⚠️ Common Mistake: Editing /etc/resolv.conf directly (gets overwritten by NetworkManager/systemd-resolved). Not knowing nsswitch.conf order.

🎓 LFCS Relevance
Networking 25%
🎯 DNS on the LFCS Exam

You'll be asked to configure DNS resolution — either by editing /etc/hosts for a quick fix, or by configuring systemd-resolved. Know the resolution order: /etc/nsswitch.conf controls whether files (hosts) or dns is checked first. The default is "files dns" — hosts file first, then DNS.

20.1 DNS Resolution Stack

How Linux Resolves a Hostname — Step by Step
  Application calls getaddrinfo("anihpj.com")
       │
       ▼
  /etc/nsswitch.conf → "hosts: files dns"
       │
       ├── ① Check /etc/hosts first (files)
       │     127.0.0.1   localhost
       │     203.0.113.10 anihpj.com   ← Match! Return this.
       │
       └── ② If not found, query DNS (dns)
              Read /etc/resolv.conf → nameserver 1.1.1.1
              Send query to 1.1.1.1 → get response → return IP
FilePurposeExample
/etc/hostsStatic name-to-IP mapping. Checked BEFORE DNS.127.0.0.1 anihpj.local
/etc/resolv.confWhich DNS servers to query. Managed by systemd-resolved on modern systems.nameserver 1.1.1.1
/etc/nsswitch.confName Service Switch — controls resolution ORDER.hosts: files dns
🔧 systemd-resolved

On modern Ubuntu, /etc/resolv.conf is a symlink to /run/systemd/resolve/stub-resolv.conf. Use resolvectl status to see current DNS configuration. To add a DNS server permanently: edit /etc/systemd/resolved.conf or use netplan's nameservers section.

20.2 Hostname Configuration

CommandWhat It Does
hostnamectlShow current hostname and system info
sudo hostnamectl set-hostname anihpj-prodSet hostname permanently (writes /etc/hostname)
hostnameShow current hostname (temporary view)
cat /etc/hostnameStatic hostname file (read at boot)

After changing hostname, add it to /etc/hosts: 127.0.1.1 anihpj-prod. This prevents sudo warnings about being unable to resolve the hostname.

20.3 Configuring a DNS Server (Bind9) — Basics

Internal DNS for anihpj.local with Bind9
  # Install: sudo apt install bind9

  # /etc/bind/named.conf.local — zone declarations:
  zone "anihpj.local" {
      type master;
      file "/etc/bind/db.anihpj.local";
  };

  # /etc/bind/db.anihpj.local — forward zone file:
  $TTL 86400
  @   IN  SOA  ns1.anihpj.local. admin.anihpj.local. (
              2026061001  ; Serial (YYYYMMDD + revision)
              3600        ; Refresh
              1800        ; Retry
              604800      ; Expire
              86400 )     ; Minimum TTL
  @       IN  NS   ns1.anihpj.local.
  ns1     IN  A    192.168.1.10
  web     IN  A    192.168.1.20
  db      IN  A    192.168.1.30
  # Now: ping web.anihpj.local → 192.168.1.20

Key Bind9 files: /etc/bind/named.conf.local (zone declarations), /etc/bind/named.conf.options (forwarders, ACLs). Forward zone = name → IP. Reverse zone = IP → name (PTR records). After editing: sudo systemctl restart bind9. Test: dig @localhost web.anihpj.local.

🔬 How DNS Caching Works — And Why It Matters

DNS caching happens at multiple levels: (1) Application: browsers cache for ~1 minute. (2) systemd-resolved: caches per the record's TTL. Clear with resolvectl flush-caches. (3) Recursive resolver: your ISP's DNS caches for TTL. (4) Authoritative: the source server sets TTL. Troubleshooting: if a DNS change "isn't working," check each cache layer. dig +trace anihpj.com shows the full resolution path from root servers down. DNSSEC adds cryptographic signatures to DNS records — prevents cache poisoning. Enable with dnssec-validation yes; in Bind9 options.

Common DNS Record Types
TypeMapsExampleUse
AName → IPv4anihpj.com. A 203.0.113.10Standard web hosting
AAAAName → IPv6anihpj.com. AAAA 2001:db8::1IPv6 web hosting
CNAMEAlias → Canonical Namewww.anihpj.com. CNAME anihpj.com.www is same server
MXDomain → Mail Serveranihpj.com. MX 10 mail.anihpj.com.Email routing
TXTArbitrary textanihpj.com. TXT "v=spf1 ..."SPF, DKIM, verification
PTRIP → Name (reverse)10.113.0.203.in-addr.arpa. PTR anihpj.com.Reverse DNS
NSDomain → Nameserveranihpj.com. NS ns1.anihpj.com.Delegation

Chapter 21: Firewall & Network Security

A server without a firewall is like a house with no doors — anyone can walk in. This chapter covers Linux firewall fundamentals: how netfilter/iptables/nftables work at the kernel level, the user-friendly ufw (Ubuntu) and firewalld (Rocky) frontends, and critical SSH hardening to protect your anihpj server from attackers.

🟡 Intermediate⏱️ ~1.5 hours🔥 Security

🎯 What You'll Learn

  • ✅ Understand how Linux firewalls work at the kernel level (netfilter)
  • ✅ Configure ufw for Ubuntu servers and firewalld for Rocky/RHEL
  • ✅ Write raw iptables rules (still tested on LFCS)
  • ✅ Harden SSH with key-only auth, non-root login, and rate limiting
🧠 Core Understanding — Chapter 21

Firewalls filter packets based on rules. UFW (Uncomplicated Firewall) is a frontend for iptables — simple syntax, persistent rules. firewalld (Rocky/RHEL) uses zones (public, internal, trusted) and services. Both ultimately write netfilter rules in the kernel. Default policy: deny incoming, allow outgoing. iptables has 3 chains: INPUT, OUTPUT, FORWARD. Rules are processed top-to-bottom — first match wins. Deep insight: a firewall doesn't make you invisible — it controls which ports respond. A closed port returns 'connection refused'; a filtered port (DROP) returns nothing (timeout).

Networking 25%

You'll be asked to configure firewall rules to allow/deny specific ports. Ubuntu uses ufw, Rocky uses firewalld. Both may appear. Also know raw iptables — it's still tested. The #1 mistake: enabling a firewall remotely without first allowing SSH (port 22). You'll lock yourself out!

21.1 How Linux Firewalls Work — iptables & nftables

Packet Flow Through iptables Chains
  INCOMING PACKET
       │
       ▼
  ┌──────────┐     ┌───────────┐     ┌───────────┐
  │ PREROUTING│────→│  FORWARD  │────→│POSTROUTING│  (routing through this host)
  │ (NAT)     │     │ (routing) │     │ (NAT)     │
  └──────────┘     └───────────┘     └───────────┘
       │                                      ↑
       │ (for local processes)                │
       ▼                                      │
  ┌──────────┐                          (outgoing packets
  │  INPUT   │                           go through OUTPUT
  │ (to us)  │                           then POSTROUTING)
  └──────────┘
       │
       ▼
  Local Process (nginx, sshd, etc.)

  iptables -L -n -v          → list all rules with packet counts
  iptables -A INPUT -p tcp --dport 22 -j ACCEPT   → allow SSH
  iptables -A INPUT -j DROP                         → default deny (LAST rule!)
🔧
1990s
ipchains

Original Linux firewall. Stateless. Replaced by iptables in kernel 2.4.

Obsolete
📜
2000s
iptables

Stateful firewall. Separate tools for IPv4, IPv6, ARP. Still widely used.

Legacy
✨
2014+
nftables

Unified framework. One tool for all protocols. Better syntax and performance.

Modern
🛡️
Always
ufw / firewalld

User-friendly frontends. ufw for Ubuntu, firewalld for Rocky. Production standard.

Recommended

21.2 ufw — Uncomplicated Firewall (Ubuntu)

Complete UFW Configuration for Anihpj Production Server
  # Reset and configure fresh
  sudo ufw reset
  sudo ufw default deny incoming
  sudo ufw default allow outgoing

  # Allow SSH (restrict to your IP in production!)
  sudo ufw allow 22/tcp

  # Allow web traffic
  sudo ufw allow 80/tcp
  sudo ufw allow 443/tcp

  # PostgreSQL: ONLY from localhost (default deny handles this)

  sudo ufw enable
  sudo ufw status verbose
CommandWhat It Does
ufw allow 22/tcpAllow SSH from anywhere
ufw allow from 10.0.0.0/8 to any port 22Allow SSH only from private network
ufw deny 5432/tcpExplicitly block PostgreSQL
ufw delete 2Delete rule #2
ufw resetClear ALL rules and disable

21.3 firewalld — Zone-Based Firewall (Rocky Linux)

ZoneDefault PolicyUse Case
publicReject incoming, allow outgoingDefault for public-facing servers
trustedAccept allInternal network, fully trusted
internalReject incoming (less strict)Internal servers with some trust
dmzReject all except selectedPublic-facing services, isolated
dropDrop all (no response)Stealth — don't even reply to scans
blockReject all (with response)Explicit rejection
CommandWhat It Does
firewall-cmd --get-active-zonesShow active zones
firewall-cmd --permanent --add-service=httpAllow HTTP permanently
firewall-cmd --permanent --add-port=8000/tcpAllow port 8000
firewall-cmd --reloadApply permanent changes
firewall-cmd --list-allShow current zone rules

21.4 NAT, Port Redirection & iptables

CommandWhat It Does
iptables -L -n -vList rules with packet/byte counts
iptables -A INPUT -p tcp --dport 22 -j ACCEPTAllow SSH (append to INPUT chain)
iptables -A INPUT -j DROPDefault deny — DROP everything else
iptables -I INPUT 1 -p tcp --dport 443 -j ACCEPTInsert HTTPS rule at position 1
iptables-save > /etc/iptables/rules.v4Save rules to survive reboot
⚠️ Modern systems prefer ufw/firewalld

iptables is still tested on the LFCS exam, but in production, use ufw (Ubuntu) or firewalld (Rocky). They're simpler, less error-prone, and integrate with systemd. iptables rules are also lost on reboot unless saved with iptables-save.

🔬 nftables — The Modern Replacement for iptables

nftables replaces iptables, ip6tables, arptables, and ebtables with ONE unified framework. Basic syntax: nft add table inet filter → nft add chain inet filter input '{ type filter hook input priority 0; }' → nft add rule inet filter input tcp dport 22 accept. nft list ruleset shows all rules. nft -f /etc/nftables.conf loads from file. Simpler syntax, better performance, IPv4+IPv6 in one table.

📜 iptables (Legacy)
# Allow SSH, HTTP, HTTPS — 6 rules for 3 services:
iptables -A INPUT -p tcp --dport 22 -j ACCEPT
ip6tables -A INPUT -p tcp --dport 22 -j ACCEPT
iptables -A INPUT -p tcp --dport 80 -j ACCEPT
ip6tables -A INPUT -p tcp --dport 80 -j ACCEPT
iptables -A INPUT -p tcp --dport 443 -j ACCEPT
ip6tables -A INPUT -p tcp --dport 443 -j ACCEPT
# Must save separately:
iptables-save > /etc/iptables/rules.v4
ip6tables-save > /etc/iptables/rules.v6
✨ nftables (Modern)
# Same rules — ONE table handles IPv4 AND IPv6:
table inet filter {
    chain input {
        type filter hook input priority 0;
        tcp dport {22, 80, 443} accept
        drop
    }
}
# Load from file:
nft -f /etc/nftables.conf
# One command, one file, both protocols.
🔀 NAT & Port Forwarding with iptables

Network Address Translation allows private IPs to access the internet through one public IP. Masquerading: iptables -t nat -A POSTROUTING -o eth0 -j MASQUERADE — all outgoing traffic appears to come from eth0's IP. Port forwarding: iptables -t nat -A PREROUTING -p tcp --dport 8080 -j DNAT --to-destination 192.168.1.100:80 — forward external port 8080 to internal server. Enable IP forwarding: echo 1 > /proc/sys/net/ipv4/ip_forward.

🚦 Rate Limiting with iptables — Prevent Brute Force Attacks
# Limit SSH connections to 5 per minute per IP:
iptables -A INPUT -p tcp --dport 22 -m state --state NEW -m recent --set
iptables -A INPUT -p tcp --dport 22 -m state --state NEW -m recent \
    --update --seconds 60 --hitcount 5 -j DROP
# After 5 new SSH connections in 60 seconds, DROP all further attempts
# This stops brute-force attacks without blocking legitimate users
🔬 Connection Tracking — How Stateful Firewalls Work

Modern firewalls are stateful — they track connections, not just individual packets. The kernel's conntrack module maintains a table of all active connections: conntrack -L lists them. conntrack -S shows statistics. Typical rule: allow ESTABLISHED and RELATED traffic back in — this automatically allows responses to outgoing connections without opening ports. iptables -A INPUT -m conntrack --ctstate ESTABLISHED,RELATED -j ACCEPT. This is the foundation of "default deny" policies that still allow internet access.

📜 TCP Wrappers — Host-Based Access Control (Legacy)

TCP Wrappers (/etc/hosts.allow and /etc/hosts.deny) provide an additional layer of access control for services compiled with libwrap. Format: sshd: 192.168.1.0/255.255.255.0 (allow SSH from local subnet). ALL: ALL in hosts.deny blocks everything not explicitly allowed. Check if a service uses wrappers: ldd /usr/sbin/sshd | grep libwrap. Note: modern systems prefer firewall rules; TCP wrappers are deprecated but still appear on the LFCS exam.

21.5 SSH Security — Hardening sshd_config

Complete Hardened sshd_config for Anihpj Production
  # /etc/ssh/sshd_config — security hardening
  PermitRootLogin no              # NEVER allow direct root login
  PasswordAuthentication no       # Force SSH key authentication only
  PubkeyAuthentication yes        # Enable public key auth
  AllowUsers anihpj owner         # Whitelist: ONLY these users can SSH
  MaxAuthTries 3                  # Limit brute-force (default is 6)
  MaxSessions 3                   # Limit concurrent sessions per user
  LoginGraceTime 30               # 30 seconds to authenticate
  ClientAliveInterval 300         # Disconnect idle clients after 5 min
  X11Forwarding no                # Disable X11 (not needed on servers)
  PermitEmptyPasswords no         # No password = no login
⚠️ Before Applying: Test Your Config!

sudo sshd -t — tests the config file syntax. Always keep one SSH session open when changing sshd_config. In a second terminal: sudo systemctl reload sshd. If the new session can connect, the config is good. If not, fix it from the still-open session.

Q8
On Rocky Linux, allow HTTPS through firewalld permanently and verify the rule is active.
Click to reveal answer
✅ Answer
sudo firewall-cmd --permanent --add-service=https
sudo firewall-cmd --reload
sudo firewall-cmd --list-services
📖 Explanation

Every running program is a process with a PID. The kernel schedules processes using the Completely Fair Scheduler (CFS). Signals (TERM, KILL, HUP) control process lifecycle — SIGTERM asks politely, SIGKILL forces termination. The flags -cmd, --permanent, --add-service control how this command behaves. Understanding what each flag does — not just memorizing the combination — lets you adapt when the exam presents a variation. Man pages are available but cost time. Know the common flags by heart; use man only for esoteric options.

Q9
What is the difference between DROP and REJECT in iptables? When would you use each?
Click to reveal answer
✅ Answer

DROP: Silently discards the packet — no response sent. The sender hangs until timeout. Use for: stealth (don't reveal the server exists). REJECT: Discards packet but sends an ICMP \"port unreachable\" response. The sender knows immediately. Use for: internal networks where you want fast failure.

Q10
You enabled ufw remotely but forgot to allow SSH. Now you're locked out. How do you recover?
Click to reveal answer
✅ Answer

If you have console access (VPS provider's web console, IPMI, physical access): log in locally and run sudo ufw disable. If no console: you're locked out — the server must be rebooted into recovery mode or the disk mounted on another system. Prevention: Always ufw allow 22/tcp BEFORE ufw enable!

📖 Explanation

Firewall rules process from top to bottom — the first match wins. Rules are evaluated in the kernel's netfilter framework for every packet. Unprotected, a Linux server on the public internet will be scanned within minutes. sudo is the key tool here. Its man page (man sudo) is available during the exam if you need to check less common options. The exam is distribution-neutral. This command works on both Ubuntu and Rocky — know which package manager to use for installation.

Chapter 22: Disks & Partitions — Dividing Your Storage

Every byte of data on your anihpj server lives on a disk — and that disk must be partitioned before it can be used. This chapter covers how Linux names storage devices, the two partition table formats (MBR vs GPT), and the tools to create and manage partitions with fdisk, gdisk, and parted.

🟡 Intermediate⏱️ ~1 hour💿 Storage

🎯 What You'll Learn

  • ✅ Understand Linux disk device naming (/dev/sda, nvme0n1, vda)
  • ✅ Compare MBR vs GPT partition tables and choose the right one
  • ✅ Create partitions with fdisk (MBR) and gdisk/parted (GPT)
🧠 Core Understanding — Chapter 22

Disks are divided into partitions defined by partition tables. MBR (legacy) supports 4 primary partitions, max 2TB. GPT (modern) supports 128 partitions, virtually unlimited size. fdisk works with MBR; gdisk with GPT; parted with both. Partitions appear as /dev/sda1, /dev/sda2. The kernel reads the partition table at boot — partprobe tells it to re-read without rebooting. Deep insight: a filesystem sits ON a partition. The partition is just a reserved range of sectors; the filesystem gives it structure.

22.1 How Linux Sees Storage Devices

Understanding lsblk Output
  $ lsblk -f
  NAME   FSTYPE  LABEL  UUID              MOUNTPOINT
  sda
  ├─sda1  vfat          AAAA-BBBB         /boot/efi
  ├─sda2  ext4          xxxx-yyyy         /boot
  └─sda3  LVM2_member   zzzz-aaaa
    ├─ubuntu--vg-root   ext4    /
    └─ubuntu--vg-swap   swap    [SWAP]
  sdb
  └─sdb1  (empty — new disk for anihpj data)
Device NameWhat It IsCommon In
/dev/sda, /dev/sdbSATA/SCSI/SAS disksPhysical servers, VMs
/dev/nvme0n1NVMe SSDModern servers, cloud
/dev/vdaVirtual diskKVM/QEMU VMs
/dev/sda1Partition 1 on sdaAll systems

lsblk = tree view of all block devices. lsblk -f adds filesystem and UUID. blkid shows UUIDs and filesystem types for all devices.

🔬 udev — Why /dev/sda Can Become /dev/sdb After Reboot

The Linux kernel does NOT guarantee persistent device names. /dev/sda and /dev/sdb are assigned in the ORDER the kernel discovers them — which depends on timing, controller scan order, and which disk spins up first. After adding a new disk, /dev/sdb might become /dev/sdc and your new disk becomes /dev/sdb. This is why /etc/fstab uses UUIDs, not device names. Persistent alternative paths (udev-created symlinks): /dev/disk/by-uuid/ — filesystem UUID (what fstab uses), /dev/disk/by-id/ — manufacturer+serial (e.g., ata-Samsung_SSD_860_SERIAL), /dev/disk/by-path/ — PCI/physical port location, /dev/disk/by-label/ — human-readable label (if set with mkfs -L). Best practice: Always use /dev/disk/by-id/ in scripts that must address a specific physical disk — it survives reboots and device reordering.

22.2 Partition Tables — MBR vs GPT

FeatureMBR (Legacy)GPT (Modern)
Max partitions4 primary (or 3 + extended)128 (practically unlimited)
Max disk size2 TB9.4 ZB (zettabytes)
Boot modeBIOS / LegacyUEFI (required for UEFI boot)
RedundancySingle copy of tableBackup copy at end of disk
When to useOld systems, small disksALWAYS for new installations

22.3 fdisk & gdisk — Partitioning Tools

CommandWhat It DoesNotes
fdisk -lList all disks and partitionsRead-only, safe
fdisk /dev/sdbOpen disk for MBR partitioningInteractive: n=new, d=delete, w=write, q=quit
gdisk /dev/sdbOpen disk for GPT partitioningSame commands as fdisk
parted /dev/sdb printList partitions (both MBR/GPT)Non-interactive mode
parted /dev/sdb mklabel gptCreate GPT partition tableDestroys all existing data!
🚀 Walkthrough: Adding a New Data Disk for Anihpj
  # SCENARIO: Cloud provider just attached a new 200GB volume to your VM.
  # Goal: Create a single GPT partition spanning the entire disk for anihpj data.

  # Step 1: Find the new disk
  $ lsblk
  NAME   MAJ:MIN RM   SIZE RO TYPE MOUNTPOINT
  sda      8:0    0    50G  0 disk
  ├─sda1   8:1    0   512M  0 part /boot/efi
  ├─sda2   8:2    0     2G  0 part /boot
  └─sda3   8:3    0  47.5G  0 part
  sdb      8:16   0   200G  0 disk          ← NEW DISK! No partitions yet.

  # Step 2: Create GPT partition table
  $ sudo parted /dev/sdb mklabel gpt
  $ sudo parted /dev/sdb print
  Partition Table: gpt                           ← GPT is now active

  # Step 3: Create a single partition using the ENTIRE disk
  $ sudo parted /dev/sdb mkpart primary ext4 0% 100%
  $ sudo parted /dev/sdb print
  Number  Start   End     Size    File system  Name     Flags
   1      1049kB  200GB   200GB                primary

  # Step 4: Tell kernel to re-read the partition table
  $ sudo partprobe /dev/sdb
  $ lsblk /dev/sdb
  NAME   MAJ:MIN RM   SIZE RO TYPE MOUNTPOINT
  sdb      8:16   0   200G  0 disk
  └─sdb1   8:17   0   200G  0 part             ← PARTITION READY!

  # Step 5: Now ready for mkfs (Chapter 23) or pvcreate (Chapter 24)

22.4 parted — Advanced Partitioning

CommandWhat It Does
parted /dev/sdb mkpart primary ext4 0% 50%Create partition using first 50% of disk
parted /dev/sdb mkpart primary ext4 50% 100%Create partition using remaining 50%
parted /dev/sdb rm 1Delete partition number 1
parted /dev/sdb resizepart 1 100%Grow partition 1 to fill disk
⚠️ ALWAYS verify the target disk before partitioning!

lsblk before any fdisk/parted command. Writing a partition table destroys existing data. A single typo (/dev/sda instead of /dev/sdb) can wipe your OS. On production servers, take a backup before partitioning.

🔬 Disk I/O Schedulers — Optimizing for Your Workload

The I/O scheduler decides the ORDER in which disk read/write requests are processed. View current: cat /sys/block/sda/queue/scheduler. Common options: mq-deadline (default, good for SSDs — low latency), kyber (modern, latency-targeted), bfq (fairness, good for HDDs). Change: echo kyber > /sys/block/sda/queue/scheduler. For anihpj: use mq-deadline for the PostgreSQL SSD, bfq for the backup HDD.

🩺 SMART — Monitor Disk Health Before It Fails

SMART (Self-Monitoring, Analysis and Reporting Technology) predicts disk failures. smartctl -a /dev/sda shows: temperature, power-on hours, reallocated sectors, pending sectors. Key fields: Reallocated_Sector_Ct > 0 → disk is failing. smartctl -t short /dev/sda runs a quick self-test. smartctl -l selftest /dev/sda shows results. Production tip: configure smartd to email alerts on disk health changes.

Q3
What's the maximum disk size MBR supports? Why is this a problem today?
Click to reveal answer
✅ Answer

MBR supports a maximum of 2 TB because it uses 32-bit sector addressing (2^32 × 512 bytes = 2TB). Any disk larger than 2TB MUST use GPT. This is a problem because modern drives (4TB, 8TB, 16TB+) are common.

Q7
What's the difference between a primary, extended, and logical partition in MBR?
Click to reveal answer
✅ Answer

MBR allows 4 primary partitions. If you need more than 4, one primary becomes an extended partition (a container), which holds multiple logical partitions. Only primary and logical partitions can hold filesystems. GPT eliminates this complexity with 128 equal partitions.

Chapter 23: Filesystems — Formatting and Mounting Storage

A partition is just raw space until you put a filesystem on it. This chapter covers Linux filesystem types (ext4, xfs, btrfs), how to format partitions with mkfs, mount them with mount, make mounts permanent with /etc/fstab, and check/repair filesystems with fsck.

🟡 Intermediate⏱️ ~1.5 hours📁 Storage

🎯 What You'll Learn

  • ✅ Compare ext4, xfs, and btrfs — when to use each
  • ✅ Format partitions with mkfs.ext4 and mkfs.xfs
  • ✅ Mount and unmount filesystems with mount/umount
  • ✅ Configure persistent mounts in /etc/fstab
  • ✅ Check and repair filesystems with fsck and xfs_repair
🧠 Core Understanding — Chapter 23

Filesystems organize data on partitions. ext4 uses inodes, block groups, and journals for crash recovery. XFS excels at large files and parallel I/O. The journal writes intent before data — if power fails, the journal replays and the filesystem stays consistent. Mounting attaches a filesystem to the directory tree — the VFS layer abstracts away the underlying FS type. /etc/fstab defines persistent mounts with 6 fields. noatime disables access time updates — significant performance boost for read-heavy workloads.

FilesystemBest ForMax SizeKey Feature

23.2 mkfs — Formatting Partitions

CommandWhat It Does
mkfs.ext4 /dev/sdb1Format partition as ext4
mkfs.xfs /dev/sdb1Format partition as xfs
mkfs.ext4 -L "anihpj-data" /dev/sdb1Format with label (human-readable name)
tune2fs -l /dev/sda1View ext4 filesystem info (creation date, mount count, features)
xfs_info /dev/sdb1View xfs filesystem info
Reading Filesystem Metadata: tune2fs -l & xfs_info Output
  $ sudo tune2fs -l /dev/sda2 | head -20
  Filesystem volume name:   
  Last mounted on:          /boot
  Filesystem UUID:          a1b2c3d4-5678-90ab-cdef-1234567890ab
  Filesystem magic number:  0xEF53
  Filesystem revision #:    1 (dynamic)
  Filesystem features:      has_journal ext_attr resize_inode dir_index
  Filesystem state:         clean
  Errors behavior:          Continue
  Filesystem OS type:       Linux
  Inode count:              131072
  Block count:              524288
  Last mount time:          Mon Jun  9 08:15:22 2026
  Last write time:          Mon Jun  9 08:15:22 2026
  Mount count:              42               ← mounted 42 times since last fsck
  Maximum mount count:      -1               ← fsck disabled (modern default)

  $ sudo xfs_info /dev/vg-data/media
  meta-data=/dev/vg-data/media  isize=512    agcount=4, agsize=6553600 blks
  data     =                     bsize=4096   blocks=26214400
  naming   =version 2            bsize=4096   ascii-ci=0, ftype=1
  log      =internal             bsize=4096   blocks=12800, version=2
  realtime =none                 extsz=4096   blocks=0, rtextents=0

  KEY INSIGHTS:
  - tune2fs shows mount count, last check, features like has_journal
  - xfs_info shows AG (Allocation Groups) — xfs splits disk into
    independent regions for parallel I/O. More AGs = more parallelism.
  - "Filesystem state: clean" = no fsck needed on next boot
🔬 /proc and /sys — The Kernel's Windows into Your System

Not all "filesystems" are on disk. /proc is a virtual filesystem (procfs) exposing kernel and process information as files. Every process has a directory: /proc/[PID]/ — check /proc/1/cmdline (how init was started), /proc/cpuinfo (CPU details), /proc/meminfo (detailed RAM breakdown), /proc/mounts (currently mounted filesystems — more accurate than /etc/mtab). /sys (sysfs) exposes kernel objects, drivers, and hardware: /sys/block/sda/ (disk properties), /sys/class/net/eth0/ (network interface), /sys/kernel/ (kernel parameters). Key difference: /proc is mostly read-only process/kernel info. /sys is more hardware/driver focused and some entries are writable (e.g., echo 1 > /sys/block/sda/device/rescan). Both are created in RAM at boot — they don't exist on any physical disk.

⚠️ mkfs DESTROYS all data on the partition!

Double-check the device name before running mkfs. Use lsblk to verify. There is NO undo. On production: blkid first to confirm the partition is empty/expected.

🔬 How Journaling Works — Why ext4/xfs Survive Power Failures

A journaling filesystem writes changes to a journal (circular log) BEFORE writing to the main filesystem. Sequence: (1) Write intended change to journal, (2) Write to main FS, (3) Mark journal entry complete. If power fails after step 1, on boot the journal is replayed — unfinished changes are completed. If power fails before step 1, nothing is lost. This is why journaling filesystems don't need fsck after a crash. ext4 journal modes: data=ordered (default, metadata journaled, data ordered), data=journal (all data journaled, slowest, safest), data=writeback (metadata only, fastest, riskiest).

🔬 Inodes — The Filesystem's Index Cards

Every file and directory has an inode — a data structure storing: permissions, owner, size, timestamps, and pointers to data blocks. NOT the filename (that's in the directory). df -i shows inode usage. Running out of inodes means "no space left" even if df -h shows free space — you can't create new files. Common cause: millions of tiny files (cache, emails, temp). Fix: delete old files, or recreate FS with more inodes: mkfs.ext4 -N 10000000 /dev/sdb1.

23.3 mount and umount — Using Filesystems

CommandWhat It Does
mount /dev/sdb1 /mnt/dataTemporary mount (lost on reboot)
mount -t ext4 /dev/sdb1 /mntSpecify filesystem type explicitly
mount -o ro /dev/sdb1 /mntRead-only mount (safe for inspection)
umount /mnt/dataUnmount (must not be in use)
umount -l /mnt/dataLazy unmount — detach now, cleanup later
df -hTShow all mounted filesystems with type and usage
findmnt /mnt/dataDetailed mount info for specific directory
🔧 Scenario: Mount the Anihpj PostgreSQL Data Disk
  # SCENARIO: Your anihpj server just got a freshly formatted 100GB xfs disk
  # for PostgreSQL data at /dev/sdb1. Mount it and make it database-ready.

  # Step 1: Create mount point
  $ sudo mkdir -p /var/lib/postgresql

  # Step 2: Get the UUID (for permanent fstab entry)
  $ sudo blkid /dev/sdb1
  /dev/sdb1: UUID="b8f3c9d1-4567-89ab-cdef-0123456789ab" TYPE="xfs"

  # Step 3: Temporary mount (test it works)
  $ sudo mount /dev/sdb1 /var/lib/postgresql
  $ df -hT /var/lib/postgresql
  Filesystem     Type  Size  Used Avail Use% Mounted on
  /dev/sdb1      xfs   100G   33M  100G   1% /var/lib/postgresql

  # Step 4: Set ownership for PostgreSQL
  $ sudo chown postgres:postgres /var/lib/postgresql
  $ sudo chmod 700 /var/lib/postgresql

  # Step 5: Make permanent — add to /etc/fstab
  $ echo "UUID=b8f3c9d1-4567-89ab-cdef-0123456789ab /var/lib/postgresql xfs defaults,nofail 0 2" | sudo tee -a /etc/fstab

  # Step 6: Test fstab before rebooting
  $ sudo mount -a          # Remounts everything from fstab — if silent, it's correct!

  # Step 7: Verify after reboot simulation
  $ findmnt /var/lib/postgresql
  TARGET               SOURCE    FSTYPE OPTIONS
  /var/lib/postgresql  /dev/sdb1 xfs    rw,relatime,attr2,inode64,noquota

23.4 /etc/fstab — Persistent Mounts

Annotated /etc/fstab for Anihpj Server
  #                        
  UUID=xxxx-yyyy        /             ext4    errors=remount-ro  0     1
  UUID=aaaa-bbbb        /boot         ext4    defaults           0     2
  UUID=cccc-dddd        /boot/efi     vfat    umask=0077         0     1

  # anihpj PostgreSQL data disk
  UUID=1234-5678  /var/lib/postgresql  ext4   defaults,nofail   0     2

  # anihpj media uploads (LVM, growable)
  UUID=8765-4321  /var/www/anihpj/media  ext4  defaults,nofail  0     2

  FIELD EXPLANATION:
  ① device: UUID (preferred) or /dev/sdb1 or LABEL=mylabel
  ② mountpoint: where to attach in the filesystem tree
  ③ type: ext4, xfs, vfat, swap, nfs, etc.
  ④ options: defaults (rw,suid,dev,exec,auto,nouser,async)
     nofail = don't halt boot if this drive is missing
  ⑤ dump: 0=don't dump, 1=dump (for backup utility)
  ⑥ pass: fsck order — 0=skip, 1=root first, 2=others
🔬 Mount Options Deep-Dive — Performance and Security

Mount options control HOW a filesystem behaves. Key options beyond defaults (which = rw,suid,dev,exec,auto,nouser,async): Performance: noatime (don't update access time — huge I/O savings, especially for databases and web servers. relatime is the modern default — updates atime only if older than mtime). data=ordered (ext4 default — journal metadata, data written first). Security: nosuid (ignore setuid bits — critical for /tmp and web-accessible mounts). noexec (prevent binary execution — use on /tmp and upload directories). nodev (ignore device files — prevents creating /dev/sda inside a mount). Anihpj example: /var/www/anihpj/media should be mounted with defaults,nosuid,noexec,nodev to prevent uploaded files from being executed or creating device nodes. /tmp should have: defaults,nosuid,noexec,nodev,noatime.

🔧 Before Rebooting: Always test fstab!

sudo mount -a mounts all entries in /etc/fstab. If it succeeds silently, your fstab is correct. If it errors, fix before rebooting — a broken fstab can prevent the system from booting!

23.5 Checking and Repairing Filesystems

CommandWhat It DoesWhen to Use
fsck /dev/sdb1Check and repair filesystemSystem won't mount; after power failure
fsck -f /dev/sdb1Force check even if marked cleanSuspected corruption but fsck skips
e2fsck -p /dev/sda1Auto-repair ext4 (no prompts)Quick fix for known ext4 issues
xfs_repair /dev/sdb1Repair xfs filesystemXFS corruption (must be unmounted!)
xfs_check /dev/sdb1Check xfs without repairDiagnostic before attempting repair
⚠️ ALWAYS unmount before running fsck!

Running fsck on a mounted filesystem can cause severe corruption. Boot into recovery mode or use a live USB if you need to check the root filesystem. umount /mnt/data first, then fsck /dev/sdb1.

23.6 Virtual Filesystems — /proc & /sys Deep-Dive 🎯

🧠 Why Virtual Filesystems Matter for LFCS

The official LFCS domain explicitly tests "Manage and configure the virtual file system." This means /proc and /sys — pseudo-filesystems that don't store data on disk but instead expose kernel data structures as files. /proc exposes process and kernel information. /sys exposes device and driver information. Together they let you read and sometimes WRITE kernel settings — no special tools needed, just cat and echo. Understanding these virtual filesystems is what separates script-kiddies from real sysadmins: when top or lsblk isn't available, you can still get everything you need from /proc and /sys.

/proc vs /sys — Two Virtual Filesystems, Two Purposes
  ╔══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════╗
  ║                         /proc (procfs)                          ║
  ║  PURPOSE: Process and kernel runtime information                ║
  ║  MOUNTED: proc on /proc type proc (rw,nosuid,nodev,noexec)     ║
  ║  KEY DIRS: /proc/PID/ — per-process info                       ║
  ║            /proc/sys/ — kernel parameters (sysctl interface)    ║
  ║            /proc/cpuinfo, /proc/meminfo, /proc/mounts           ║
  ║  CAN WRITE? YES — /proc/sys/ entries are writable (tunables)   ║
  ╚══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════╝

  ╔══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════╗
  ║                         /sys (sysfs)                            ║
  ║  PURPOSE: Device, driver, and kernel subsystem information      ║
  ║  MOUNTED: sysfs on /sys type sysfs (rw,nosuid,nodev,noexec)    ║
  ║  KEY DIRS: /sys/class/ — devices grouped by type               ║
  ║            /sys/block/ — block devices (disks)                  ║
  ║            /sys/devices/ — physical device tree                 ║
  ║            /sys/kernel/ — kernel tuning (newer than /proc/sys)  ║
  ║  CAN WRITE? YES — device power states, driver parameters       ║
  ╚══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════╝
Virtual FileWhat It ShowsPractical UseAnihpj Example
/proc/cpuinfoCPU model, cores, flags, MHzVerify hardware before installinggrep -c processor /proc/cpuinfo → number of CPU cores
/proc/meminfoTotal RAM, free, buffers, swapMemory sizing for DB, web servergrep MemTotal /proc/meminfo → plan PostgreSQL shared_buffers
/proc/mountsAll currently mounted filesystemsCheck if mount succeededgrep /var/www /proc/mounts → verify anihpj data mount
/proc/partitionsAll block devices with major/minorSee what disks kernel detectsCheck if new disk is visible before partitioning
/proc/filesystemsFilesystems the kernel supportsSee if xfs/btrfs is compiled inVerify kernel supports your chosen FS
/proc/sys/vm/swappinessSwap tendency (0-100)Read/Write kernel tunableecho 10 > /proc/sys/vm/swappiness — tune for DB server
/proc/sys/net/ipv4/ip_forwardIP forwarding (0=off, 1=on)Enable routing/NATEnable for container networking
/sys/class/net/eth0/speedLink speed (1000=1Gbps)Verify NIC speed negotiatedCheck if server is on 1Gbps or 100Mbps
/sys/block/sda/queue/schedulerI/O scheduler (mq-deadline, none)Tune for SSD vs HDDecho none > /sys/block/sda/queue/scheduler for NVMe SSD
/sys/block/sda/sizeDisk size in 512-byte sectorsVerify disk size detectedMultiply by 512 to get bytes
✅ /proc — Process Internals Exposed
# Every PID has a directory in /proc:
ls /proc/$$/    # $$ = current shell's PID

# Key per-process files:
/proc/PID/cmdline    # Exact command that started it
/proc/PID/environ    # Environment variables (null-separated)
/proc/PID/cwd        # Symlink to current working dir
/proc/PID/fd/        # All open file descriptors
/proc/PID/maps        # Memory map (loaded libraries)
/proc/PID/limits      # Resource limits (ulimit values)
/proc/PID/status      # Human-readable process state

# Find what file a process has open:
ls -la /proc/$(pgrep nginx | head -1)/fd/
# 0 -> /dev/null, 3 -> /var/log/nginx/access.log

# Recover a deleted but still-open file:
cp /proc/PID/fd/3 /tmp/recovered.log
✅ /sys — Devices & Drivers Exposed
# Network interface info:
cat /sys/class/net/eth0/address    # MAC address
cat /sys/class/net/eth0/mtu        # MTU size
cat /sys/class/net/eth0/operstate  # up or down

# Disk/block device info:
ls /sys/block/                     # All block devices
cat /sys/block/sda/removable       # 0=fixed, 1=removable
cat /sys/block/sda/queue/rotational  # 0=SSD, 1=HDD

# Power management:
cat /sys/power/state               # Supported sleep states

# Kernel parameters (sysctl alternative):
cat /proc/sys/net/ipv4/ip_forward
# Writing to /proc/sys is equivalent to sysctl -w:
echo 1 > /proc/sys/net/ipv4/ip_forward
# Same as: sysctl -w net.ipv4.ip_forward=1
💡 The LFCS Virtual FS Trick — When Tools Fail, Go to /proc

On the LFCS exam, you might find yourself in a minimal recovery environment where top, free, lscpu aren't available. Everything you need is in /proc: cat /proc/cpuinfo (CPU), cat /proc/meminfo (RAM), cat /proc/partitions (disks), cat /proc/mounts (what's mounted). This knowledge can save you when standard tools are missing. Exam scenario: You boot into emergency mode and need to fix /etc/fstab. mount doesn't work? cat /proc/mounts shows what's actually mounted. lsblk missing? cat /proc/partitions shows all disks.

⚠️ Writing to /proc and /sys — Immediate, But NOT Persistent

Changes made by writing to /proc/sys/ or /sys/ take effect IMMEDIATELY but are lost on reboot. For persistence: /proc/sys/ values → add to /etc/sysctl.conf or /etc/sysctl.d/*.conf. /sys/ values → add to /etc/rc.local, a systemd service, or udev rules. LFCS exam tip: If the task says "set kernel parameter X" without mentioning persistence, sysctl -w or echo > /proc/sys/ is fine. If it says "persistently" or "permanent," you MUST add it to /etc/sysctl.conf or /etc/sysctl.d/.

Q5
What is the difference between ext4 and xfs? When would you choose xfs for anihpj?
Click to reveal answer
✅ Answer

ext4 is the general-purpose Linux filesystem — stable, well-tested, good for OS and small-to-medium files. xfs is optimized for large files and high concurrency — better for databases, large media files, and backup storage. For anihpj: use xfs for /var/lib/postgresql (database) and /backups (large sequential writes). Use ext4 for general directories.

📖 Explanation

Every running program is a process with a PID. The kernel schedules processes using the Completely Fair Scheduler (CFS). Signals (TERM, KILL, HUP) control process lifecycle — SIGTERM asks politely, SIGKILL forces termination. /var/lib/postgresql is the key tool here. Its man page (man /var/lib/postgresql) is available during the exam if you need to check less common options. Flag hard tasks and return later. Spending 15 minutes on one task guarantees you'll run out of time for 3-4 easier ones.

What does the "pass" field in /etc/fstab control? What values are valid?
Click to reveal answer
✅ Answer

The 6th field controls fsck order at boot. Values: 0 = don't check. 1 = check first (root filesystem only!). 2 = check after root (all other filesystems). Multiple filesystems can have pass=2 — they're checked in parallel.

Chapter 24: LVM — Logical Volume Management

LVM is the storage administrator's superpower. It abstracts physical disks into flexible pools of storage that can be resized, combined, and snapshotted — all without unmounting or reformatting. This chapter covers the complete LVM workflow: creating Physical Volumes, pooling them into Volume Groups, carving out Logical Volumes, and extending them live when your anihpj uploads directory runs out of space.

🟡 Intermediate⏱️ ~1.5 hours🗄️ Storage

🎯 What You'll Learn

  • ✅ Understand the LVM layer cake: PV → VG → LV → Filesystem → Mount
  • ✅ Create complete LVM storage from scratch
  • ✅ Extend logical volumes online without downtime
  • ✅ Create and use LVM snapshots for safe migrations
🧠 Core Understanding — Chapter 24

LVM adds a layer of abstraction between physical disks and filesystems. Three layers: PV (physical volume — the actual disk), VG (volume group — pool of PVs), LV (logical volume — what you format and mount). The magic: you can add PVs to a VG while the system is running, then extend LVs and resize filesystems ONLINE. No unmounting, no downtime. Snapshots create point-in-time copies using copy-on-write — minimal space, instant creation. Deep insight: LVM turns storage from rigid physical constraints into flexible logical pools.

🧠 Core Understanding — Chapter 24

LVM adds a layer of abstraction between physical disks and filesystems. Three layers: PV (physical volume — the actual disk), VG (volume group — pool of PVs), LV (logical volume — what you format and mount). The magic: you can add PVs to a VG while the system is running, then extend LVs and resize filesystems ONLINE. No unmounting, no downtime. Snapshots create point-in-time copies using copy-on-write — minimal space, instant creation. Deep insight: LVM turns storage from rigid physical constraints into flexible logical pools.

🎯 LFCS Exam Preparation — Chapter 24 Quick Reference

⌨️ Key Commands: pvcreate, vgcreate, lvcreate -L SIZE -n name vg, lvextend -L +SIZE /dev/vg/lv, resize2fs, xfs_growfs, pvs, vgs, lvs

📋 Exam Focus: LVM provides flexible storage. LFCS tests creating PVs, VGs, and LVs, then extending them online. Master the PV→VG→LV hierarchy.

⚠️ Common Mistake: Extending LV but forgetting to resize the filesystem (resize2fs for ext4, xfs_growfs for XFS). Running out of space in VG.

🎓 LFCS Relevance
Storage Management 20%
🎯 LVM on the LFCS Exam

LVM is heavily tested. You'll be given raw disks and asked to create a complete LVM setup: PV → VG → LV → format → mount → fstab. Know the difference between extending the LV (lvextend) and growing the filesystem (resize2fs for ext4, xfs_growfs for xfs). They are TWO separate steps!

24.1 Why LVM? — The Flexibility Problem

The LVM Layer Cake — PV → VG → LV
  LOGICAL VOLUMES (what you actually use — /dev/vgname/lvname)
  ┌───────────────────┐  ┌────────────────┐  ┌───────────────┐
  │  lv-root (50GB)   │  │  lv-data (20GB)│  │  lv-var (10GB)│
  └───────────────────┘  └────────────────┘  └───────────────┘
                         │
  VOLUME GROUP (the pool — ubuntu-vg)
  ┌────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │  Total: 80GB = /dev/sda3 (50GB) + /dev/sdb1 (30GB)    │
  └────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
                         │
  PHYSICAL VOLUMES (raw storage — pvcreate'd)
  ┌─────────────────────┐      ┌─────────────────────────┐
  │  /dev/sda3 (50GB)   │      │  /dev/sdb1 (30GB)       │
  └─────────────────────┘      └─────────────────────────┘
❌ Without LVM

Fixed partitions. Resizing requires: unmount → backup → delete partition → create larger → restore. DOWNTIME. Risk of data loss.

✅ With LVM

Flexible volumes. Resizing: add disk to VG → lvextend → resize2fs. ONLINE. No downtime. Minutes, not hours.

24.2 Creating LVM from Scratch

StepCommandWhat It Does
1. Initializepvcreate /dev/sdb1Mark partition as LVM Physical Volume
2. Create Poolvgcreate anihpj-vg /dev/sdb1Create Volume Group (storage pool)
3. Create Volumelvcreate -L 100G -n data anihpj-vgCreate 100GB Logical Volume named "data"
4. Formatmkfs.ext4 /dev/anihpj-vg/dataFormat the new LV
5. Mountmount /dev/anihpj-vg/data /dataMake it usable
6. Make PermanentAdd to /etc/fstabMount automatically at boot
🔧 Useful LVM Inspection Commands

pvs / pvdisplay — list Physical Volumes. vgs / vgdisplay — list Volume Groups. lvs / lvdisplay — list Logical Volumes. The short forms (pvs, vgs, lvs) are scriptable; the long forms show detailed info.

24.3 Extending and Resizing LVM Volumes

Scenario: Anihpj Uploads Disk at 90% — Extend Without Downtime
  # 1. Add new physical disk and create a partition
  sudo parted /dev/sdc mklabel gpt
  sudo parted /dev/sdc mkpart primary 0% 100%

  # 2. Initialize as PV and add to the volume group
  sudo pvcreate /dev/sdc1
  sudo vgextend anihpj-vg /dev/sdc1

  # 3. Extend the logical volume by 200GB
  sudo lvextend -L +200G /dev/anihpj-vg/data

  # 4. Grow the filesystem (depends on type):
  sudo resize2fs /dev/anihpj-vg/data        # ext4 — unmounted or mounted
  # OR:
  sudo xfs_growfs /var/www/anihpj/media     # xfs — MUST be mounted!

  RESULT: /media grew from 90% full to 30% full — zero downtime!

24.4 LVM Snapshots — Point-in-Time Copies

CommandWhat It Does
lvcreate -L 2G -s -n data-snap /dev/anihpj-vg/dataCreate a 2GB snapshot of the data LV
mount /dev/anihpj-vg/data-snap /mnt/snapshotMount the snapshot (read-only preferred)
lvremove /dev/anihpj-vg/data-snapDelete the snapshot when done
🔬 LVM Striping & Mirroring — Performance and Redundancy

Beyond basic linear LVs, LVM supports RAID-like configurations. Striping (RAID 0 — performance): lvcreate --type striped -i 2 -L 50G -n data-fast anihpj-vg /dev/sdb1 /dev/sdc1 — stripes data across 2 PVs. Reads and writes are parallelized → near-double throughput. Best for: temporary/scratch data where speed matters more than safety. ⚠️ If ANY PV fails, ALL data is lost (no redundancy). Mirroring (RAID 1 — redundancy): lvcreate --type raid1 -m1 -L 50G -n data-safe anihpj-vg /dev/sdb1 /dev/sdc1 — mirrors data to 2 PVs. ⚠️ Uses more space (50GB LV needs 100GB raw). Can survive a single disk failure. Verify with lvs -a -o name,attr,size — mirrored LVs show 'r' attribute. Striping + Mirroring (RAID 10): lvcreate --type raid10 -i 2 -m1 -L 50G -n data-best anihpj-vg /dev/sd{b,c,d,e}1 — both fast AND redundant, needs 4+ PVs. Anihpj: Use linear LVs (default) for most data. Use RAID1 for critical DB volumes if you have spare disks. Use striped for /tmp (speed, data is disposable).

🔧 Use Case: Safe Django Database Migrations

Before running python manage.py migrate: create an LVM snapshot of the PostgreSQL data LV. If the migration corrupts data, unmount the production LV and copy from the snapshot. Once verified: lvremove the snapshot. The snapshot only needs enough space to hold CHANGES during its lifetime — not a full copy of the original.

🔬 Thin Provisioning — Overcommit Storage, Allocate on Demand

Thin pools let you create LVs larger than the physical storage you have — storage is allocated as data is written, not upfront. Create: lvcreate --type thin-pool -L 100G vg-data/thinpool, then lvcreate --type thin -V 500G --thinpool vg-data/thinpool -n thin-lv. The LV shows 500GB but only uses what's written. Monitor: lvs -a shows Data% and Meta%. ⚠️ If the thin pool fills up, ALL thin LVs in it become read-only. Always monitor and extend before 80%.

⚡ LVM Cache — SSD-Accelerated HDD Storage

Combine an SSD (fast) with an HDD (large) using LVM cache: frequently accessed data lives on SSD, bulk data on HDD. lvcreate --type cache --cachemode writethrough -L 50G -n cache-lv vg-data/data /dev/nvme0n1p1. This gives near-SSD performance for your HDD-hosted LVs. Perfect for: PostgreSQL data on large HDD with NVMe cache, or media storage with hot-files accelerated.

📊 Chapter 24 Visual Summary

🧱
PV → VG → LVpvcreate→vgcreate→lvcreate. Physical→Pool→Logical. Abstract hardware from usage.
📈
Extend Onlinevgextend→lvextend→resize2fs/xfs_growfs. Grow storage without unmounting.
📸
SnapshotsPoint-in-time copy. Safe migrations. Delete with lvremove when done.

What's the difference between lvextend and resize2fs? Why are both needed?
Click to reveal answer
✅ Answer

lvextend grows the block device (the LV) — it makes the container bigger. resize2fs grows the filesystem INSIDE the container to fill the new space. Both are needed because the container and its contents are separate layers. For xfs: xfs_growfs replaces resize2fs and requires the filesystem be mounted.

Q6
You need to reduce an ext4 LV from 100GB to 50GB. What are the steps and why is this risky?
Click to reveal answer
✅ Answer
# 1. UNMOUNT first (required for shrink)
sudo umount /data
# 2. Check filesystem
sudo e2fsck -f /dev/vg-data/media
# 3. Shrink filesystem FIRST (before LV!)
sudo resize2fs /dev/vg-data/media 50G
# 4. Then shrink the LV
sudo lvreduce -L 50G /dev/vg-data/media
# 5. Remount
sudo mount /data

Risky: If you shrink the LV BEFORE the filesystem, you truncate data. ALWAYS shrink filesystem first. Backup before any shrink operation. xfs CANNOT be shrunk — only ext4 supports online/offline shrinking.

📖 Explanation

Mounting attaches a filesystem to the directory tree. /etc/fstab defines persistent mounts read at boot. A single typo in fstab can drop the system into emergency mode — always test with mount -a. sudo is the key tool here. Its man page (man sudo) is available during the exam if you need to check less common options. Verify with df -h or mount | grep mountpoint. For fstab changes, run mount -a to test without rebooting. Reboot once before submitting (last 5 minutes). This catches non-persistent configs and broken fstab entries before the grader sees them.

Q8
What happens when an LVM snapshot runs out of space? How do you prevent this?
Click to reveal answer
✅ Answer

When a snapshot fills up, it becomes invalid (I/O errors on access) — the snapshot is automatically disabled. Prevention: (1) Allocate enough space for expected changes during the snapshot lifetime. (2) Monitor with lvs — the Data% column shows snapshot usage. (3) Auto-extend with /etc/lvm/lvm.conf: snapshot_autoextend_threshold = 70 and snapshot_autoextend_percent = 20.

📖 Explanation

Every running program is a process with a PID. The kernel schedules processes using the Completely Fair Scheduler (CFS). Signals (TERM, KILL, HUP) control process lifecycle — SIGTERM asks politely, SIGKILL forces termination. lvs is the key tool here. Its man page (man lvs) is available during the exam if you need to check less common options. If a task says "make persistent" or "survive reboot," you MUST write to a file in /etc/. This is the #1 reason candidates lose points.

Chapter 25: Swap, NFS & Remote Storage

Not all storage is local. This chapter covers swap space (virtual memory on disk), NFS (network file sharing between Linux servers), and iSCSI (remote block storage). You'll learn when to use each, how to configure them, and how they fit into the anihpj storage strategy — including the critical 3-2-1 backup rule.

🟡 Intermediate⏱️ ~1 hour💾 Storage

🎯 What You'll Learn

  • ✅ Create and manage swap space (partitions and files)
  • ✅ Set up NFS server and client for shared file access
  • ✅ Understand iSCSI for remote block storage
  • ✅ Apply the 3-2-1 backup strategy to anihpj
🧠 Core Understanding — Chapter 25

Swap extends RAM by using disk space. When RAM is full, the kernel moves inactive pages to swap — this is paging. Linux can use swap partitions or swap files. swappiness (0-100) controls how aggressively the kernel swaps. NFS is a distributed filesystem — a server exports directories, clients mount them. NFSv4 uses TCP and supports Kerberos authentication. Deep insight: swap is NOT 'extra RAM' — it's an emergency buffer. Excessive swapping (thrashing) makes the system unusably slow. Monitor with vmstat.

🧠 Core Understanding — Chapter 25

Swap extends RAM by using disk space. When RAM is full, the kernel moves inactive pages to swap — this is paging. Linux can use swap partitions or swap files. swappiness (0-100) controls how aggressively the kernel swaps. NFS is a distributed filesystem — a server exports directories, clients mount them. NFSv4 uses TCP and supports Kerberos authentication. Deep insight: swap is NOT 'extra RAM' — it's an emergency buffer. Excessive swapping (thrashing) makes the system unusably slow. Monitor with vmstat.

⚠️ Common Mistake: Forgetting _netdev option for NFS in fstab (mount fails at boot if network isn't ready). Not setting proper NFS export permissions.

You may be asked to create and enable swap, or configure an NFS client mount. Know both swap partition (mkswap) and swap file (dd + mkswap) approaches. For NFS: know the /etc/exports format, exportfs -a, and the client mount syntax.

25.1 SWAP — Virtual Memory Extension

MethodCommandBest For
Swap Partitionmkswap /dev/sdb2 && swapon /dev/sdb2Dedicated disk, predictable size
Swap Filedd if=/dev/zero of=/swapfile bs=1G count=8 && chmod 600 /swapfile && mkswap /swapfile && swapon /swapfileCloud VMs, no free partitions
View active swapswapon -s or free -hCheck what's currently used
Disable swapswapoff /dev/sdb2Remove swap before repartitioning
Persist in fstab/dev/sdb2 swap swap defaults 0 0Automatically enabled at boot

When to use swap: Always have some swap (1-2x RAM). It prevents OOM kills during memory spikes. Swapiness (/proc/sys/vm/swappiness, default 60): lower values prefer RAM, higher values prefer swap. For database servers: set swappiness=10 to keep PostgreSQL in RAM.

🔧 Real-World: "The Uploads Disk Is Full!" — Storage Emergency on Anihpj

Situation: Users can't upload images. df -h shows /media at 100%. You have a new 500GB disk (/dev/sdc) ready.

  1. Diagnose: df -h /media → 100% full. du -sh /media/* | sort -rh | head → images consuming 190GB.
  2. Add disk to LVM: pvcreate /dev/sdc1 && vgextend anihpj-vg /dev/sdc1
  3. Grow the volume ONLINE: lvextend -L +400G /dev/anihpj-vg/media && resize2fs /dev/anihpj-vg/media
  4. Verify: df -h /media → 450GB total, 42% used. Uploads work again!

Time elapsed: 3 minutes. Downtime: ZERO. This is why LVM exists.

25.2 NFS — Network File System (File Sharing)

NFS Server + Client Setup for Anihpj Media Uploads
  # === SERVER SIDE (nfs-server) ===
  sudo apt install nfs-kernel-server
  sudo mkdir -p /var/www/anihpj/media

  # /etc/exports — define what to share:
  /var/www/anihpj/media  192.168.1.0/24(rw,sync,no_subtree_check)

  sudo exportfs -a    # apply exports
  sudo exportfs -v    # verify

  # === CLIENT SIDE (app-server-1, app-server-2) ===
  sudo apt install nfs-common
  sudo mount -t nfs nfs-server:/var/www/anihpj/media /mnt/nfs-media

  # /etc/fstab (client — persistent):
  nfs-server:/var/www/anihpj/media  /mnt/nfs-media  nfs  defaults,_netdev  0  0
OptionMeaning
rwRead-write access
syncWrite immediately (safer, slower)
no_subtree_checkSkip verification (faster, default)
_netdev (client)Wait for network before mounting

25.3 iSCSI — Remote Block Storage

iSCSI presents a remote disk as a local block device (/dev/sdb). Unlike NFS (file-level), iSCSI is block-level — the client formats it with its own filesystem. Used for databases that need raw disk performance over the network.

📁 NFS — File-Level

Server manages the filesystem. Multiple clients can read/write the SAME files simultaneously. Simple to set up. Best for: shared media directories, home directories, config files.

💾 iSCSI — Block-Level

Client sees a raw disk and formats it with its OWN filesystem. Only ONE client can mount at a time (without cluster FS). Performs like a local disk. Best for: database storage, VM disk images.

CommandWhat It Does
iscsiadm -m discovery -t st -p 192.168.1.100Discover available iSCSI targets
iscsiadm -m node --loginConnect to discovered target
iscsiadm -m sessionShow active iSCSI sessions
NFS vs iSCSI vs Local Storage — Remote Storage Options
TechnologyTypeUse CaseLFCS Tested
NFSFile-level (NAS)Shared /media across web servers. Simple, mature.✅ mount, fstab, exports
iSCSIBlock-level (SAN)Remote disk for DB. Appears as /dev/sdb.✅ iscsiadm discovery
Local FSDirect-attach (DAS)PostgreSQL data, OS. Fastest, simplest.✅ mkfs, mount
🔬 NFS v3 vs v4 — Which Version Should You Use?

NFSv3: Older, simpler. Uses separate mount/lock/status protocols (portmapper/rpcbind required). Stateless-ish. UID/GID-based auth (no Kerberos). Good for simple LAN setups. NFSv4: Modern. Single protocol on port 2049 (no portmapper needed). Stateful (better caching, delegations). Supports Kerberos authentication (krb5p = encrypt ALL traffic). Pseudo-filesystem (exports appear under a single root). File locking is built-in (no separate lockd). For anihpj: Use NFSv4 with krb5p for production NFS. Commands: rpcinfo -p server shows RPC services. showmount -e server lists NFS exports (v3 only — v4 uses the pseudo-filesystem). The kernel negotiates the highest version automatically — check with nfsstat -m or mount | grep nfs.

🔬 autofs — Mount on Demand, Unmount When Idle

autofs mounts NFS/Samba shares automatically when accessed and unmounts them after a period of inactivity. Install: apt install autofs. Configure /etc/auto.master: /mnt/nfs /etc/auto.nfs --timeout=60. Then /etc/auto.nfs: backups -rw nfs-server:/backups/anihpj. Now ls /mnt/nfs/backups triggers the mount automatically. systemctl restart autofs. Perfect for: backup mounts that are only used during nightly jobs.

25.4 Disk Usage Analysis — Finding What Eats Your Space

CommandWhat It DoesExample
df -hTDisk space per filesystem with typedf -hT /var → check specific mount
du -sh /var/*Summary size of each subdirectorydu -sh /var/* | sort -rh | head -10
du -ah /var/logShow ALL files (not just dirs)du -ah /var/log | grep "\.log$"
du --max-depth=1 -h /One level deep, human-readableGreat for finding what fills root
ncdu /Interactive ncurses browserncdu /var → arrow keys, d=delete
find / -type f -size +100MFiles larger than 100MBfind /var -type f -size +1G -exec ls -lh {} \;
find / -type f -mtime +30 -size +50MOld large files (candidates for cleanup)Files >50MB, unmodified in 30+ days

Common disk hogs in production: (1) Log files — /var/log/syslog, journald (journalctl --disk-usage). (2) Package cache — apt clean or dnf clean all. (3) Docker images — docker system prune -a. (4) Old kernels — dpkg --list | grep linux-image. (5) Core dumps — /var/lib/systemd/coredump/. (6) Database WAL files — pg_wal/ in PostgreSQL.

🔧 Pro Tip: Find Today's Largest New Files

find / -type f -mtime -1 -size +10M -exec ls -lh {} \; 2>/dev/null | sort -k5 -rh | head -20 — find files created/modified in the last 24 hours over 10MB, sorted by size. This catches runaway log files, unexpected core dumps, or a forgotten mysqldump filling /tmp.

💡 Anihpj Storage Strategy: PostgreSQL data → LOCAL ext4 on LVM (fast!). User uploads → LOCAL ext4 on LVM (growable). Backups → NFS to NAS (off-server safety). Static files → LOCAL (Nginx cache). 3-2-1 Backup Rule: 3 copies of data, 2 different media types, 1 copy off-site. Anihpj example: Copy 1 = production LVM, Copy 2 = local /backups disk (nightly pg_dump), Copy 3 = NFS mount to NAS (rsync'd after backup).

Click to reveal answer
✅ Answer

Lower values prefer RAM over swap. For database servers, 10 keeps PostgreSQL in RAM and only swaps under extreme pressure.

Chapter 26: SSH — Secure Remote Access

SSH is the sysadmin's lifeline to every Linux server. It encrypts ALL traffic between you and your anihpj server — login credentials, commands, file transfers, even database queries tunneled through it. This chapter covers the SSH protocol, server configuration (sshd_config), key-based authentication, port forwarding, client config files, and production hardening.

🔴 Advanced⏱️ ~1.5 hours🔐 Security

🎯 What You'll Learn

  • ✅ Understand the SSH protocol — encryption, authentication, integrity
  • ✅ Install and configure sshd with secure production settings
  • ✅ Set up SSH key-based authentication (Ed25519)
  • ✅ Use SSH port forwarding for secure tunnels
  • ✅ Harden SSH: disable root login, disable passwords, change port
🧠 Core Understanding — Chapter 26

SSH creates an encrypted tunnel between client and server. Public-key crypto: you have a private key (never shared) and a public key (goes on servers). The server encrypts a challenge with your public key; only your private key can decrypt it — proving your identity without sending the key. Host keys prevent MITM attacks — the server proves its identity first. ssh-agent caches decrypted keys in memory. Agent forwarding lets you hop through servers without copying keys. Deep insight: SSH is not just for remote shells — it tunnels TCP connections, proxies X11, and transfers files (scp/sftp).

The server encrypts a challenge with your public key; only your private key can decrypt it — proving your identity without sending the key. Host keys prevent MITM attacks — the server proves its identity first. ssh-agent caches decrypted keys in memory. Agent forwarding lets you hop through servers without copying keys. Deep insight: SSH is not just for remote shells — it tunnels TCP connections, proxies X11, and transfers files (scp/sftp).

🎯 LFCS Exam Preparation — Chapter 26 Quick Reference

📋 Exam Focus: SSH is the primary remote administration tool. LFCS tests key generation, key-based auth setup, and server hardening. ALWAYS test config with sshd -t.

⚠️ Common Mistake: Locking yourself out by misconfiguring SSH. Always keep a second terminal open when editing sshd_config.

🎓 LFCS Relevance
Service Configuration 20%
🎯 SSH on the LFCS Exam

You'll need to configure sshd, set up key-based auth, and troubleshoot connection issues. Key files: /etc/ssh/sshd_config (server), ~/.ssh/config (client), ~/.ssh/authorized_keys (allowed keys). Always test config with sshd -t before restarting! Wrong permissions on ~/.ssh (must be 700) or authorized_keys (must be 600) are the #1 cause of key auth failures.

26.1 SSH Server (sshd_config)

How SSH Works — The Encrypted Handshake
  CLIENT (your laptop)                    SERVER (anihpj production)
  ─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
  ① TCP CONNECT to port 22
     ─────────────────────────────────────▶  sshd listening on :22

  ② VERSION EXCHANGE
     "SSH-2.0-OpenSSH_9.3"  ───────────▶  "SSH-2.0-OpenSSH_9.3"
     (agree on protocol version)

  ③ KEY EXCHANGE (Diffie-Hellman)
     ◀══════════════════════════════════▶  Both sides compute a
         (mathematical agreement)           SHARED SESSION KEY
         🔑 Session key is NEVER             without ever sending
            transmitted over network!        it across the network

  ④ SERVER AUTHENTICATION
     ◀───────────────────────────────────  Server presents its
         "Here's my HOST KEY"              HOST KEY fingerprint.
         (you verify on first connect)     Stored in ~/.ssh/known_hosts

  ⑤ USER AUTHENTICATION
     Method A: Password
       "password: ******"  ──────────────▶  Check against /etc/shadow
     Method B: PUBLIC KEY (recommended!)
       "I'll prove I have the             ◀  "Here's a random challenge,
        private key for this                encrypt it with user's public key"
        public key in authorized_keys"

  ⑥ 🔒 ENCRYPTED SESSION ESTABLISHED
     All subsequent data encrypted with AES-256 / ChaCha20
     ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
     │  🔐 EVERYTHING ENCRYPTED: commands, output, files, TCP │
     │     tunnels. Even if someone snoops, they see garbage.  │
     └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
File / CommandWhat It IsKey Directives
/etc/ssh/sshd_configSSH daemon (server) configPort, PermitRootLogin, PasswordAuthentication
systemctl status sshdCheck if SSH server is runningActive: active (running)
sshd -tTest config syntax before reloadingNo output = OK. ALWAYS run this first!
systemctl reload sshdApply config changes without dropping connectionsExisting sessions survive reload
Complete sshd_config for Anihpj Production Server
  # /etc/ssh/sshd_config — HARDENED configuration for anihpj
  Port 22                          # Default port (consider changing to reduce noise)
  Protocol 2                       # SSH protocol version 2 ONLY (v1 is insecure)
  HostKey /etc/ssh/ssh_host_ed25519_key   # Modern, fast, secure key type

  # AUTHENTICATION — KEY-ONLY IN PRODUCTION
  PermitRootLogin no               # NEVER allow direct root SSH login!
  PasswordAuthentication no         # Disable password login (key-only)
  PubkeyAuthentication yes          # Enable public key authentication
  ChallengeResponseAuthentication no # Disable keyboard-interactive

  # SESSION LIMITS
  MaxAuthTries 3                    # Disconnect after 3 failed attempts
  MaxSessions 10                    # Max simultaneous sessions per connection
  ClientAliveInterval 300          # Send keepalive every 5 min (detect dead clients)
  ClientAliveCountMax 3            # Disconnect after 3 missed keepalives (15 min)

  # ACCESS CONTROL
  AllowUsers anihpj-deploy admin   # WHITELIST: only these users can SSH in
  # DenyUsers  baduser             # BLACKLIST alternative (AllowUsers is stronger)

  # SECURITY HARDENING
  X11Forwarding no                 # Disable GUI forwarding (not needed on server)
  PermitTunnel no                  # Disable tunneling unless needed
  AllowTcpForwarding no            # Disable port forwarding unless needed
  PermitUserEnvironment no         # Prevent users from setting env vars via SSH

  # LOGGING
  SyslogFacility AUTH              # Log to /var/log/auth.log
  LogLevel VERBOSE                 # Log connection attempts (helps fail2ban)

  # After editing: sudo sshd -t && sudo systemctl reload sshd

26.2 SSH Key Management

CommandWhat It DoesWhen to Use
ssh-keygen -t ed25519 -C "anihpj-deploy"Generate Ed25519 key pair (recommended!)Creating new keys — faster & more secure than RSA
ssh-keygen -t rsa -b 4096 -C "legacy"Generate RSA 4096-bit key pairCompatibility with old systems
ssh-copy-id user@serverCopy public key to server's authorized_keysFirst-time setup — easiest method
cat ~/.ssh/id_ed25519.pubView your public key (safe to share)Manual key sharing or pasting into cloud console
ssh-add ~/.ssh/id_ed25519Add private key to SSH agent (cache passphrase)Avoid typing passphrase repeatedly
⚠️ SSH Key Permissions are CRITICAL!

Wrong permissions = SSH silently ignores your keys. Must be: chmod 700 ~/.ssh (directory — owner only). chmod 600 ~/.ssh/id_ed25519 (private key — owner read/write only). chmod 644 ~/.ssh/id_ed25519.pub (public key — world-readable is fine). chmod 600 ~/.ssh/authorized_keys (on server — owner read/write only). If SSH key auth fails: tail -f /var/log/auth.log on the server — it will tell you EXACTLY which file has wrong permissions.

🔬 Ed25519 vs RSA — Why Ed25519 Wins

Ed25519 keys are: (1) Faster — 256-bit keys with same security as 3072-bit RSA. (2) Smaller — public key is 68 chars vs 700+ for RSA. (3) More secure — resistant to side-channel attacks that affect RSA. (4) Modern — supported by OpenSSH 6.5+ (2014). For new deployments: ALWAYS use Ed25519. Use RSA only for legacy systems that don't support it. The LFCS exam accepts both — show you know the difference!

🔬 How Diffie-Hellman Key Exchange Actually Works (Simplified)

The magic: two parties agree on a shared secret that was NEVER transmitted. Simplified with colors: (1) Alice and Bob agree on a public color (yellow). (2) Each picks a SECRET color (Alice=red, Bob=blue). (3) Each mixes their secret with the public color (Alice=orange, Bob=green) and sends the mixture. (4) Each adds their own secret to the received mixture. Alice: green+red = brown. Bob: orange+blue = brown. Both now have brown — the shared secret! An eavesdropper sees yellow, orange, and green — but can't figure out brown without knowing red or blue. Real DH uses modular exponentiation instead of colors: g^a mod p where only g and p are public. Computing a from g^a mod p is the discrete logarithm problem — mathematically infeasible for large numbers. The shared secret becomes the session key for AES-256 encryption. This is why SSH is secure even on untrusted networks.

⚠️ SSH Agent Forwarding — The Hidden Danger

SSH agent forwarding (ssh -A or ForwardAgent yes in config) lets you use your local SSH keys on a remote server. The danger: if the remote server is compromised, an attacker can use your forwarded agent to authenticate to ANY server your key has access to. They don't steal your private key — they use the agent socket while you're connected. Never use agent forwarding on untrusted servers. Safer alternative: ProxyJump (ssh -J bastion target) which tunnels the connection through an intermediate host without exposing your keys. Another alternative: use separate keys with limited scope per server.

26.3 SSH Troubleshooting

SSH Troubleshooting Decision Tree
  SSH FAILS TO CONNECT?
      │
      ├─ "Connection refused"
      │   ├─ sshd running? → systemctl status sshd
      │   ├─ Correct port?  → ss -tlnp | grep 22
      │   └─ Firewall?      → ufw status, iptables -L
      │
      ├─ "Connection timed out"
      │   ├─ Can ping?      → ping server-ip
      │   ├─ Port open?     → nc -zv server 22
      │   └─ Cloud SG?      → Check AWS/Azure security group
      │
      ├─ "Permission denied (publickey)"
      │   ├─ Key in authorized_keys? → cat ~/.ssh/authorized_keys
      │   ├─ Permissions?    → chmod 700 ~/.ssh; chmod 600 ~/.ssh/authorized_keys
      │   ├─ Right key?      → ssh -i /path/to/key user@host
      │   └─ Check server log → tail -f /var/log/auth.log
      │
      ├─ "Host key verification failed"
      │   ├─ Expected change? → ssh-keygen -R hostname
      │   └─ UNEXPECTED?      → ⚠️ POSSIBLE MITM ATTACK! Verify with admin.
      │
      └─ "Too many authentication failures"
          ├─ Too many keys in agent? → ssh -o IdentitiesOnly=yes
          └─ Try specific key: ssh -i ~/.ssh/id_ed25519 -o IdentitiesOnly=yes user@host
🔬 How known_hosts Prevents MITM Attacks

On your FIRST SSH connection to a server, you see: "The authenticity of host 'anihpj.com (203.0.113.50)' can't be established. ED25519 key fingerprint is SHA256:abc123... Are you sure you want to continue?" This is the most important security prompt in SSH. If you type "yes", the server's public host key is saved in ~/.ssh/known_hosts. On every FUTURE connection, SSH verifies the server's presented key MATCHES the saved one. If they don't match, SSH screams "HOST KEY VERIFICATION FAILED" and refuses to connect. This protects against MITM (Man-in-the-Middle) attacks: if someone intercepts your connection and presents a fake server, the key won't match and SSH warns you. When to trust the warning: Server was reinstalled, IP reassigned, or you're connecting to a DIFFERENT server at the same IP. When to PANIC: You didn't expect the key to change — someone might be intercepting your traffic. Fix: ssh-keygen -R hostname removes the old key so you can accept the new one. Never blindly type "yes" to a changed host key — verify with the server admin first.

SymptomLikely CauseFix
"Connection refused"sshd not running or wrong portsystemctl status sshd, check ss -tlnp | grep 22
"Permission denied (publickey)"Key not in authorized_keys OR wrong permissionsCheck ~/.ssh/authorized_keys, run chmod 600 ~/.ssh/*
"Host key verification failed"Server's host key changed (reinstall/IP change)ssh-keygen -R hostname to remove old key
"Connection timed out"Firewall blocking port 22Check UFW: ufw status, cloud security group rules
SSH hangs after "Connecting..."DNS reverse lookup slow/failingAdd UseDNS no to sshd_config on server
"Too many authentication failures"SSH agent offering too many keysssh -o IdentitiesOnly=yes -o PubkeyAuthentication=no user@host
🔧 Debug SSH Like a Pro

ssh -vvv user@server — triple verbose mode shows the ENTIRE handshake: key exchange, offered keys, accepted auth methods, and the exact reason for failure. On the server side: tail -f /var/log/auth.log shows sshd's perspective. These two together solve 99% of SSH problems.

🔬 SSH Port Forwarding Deep-Dive — Three Types of Tunnels

SSH can tunnel TCP connections through its encrypted channel — turning SSH into a poor-man's VPN. Type 1 — Local Forward (most common): ssh -L 5433:localhost:5432 user@server. Traffic to YOUR port 5433 → encrypted over SSH → server's localhost:5432. Use: access remote PostgreSQL without exposing it to the internet. Type 2 — Remote Forward (reverse tunnel): ssh -R 8080:localhost:80 user@public-server. Traffic to public-server:8080 → encrypted back to YOUR localhost:80. Use: expose your dev server behind NAT to a public server. Type 3 — Dynamic SOCKS Proxy: ssh -D 1080 user@server. Creates a SOCKS5 proxy on your local port 1080. Configure browser to use localhost:1080 as proxy → ALL browser traffic tunnels through the server. Use: browse internet as if you're at the server's location, bypass geo-restrictions.

26.4 SSH Hardening

⚠️ The Single Biggest SSH Mistake

Leaving PasswordAuthentication yes on a public-facing server. Within MINUTES of going online, bots will start guessing passwords: root/admin/ubuntu/123456 — thousands of attempts per day. Even a "strong" 12-character password can be brute-forced given enough time. SSH keys (Ed25519) are mathematically impossible to brute-force. PasswordAuthentication no is the single most impactful security change you can make. Every other hardening measure is secondary.

🔴 Password Authentication

Bots guess passwords 24/7. Even strong passwords can be keylogged or phished. Server logs fill with "Failed password for root from 103.x.x.x". A single weak user password = full server compromise.

🟢 SSH Key Authentication

Ed25519 key = 256 bits of cryptographic proof. Cannot be brute-forced. Cannot be keylogged (private key never leaves your machine). Pair with a passphrase for 2FA-like protection.

The SSH Hardening Ladder — From Default to Fortress
  LEVEL 1: DEFAULT (INSECURE)
  ├─ Port 22, root login allowed, password auth enabled
  └─ 🔴 Bots WILL find you and try passwords within MINUTES

    ▼

  LEVEL 2: BASIC HARDENING
  ├─ PermitRootLogin no
  ├─ PasswordAuthentication no (key-only)
  └─ 🔶 Stops ALL password-guessing attacks

    ▼

  LEVEL 3: INTERMEDIATE
  ├─ Change port to 2222 (reduces automated scans by 99%)
  ├─ AllowUsers whitelist (only specific users can SSH)
  ├─ MaxAuthTries 3
  └─ 🔶 Dramatically reduces attack surface

    ▼

  LEVEL 4: ADVANCED
  ├─ fail2ban: auto-ban IPs after 5 failed attempts
  ├─ Port knocking: SSH port hidden until secret sequence
  ├─ 2FA: Google Authenticator + SSH key
  └─ 🟢 Production-grade security

    ▼

  LEVEL 5: ENTERPRISE
  ├─ SSH Certificate Authority (signed keys with expiry)
  ├─ Bastion host (jump server, single SSH entry point)
  ├─ Session recording (audit all SSH commands)
  └─ 🟢 Zero-trust architecture
DirectiveRecommended ValueWhy
PermitRootLoginnoForce sudo via personal account. Audit trail.
PasswordAuthenticationnoKeys are un-bruteforceable. Passwords are not.
Port2222 (non-default)Eliminates 99% of automated SSH scan noise.
AllowUsersWhitelist specific usersEven if someone steals a key, they need the username too.
MaxAuthTries3Disconnect after 3 failures. Works with fail2ban.

26.5 SSH Config File (~/.ssh/config)

Client-Side ~/.ssh/config — Your SSH Shortcut File
  # ~/.ssh/config — save typing with aliases and defaults
  # chmod 600 ~/.ssh/config (must be owner-only!)

  # === ANIHPJ PRODUCTION ===
  Host anihpj-prod
      HostName 203.0.113.50
      User anihpj-deploy
      Port 2222
      IdentityFile ~/.ssh/anihpj_ed25519
      IdentitiesOnly yes          # Only try THIS key
      ServerAliveInterval 60      # Keep connection alive

  # === ANIHPJ STAGING ===
  Host anihpj-staging
      HostName staging.anihpj.com
      User anihpj-deploy
      IdentityFile ~/.ssh/anihpj_ed25519

  # === DATABASE TUNNEL (access PostgreSQL via SSH) ===
  Host anihpj-db-tunnel
      HostName 203.0.113.50
      User anihpj-deploy
      IdentityFile ~/.ssh/anihpj_ed25519
      LocalForward 5432 localhost:5432   # /dbs/port-forwarding/idioms

  # === GLOBAL DEFAULTS ===
  Host *
      ServerAliveInterval 120     # Send keepalive every 2 min
      ForwardAgent no             # Don't forward SSH agent (security!)
      StrictHostKeyChecking ask   # Prompt on new host keys

  # NOW: Instead of:
  #   ssh -i ~/.ssh/anihpj_ed25519 -p 2222 anihpj-deploy@203.0.113.50
  # Just type:
  #   ssh anihpj-prod
DirectiveExampleWhat It Does
HostHost anihpj-prodAlias name — what you type after ssh
HostNameHostName 203.0.113.50Real server IP or FQDN
UserUser deployDefault SSH username (skip user@ in commands)
PortPort 2222Non-default SSH port
IdentityFileIdentityFile ~/.ssh/anihpj_ed25519Which private key to use
IdentitiesOnlyIdentitiesOnly yesOnly try THIS key (ignore ssh-agent keys)
LocalForwardLocalForward 5433 localhost:5432Tunnel local port to remote host:port
ProxyJumpProxyJump bastion.anihpj.comJump through bastion host to reach target
ServerAliveIntervalServerAliveInterval 60Send keepalive every 60s (prevents timeout)

StrictHostKeyCheckingStrictHostKeyChecking askPrompt on new host keys (security default)
❌ WITHOUT ~/.ssh/config

ssh -i ~/.ssh/anihpj_ed25519 -p 2222 anihpj-deploy@203.0.113.50
Every. Single. Time. You must remember the port, user, key path, and IP.

✅ WITH ~/.ssh/config

ssh anihpj-prod
That's it. Tab-completes. All settings applied automatically from the config file.

🔬 ProxyJump — The Safe Way to Reach Internal Servers

Many organizations have a bastion/jump host — the ONLY server exposed to the internet. Internal servers (databases, staging, monitoring) sit behind it with no public IP. Instead of SSH-ing into the bastion THEN SSH-ing again, use ProxyJump: ssh -J bastion.anihpj.com internal-db.anihpj.local. The connection is tunneled THROUGH the bastion — your keys stay on your laptop. In ~/.ssh/config: Host internal-db
HostName 10.0.1.50
User deploy
ProxyJump bastion.anihpj.com. This is why ProxyJump replaces the dangerous ssh -A (agent forwarding) — same result, zero key exposure.

Configure sshd to: disable root login, disable password authentication, and limit SSH to users "admin" and "deploy" only.
Click to reveal answer
✅ Answer

PermitRootLogin no
PasswordAuthentication no
AllowUsers admin deploy
# Test and reload:
sudo sshd -t && sudo systemctl reload sshd
📖 Explanation

systemd manages every service on modern Linux. systemctl start activates a unit now; systemctl enable creates the symlink for auto-start at boot. You need both for a persistent service. PermitRootLogin is the key tool here. Its man page (man PermitRootLogin) is available during the exam if you need to check less common options. Verify with systemctl status unit-name. Look for "Active: active (running)" and check the PID. If it failed, journalctl -xeu unit-name shows why. Man pages are available but cost time. Know the common flags by heart; use man only for esoteric options.
