You changed sshd_config and ran "systemctl restart sshd". Now you can't SSH in. What should you have done differently?
Click to reveal answer
✅ Answer
# ALWAYS do this sequence:
sudo sshd -t              # 1. TEST config first!
sudo systemctl reload sshd  # 2. RELOAD (not restart!) — existing session stays alive

# NEVER "systemctl restart sshd" because:
# - Kills your current SSH session
# - If config is broken, sshd won't start → LOCKED OUT

# Recovery (if you have console access):
# Boot into recovery mode or use cloud console to fix the config
# Or: schedule a "sanity reboot" with "shutdown -r +5" before risky changes
#     → if you break SSH, the server reboots in 5 min with old config
📖 Explanation

systemd manages every service on modern Linux. systemctl start activates a unit now; systemctl enable creates the symlink for auto-start at boot. You need both for a persistent service. The flags -t control how this command behaves. Understanding what each flag does — not just memorizing the combination — lets you adapt when the exam presents a variation. Verify with systemctl status unit-name. Look for "Active: active (running)" and check the PID. If it failed, journalctl -xeu unit-name shows why. Reboot once before submitting (last 5 minutes). This catches non-persistent configs and broken fstab entries before the grader sees them.

Chapter 27: Web Servers — Nginx & Apache

Every web request to anihpj.com hits a web server first. This chapter covers the two dominant Linux web servers: Nginx (the modern event-driven reverse proxy) and Apache (the process-based workhorse). You'll learn their architectural differences, how to configure Nginx as a reverse proxy for Gunicorn/Django, set up SSL/TLS with Let's Encrypt, and handle Apache basics for the LFCS exam.

🔴 Advanced⏱️ ~2 hours🌐 Web

🎯 What You'll Learn

  • ✅ Compare Nginx (event-driven) vs Apache (process-based) architectures
  • ✅ Install and configure Nginx with virtual hosts (server blocks)
  • ✅ Build a complete Nginx reverse proxy config for anihpj + Gunicorn
  • ✅ Enable HTTPS with Let's Encrypt (Certbot) — zero downtime
  • ✅ Understand Apache2 virtual hosts and module management
🧠 Core Understanding — Chapter 27

Nginx uses an event-driven, asynchronous architecture — one master process + multiple worker processes, each handling thousands of connections concurrently. Contrast with Apache: Apache creates a thread per connection; Nginx uses non-blocking I/O with epoll. This is why Nginx handles high concurrency with minimal resources. Reverse proxy: client → Nginx → backend (Gunicorn). Nginx buffers slow clients, handles SSL, and serves static files — the backend only handles application logic.

27.1 Nginx vs Apache — Architecture Differences

FeatureNginxApache
ArchitectureEvent-driven, asynchronous, single-threaded worker processesProcess/thread per connection (prefork/worker/event MPMs)
ConcurrencyHandles 10,000+ connections with few workers (C10K)Each connection consumes a process/thread — more RAM
Static FilesExcellent — serves directly from disk with minimal overheadGood, but more overhead per request
Dynamic ContentReverse proxy to backend (Gunicorn, uWSGI, PHP-FPM)Modules run code in-process (mod_php, mod_python)
Config StyleClean, block-based. server { } and location { } blocksXML-like. Directory-based .htaccess overrides.
.htaccessNOT supported (by design — faster without per-dir checks)Supported — allows per-directory config overrides
Best ForReverse proxy, load balancing, static files, high concurrencyShared hosting, legacy apps needing .htaccess
🟢 Nginx (Event-Driven)

1 worker process handles thousands of connections simultaneously using epoll/kqueue. Like a restaurant with one super-efficient waiter who never stops moving. Anihpj choice: Nginx as reverse proxy.

🔵 Apache (Process-Based)

Each connection gets its own process/thread. Like a restaurant with one waiter per table. More resource usage but simpler mental model. Anihpj choice: Not used; Nginx is primary.

🔬 How epoll Makes Nginx So Fast — The Event Loop Explained

Traditional servers (Apache prefork) create one process PER connection. 1,000 concurrent users = 1,000 processes, each consuming ~2-10MB RAM. That's 2-10GB just for idle connections! Nginx uses epoll (Linux) / kqueue (BSD): the kernel maintains a list of file descriptors (sockets) and wakes up Nginx ONLY when data is ready. One worker process with epoll can handle 10,000+ idle connections using almost no CPU. The event loop: (1) Register all sockets with epoll, (2) Go to sleep — kernel does the waiting, (3) Kernel wakes Nginx: "data ready on socket #42", (4) Nginx handles that ONE socket, (5) Go back to sleep. No polling, no per-connection processes, minimal context switching. Analogy: Apache = 1,000 waiters each watching one table. Nginx = 1 waiter with a pager that buzzes when ANY table needs attention.

🔬 UNIX Socket vs TCP Socket — Why Gunicorn Uses a File

Nginx talks to Gunicorn via /run/anihpj/anihpj.sock — a UNIX domain socket. Why not TCP on localhost:8000? Performance: UNIX sockets bypass the TCP/IP stack entirely — no packetization, no TCP handshake, no congestion control. Data is copied directly between processes in the kernel. Security: UNIX sockets respect filesystem permissions (chmod 660, chown anihpj:www-data) — only specific users/groups can connect. TCP on localhost:8000 can be connected to by ANY local user. No port conflicts: You can have unlimited UNIX sockets, but only one service per TCP port. The downside: UNIX sockets only work on the same machine (no remote connections). For anihpj: Nginx and Gunicorn are on the SAME server, so the UNIX socket is perfect.

27.3 Virtual Host for anihpj

🔧 Real-World: "Nginx 502 Bad Gateway" — What Happened to Anihpj?

Situation: Users report anihpj.com showing "502 Bad Gateway." You SSH in to investigate.

  1. Check Nginx error log: tail -50 /var/log/nginx/anihpj-error.log → "connect() to unix:/run/anihpj/anihpj.sock failed (111: Connection refused)"
  2. Check Gunicorn: systemctl status anihpj → inactive (dead). Gunicorn crashed!
  3. Check journal: journalctl -u anihpj --since "10 min ago" → "ModuleNotFoundError: No module named 'django'" — someone updated the virtualenv without reinstalling deps.
  4. Fix: source /var/www/anihpj/venv/bin/activate && pip install -r requirements.txt && systemctl restart anihpj
  5. Verify: curl -I https://anihpj.com → HTTP/2 200. Back online!

Root cause: Gunicorn crashed because Django wasn't importable. Nginx correctly returned 502 (upstream unreachable). Lesson: Always check BOTH nginx error log AND the upstream service when debugging 502 errors.

Complete Nginx Config for Anihpj — Reverse Proxy to Gunicorn
  # /etc/nginx/sites-available/anihpj
  # After editing: sudo nginx -t && sudo systemctl reload nginx

  # === HTTP (Port 80) — Redirect ALL traffic to HTTPS ===
  server {
      listen 80;
      server_name anihpj.com www.anihpj.com;

      # Redirect to HTTPS (301 permanent)
      return 301 https://$server_name$request_uri;
  }

  # === HTTPS (Port 443) — The REAL server block ===
  server {
      listen 443 ssl http2;              # HTTP/2 for faster page loads
      server_name anihpj.com www.anihpj.com;

      # SSL CERTIFICATES (from Let's Encrypt / Certbot)
      ssl_certificate     /etc/letsencrypt/live/anihpj.com/fullchain.pem;
      ssl_certificate_key /etc/letsencrypt/live/anihpj.com/privkey.pem;

      # SECURITY HEADERS
      add_header Strict-Transport-Security "max-age=63072000" always;
      add_header X-Frame-Options DENY;
      add_header X-Content-Type-Options nosniff;

      # LOGS
      access_log /var/log/nginx/anihpj-access.log;
      error_log  /var/log/nginx/anihpj-error.log;

      # CLIENT MAX BODY SIZE (for jobpost file uploads)
      client_max_body_size 10M;

      # === STATIC FILES — Served DIRECTLY by Nginx (fast!) ===
      location /static/ {
          alias /var/www/anihpj/staticfiles/;
          expires 30d;                    # Cache for 30 days
          add_header Cache-Control "public, immutable";
      }

      # === MEDIA FILES — User uploads (jobpost images) ===
      location /media/ {
          alias /var/www/anihpj/media/;
      }

      # === EVERYTHING ELSE → Gunicorn (Django app) ===
      location / {
          proxy_pass http://unix:/run/anihpj/anihpj.sock;

          # Pass original request info to Django
          proxy_set_header Host $http_host;
          proxy_set_header X-Real-IP $remote_addr;
          proxy_set_header X-Forwarded-For $proxy_add_x_forwarded_for;
          proxy_set_header X-Forwarded-Proto $scheme;

          # Timeout settings
          proxy_connect_timeout 60s;
          proxy_read_timeout 60s;
      }
  }

  KEY DIRECTIVES EXPLAINED:
  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │ listen 443 ssl http2     → Listen on HTTPS with HTTP/2          │
  │ server_name anihpj.com   → This block handles requests for      │
  │                            anihpj.com ONLY (virtual hosting)    │
  │ location /static/         → URL path matching: /static/* files   │
  │ alias /var/www/...        → Map URL path to filesystem path      │
  │ proxy_pass http://unix:   → Forward to Gunicorn via UNIX socket  │
  │ proxy_set_header          → Inject headers so Django knows the   │
  │                            original client IP and protocol       │
  │ client_max_body_size 10M  → Allow file uploads up to 10MB       │
  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

🔬 Why HTTPS Matters for Anihpj

Without HTTPS: (1) Passwords sent in plaintext — anyone on the WiFi can see them. (2) Session cookies stolen — attacker hijacks user accounts. (3) Browsers show "Not Secure" warning — users leave. (4) Google ranks HTTP sites lower. With HTTPS + HSTS: browsers refuse to connect over HTTP. Certificates are FREE with Let's Encrypt — there's no excuse not to use HTTPS in production.

27.6 Nginx Load Balancer — Distributing Traffic 🎯

🧠 Why Load Balancers Matter for LFCS

The official LFCS domain explicitly lists "Implement reverse proxies and load balancers." A reverse proxy forwards requests to ONE backend; a load balancer distributes requests across MULTIPLE backends. This is how high-traffic sites stay up — if one Gunicorn worker crashes, the load balancer routes traffic to the healthy ones. For anihpj in production, you'd run 3-4 Gunicorn workers on different ports and have Nginx distribute traffic among them.

Load Balancer Architecture — Anihpj Production Setup
                        INTERNET
                           │
                    ┌──────▼──────┐
                    │   Nginx LB  │  (anihpj.com:443)
                    │ :80 → :443  │  SSL Termination + Load Balancing
                    └──┬──┬──┬───┘
                       │  │  │  │
              ┌────────┘  │  │  └────────┐
              ▼           ▼  ▼           ▼
        ┌──────────┐ ┌──────────┐ ┌──────────┐
        │ Gunicorn │ │ Gunicorn │ │ Gunicorn │
        │  :8001   │ │  :8002   │ │  :8003   │
        │ Worker 1 │ │ Worker 2 │ │ Worker 3 │
        └────┬─────┘ └────┬─────┘ └────┬─────┘
             │            │            │
             └────────────┼────────────┘
                          │
                   ┌──────▼──────┐
                   │ PostgreSQL  │
                   │   :5432     │
                   └─────────────┘
Load Balancing MethodHow It WorksBest ForExample
Round-Robin (default)Requests distributed evenly in order: W1 → W2 → W3 → W1...Stateless apps with similar server specsGeneral web apps, REST APIs
Least ConnectionsSend to backend with fewest active connectionsRequests with varying processing timesLong-lived WebSocket connections
IP HashHash of client IP determines backend. Same IP → same backendSession stickiness without cookiesShopping carts, login sessions
WeightedBackends given weight. weight=3 gets 3x traffic of weight=1Heterogeneous servers (bigger server = more weight)Canary deployments, A/B testing
Least Time (NGINX Plus)Send to backend with lowest avg response time + fewest connectionsPerformance-sensitive appsHigh-frequency trading, real-time APIs
✅ Nginx Upstream — Practical Anihpj Load Balancer
# /etc/nginx/sites-available/anihpj
upstream anihpj_backend {
    # Round-robin (default) — distribute evenly
    server 127.0.0.1:8001;
    server 127.0.0.1:8002;
    server 127.0.0.1:8003;

    # Keep connections alive for reuse
    keepalive 32;
}

upstream anihpj_backend_weighted {
    # Weighted — bigger server gets more traffic
    server 127.0.0.1:8001 weight=3;  # 8-core machine
    server 127.0.0.1:8002 weight=1;  # 2-core machine
}

upstream anihpj_backend_ip_hash {
    # Sticky sessions — same client → same backend
    ip_hash;
    server 127.0.0.1:8001;
    server 127.0.0.1:8002;
    server 127.0.0.1:8003;
}

server {
    listen 443 ssl;
    server_name anihpj.com;

    location / {
        proxy_pass http://anihpj_backend;
        proxy_set_header Host $host;
        proxy_set_header X-Real-IP $remote_addr;
        proxy_set_header X-Forwarded-For $proxy_add_x_forwarded_for;
        proxy_set_header X-Forwarded-Proto $scheme;

        # Timeouts — prevents hanging connections
        proxy_connect_timeout 60s;
        proxy_read_timeout 60s;
        proxy_send_timeout 60s;
    }

    location /static/ {
        alias /var/www/anihpj/static/;
        expires 30d;
    }
}
❌ Common Mistakes with Load Balancers
# MISTAKE 1: No health checks — Nginx sends
# traffic to dead backends!
# FIX: Add health check parameters:
upstream anihpj_backend {
    server 127.0.0.1:8001 max_fails=3 fail_timeout=30s;
    server 127.0.0.1:8002 max_fails=3 fail_timeout=30s;
    # After 3 failures in 30s, mark as DOWN
    # Tries again after 30s
}

# MISTAKE 2: Forgetting backup server
# FIX: Designate a backup for emergencies:
upstream anihpj_backend {
    server 127.0.0.1:8001;
    server 127.0.0.1:8002;
    server 127.0.0.1:8003 backup;  # Only used
    # when ALL others are down
}

# MISTAKE 3: Sticky sessions without session store
# ip_hash breaks if clients change IPs (mobile)
# FIX: Use Redis-backed Django sessions instead
💡 Health Checks — Keep Traffic Off Broken Backends

max_fails=N fail_timeout=T: If a backend fails N times within T seconds, Nginx marks it as DOWN for T seconds, then retries. Anihpj setup: Each Gunicorn worker on a different port (8001/8002/8003) started by separate systemd units OR via Gunicorn's built-in --workers 3. Active health checks (NGINX Plus only): health_check uri=/health interval=5s fails=2 passes=3; — Nginx proactively pings /health endpoint. Passive health checks (NGINX OSS): Nginx detects failures from actual traffic. Debug: curl -I http://127.0.0.1:8001/health — manually check each backend before adding to upstream.

🔬 Load Balancer vs Reverse Proxy — What's the Difference?

A reverse proxy sits in front of ONE or MORE backends — its primary job is SSL termination, caching, and security. A load balancer is a type of reverse proxy whose PRIMARY job is distributing traffic across multiple backends for high availability and horizontal scaling. In practice, Nginx does both — every load balancer IS a reverse proxy, but not every reverse proxy configuration includes load balancing. LFCS exam tip: If the task says "configure a reverse proxy," set up proxy_pass to one backend. If it says "implement a load balancer," configure an upstream block with multiple servers.

Starting Multiple Gunicorn Workers for Load Balancing
  # Option A: Gunicorn manages workers internally
  # (Simpler — one systemd unit, Gunicorn forks workers)
  gunicorn anihpj.wsgi:application       --workers 3       --bind 127.0.0.1:8000

  # Option B: Separate Gunicorn instances per port
  # (More control — isolate crashes, different configs)
  gunicorn anihpj.wsgi:application --bind 127.0.0.1:8001
  gunicorn anihpj.wsgi:application --bind 127.0.0.1:8002
  gunicorn anihpj.wsgi:application --bind 127.0.0.1:8003

  # Option B with systemd (production grade):
  # anihpj@.service (template unit)
  # systemctl start anihpj@8001 anihpj@8002 anihpj@8003

Q1
Install Nginx and create a virtual host for anihpj.com that listens on port 80 and serves files from /var/www/anihpj.
Click to reveal answer
✅ Answer
sudo apt install nginx
sudo nano /etc/nginx/sites-available/anihpj

📖 Explanation

systemd manages every service on modern Linux. systemctl start activates a unit now; systemctl enable creates the symlink for auto-start at boot. You need both for a persistent service. sudo is the key tool here. Its man page (man sudo) is available during the exam if you need to check less common options. Verify with systemctl status unit-name. Look for "Active: active (running)" and check the PID. If it failed, journalctl -xeu unit-name shows why. On the exam, verify your result immediately — a single unverified typo can cascade into multiple failed tasks.

Q2
What's the difference between sites-available and sites-enabled in Nginx?
Click to reveal answer
✅ Answer

sites-available/ stores ALL virtual host config files — active or not. sites-enabled/ contains ONLY symlinks to active sites. Nginx only reads from sites-enabled/. This lets you disable a site by removing the symlink without deleting the config file. Pattern: write in available, enable with symlink, test, reload.

📖 Explanation

KVM turns the Linux kernel into a Type 1 hypervisor — VMs run directly on hardware with near-native performance. libvirt provides the management layer; virsh is its command-line interface. The flags -available, -enabled, -enabled control how this command behaves. Understanding what each flag does — not just memorizing the combination — lets you adapt when the exam presents a variation. Practice this in your lab VM until you can type it from memory. The 2-hour timer is unforgiving if you're looking up every command.

Q3
Configure Nginx to redirect all HTTP (port 80) traffic to HTTPS (port 443) for anihpj.com.
Click to reveal answer
✅ Answer
server {
    listen 80;
    server_name anihpj.com www.anihpj.com;
    return 301 https://$server_name$request_uri;
}
📖 Explanation

Every running program is a process with a PID. The kernel schedules processes using the Completely Fair Scheduler (CFS). Signals (TERM, KILL, HUP) control process lifecycle — SIGTERM asks politely, SIGKILL forces termination. server is the key tool here. Its man page (man server) is available during the exam if you need to check less common options. If a task says "make persistent" or "survive reboot," you MUST write to a file in /etc/. This is the #1 reason candidates lose points.

Q7
Why does Nginx NOT support .htaccess files? What's the advantage of this design?
Click to reveal answer
✅ Answer

Nginx intentionally does NOT support per-directory config files (.htaccess). Reason: Apache checks .htaccess in EVERY directory in the path for EVERY request — this is slow. Nginx's approach: all config is in the central server blocks — read once at startup, no per-request filesystem checks. Result: Nginx is faster for static files and uses less CPU. The trade-off: you can't let users override config in their directories (which shared hosting needs).

📖 Explanation

tar bundles files into one archive while preserving permissions, ownership, and directory structure. Compression is a separate step — that's why the flags combine: -c create, -z gzip, -f file. The flags -directory, -request, -off control how this command behaves. Understanding what each flag does — not just memorizing the combination — lets you adapt when the exam presents a variation. Man pages are available but cost time. Know the common flags by heart; use man only for esoteric options.

Q9
You changed Nginx config and ran "systemctl restart nginx". Why is reload usually better?
Click to reveal answer
✅ Answer

systemctl reload nginx tells the master process to re-read config and gracefully restart workers — existing connections finish, new connections use new config. ZERO downtime. systemctl restart nginx KILLS all workers immediately, dropping active connections. Use reload for config changes, restart only when nginx itself is broken or after package upgrades.

Chapter 28: PostgreSQL — Database Server Configuration

PostgreSQL stores every job posting, user profile, and application on anihpj. This chapter covers installing PostgreSQL, understanding its two critical config files (postgresql.conf and pg_hba.conf), creating the anihpj database and user with proper privileges, backup/restore strategies, and performance tuning basics for production.

🔴 Advanced⏱️ ~1.5 hours🗄️ Database

🎯 What You'll Learn

  • ✅ Install PostgreSQL and understand its directory structure
  • ✅ Configure postgresql.conf (server settings) and pg_hba.conf (authentication)
  • ✅ Create the anihpj database, user, and grant proper privileges
  • ✅ Backup and restore databases with pg_dump and pg_restore
  • ✅ Tune PostgreSQL memory settings for production performance
🧠 Core Understanding — Chapter 28

PostgreSQL is a relational database that uses MVCC (Multi-Version Concurrency Control) — readers never block writers and vice versa. Each transaction sees a snapshot of the database. WAL (Write-Ahead Log) records changes before they're written to data files — crash recovery replays WAL. VACUUM reclaims space from dead tuples (old row versions). Connection pooling (PgBouncer) is essential for web apps — creating connections is expensive. Deep insight: PostgreSQL doesn't overwrite rows on UPDATE — it creates a new version and marks the old one as dead. This is why VACUUM is necessary.

28.1 Installing PostgreSQL

PostgreSQL Directory Structure — What Goes Where
  /etc/postgresql/15/main/          ← CONFIGURATION (what you edit)
  ├── postgresql.conf                ← Server settings: port, memory, SSL
  ├── pg_hba.conf                    ← Authentication: who can connect
  ├── pg_ident.conf                  ← User name mapping (rarely used)
  └── environment                    ← Environment variables for PostgreSQL

  /var/lib/postgresql/15/main/       ← DATA DIRECTORY (where your data lives)
  ├── base/                          ← Actual database files (one subdir per DB)
  │   ├── 1/                         ← Template database
  │   ├── 13765/                     ← anihpj_db (OID = 13765)
  │   │   ├── 12345                  ← jobpost_jobpost table file
  │   │   └── 12345_fsm              ← Free space map for that table
  │   └── ...
  ├── pg_wal/                        ← Write-Ahead Log (crash recovery)
  ├── pg_stat/                       ← Statistics (query planner uses this)
  ├── pg_logical/                    ← Logical replication data
  └── PG_VERSION                     ← File containing "15" (version marker)

  /usr/lib/postgresql/15/bin/        ← EXECUTABLES
  ├── postgres                       ← The database engine itself
  ├── pg_dump / pg_restore           ← Backup/restore tools
  ├── psql                           ← Interactive SQL client
  └── pg_ctl                         ← Start/stop/reload control

  /var/log/postgresql/               ← LOG FILES
  └── postgresql-15-main.log         ← Main log (errors, slow queries, connections)

  KEY INSIGHT: Config is in /etc/, data is in /var/lib/, binaries in /usr/lib/,
  logs in /var/log/.  Back up /var/lib/postgresql/15/main/ — that's your data.
  Never lose pg_wal/ — it's your crash recovery safety net.
Command / PathWhat It Is
apt install postgresql postgresql-contribInstall PostgreSQL + extra modules (pgcrypto, etc.)
/etc/postgresql/15/main/Config directory (15 = version number)
/var/lib/postgresql/15/main/Data directory (actual database files on disk)
systemctl status postgresqlCheck if PostgreSQL is running
sudo -u postgres psqlConnect as the postgres superuser
pg_lsclustersList all PostgreSQL clusters, versions, and status
🔬 The "postgres" User — Linux User vs Database Role

PostgreSQL creates a Linux system user called postgres during installation. This user has NO password (locked account) and NO login shell — you can only switch to it via sudo -u postgres. Inside PostgreSQL, there's also a database ROLE called postgres which is the superuser. When you run sudo -u postgres psql, you connect as the Linux postgres user, and PostgreSQL's "peer" authentication (in pg_hba.conf) automatically logs you in as the postgres database role. No password needed — this is the DEFAULT secure setup.

28.2 Configuration Files

The Two PostgreSQL Config Files — What Each Controls
  /etc/postgresql/15/main/
  ├── postgresql.conf      ← SERVER SETTINGS (how PostgreSQL runs)
  │   • listen_addresses = 'localhost'    # Only local connections (secure!)
  │   • port = 5432                       # Default PostgreSQL port
  │   • max_connections = 100             # Max simultaneous connections
  │   • shared_buffers = 128MB            # Memory for caching data
  │   • effective_cache_size = 4GB        # Hint for query planner
  │   • work_mem = 4MB                    # Memory per sort/hash operation
  │   • log_destination = 'stderr'        # Where to write logs
  │   • logging_collector = on            # Enable log file collection
  │   • log_directory = 'log'             # Log file location
  │
  └── pg_hba.conf          ← AUTHENTICATION (WHO can connect, and HOW)
      # TYPE  DATABASE    USER        ADDRESS          METHOD
      local   all         postgres                    peer
      local   all         all                         peer
      host    all         all         127.0.0.1/32    md5
      host    all         all         ::1/128         md5

      FORMAT:  type  database  user  address  auth_method

      type:     local (Unix socket) / host (TCP/IP) / hostssl (TLS only)
      database: all / specific_database_name
      user:     all / specific_user_name
      address:  CIDR for TCP connections (e.g., 192.168.1.0/24)
      method:   peer (OS user match) / md5 (password hash) / scram-sha-256
                trust (NO password — NEVER in production!)
SettingWhat It ControlsAnihpj Recommendation
listen_addressesWhich IPs PostgreSQL listens on'localhost' — only app server can connect
max_connectionsHow many simultaneous DB connections20-50 (Gunicorn workers × connection pool)
shared_buffersMemory for caching data pages25% of system RAM (e.g., 1GB on 4GB server)
sslEnable TLS for client connectionson if connecting over network

28.3 Creating the anihpj Database & User

🔧 Real-World: "Django Can't Connect to PostgreSQL" — Debugging Connection Refused

Situation: python manage.py migrate fails with "could not connect to server: Connection refused. Is the server running on host 'localhost' (127.0.0.1)?"

  1. Check PostgreSQL is running: systemctl status postgresql → active ✅
  2. Check listening interfaces: ss -tlnp | grep 5432 → NOTHING! PostgreSQL isn't listening!
  3. Check postgresql.conf: grep listen_addresses /etc/postgresql/15/main/postgresql.conf → listen_addresses = '' (EMPTY means no TCP, only Unix sockets!)
  4. Fix: sudo sed -i "s/listen_addresses = ''/listen_addresses = 'localhost'/" /etc/postgresql/15/main/postgresql.conf && sudo systemctl restart postgresql
  5. Check pg_hba.conf: Ensure there's a line: host anihpj_db anihpj_user 127.0.0.1/32 md5
  6. Test: PGPASSWORD='pass' psql -h localhost -U anihpj_user -d anihpj_db -c "SELECT 1" → 1. Fixed!

Key insight: Empty/blank listen_addresses = Unix sockets only (peer auth). 'localhost' = TCP on 127.0.0.1 + Unix sockets. Django needs TCP to connect via localhost.

Complete SQL Setup for Anihpj Database
  # Connect as PostgreSQL superuser
  sudo -u postgres psql

  -- 1. Create the database
  CREATE DATABASE anihpj_db;

  -- 2. Create the application user (what Django uses to connect)
  CREATE USER anihpj_user WITH PASSWORD 'generate-a-strong-random-password-here';

  -- 3. Grant all privileges on the database to our user
  GRANT ALL PRIVILEGES ON DATABASE anihpj_db TO anihpj_user;

  -- 4. Make our user the database owner (can create/drop tables)
  ALTER DATABASE anihpj_db OWNER TO anihpj_user;

  -- 5. Connect to the database and grant schema permissions
  \c anihpj_db
  GRANT ALL ON SCHEMA public TO anihpj_user;
  GRANT CREATE ON SCHEMA public TO anihpj_user;

  -- 6. Verify
  \l anihpj_db    -- list database details (owner should be anihpj_user)
  \du anihpj_user -- list user details

  -- 7. Test connection (from shell, not psql):
  PGPASSWORD='the-password' psql -h localhost -U anihpj_user -d anihpj_db -c "SELECT 1;"
  # Should return:  ?column?  |  1

  # IMPORTANT: Store the password in Django's .env file:
  # DATABASE_URL=postgres://anihpj_user:password@localhost:5432/anihpj_db
💡 The Golden Rule of Database Security

PostgreSQL should NEVER listen on a public IP address. Always listen_addresses = 'localhost'. If Django and PostgreSQL are on the same server (which they should be for most deployments), there's ZERO reason for PostgreSQL to accept network connections from anywhere but 127.0.0.1. If you need remote access: use an SSH tunnel (ssh -L 5432:localhost:5432 user@server), NEVER open port 5432 to the internet. Thousands of PostgreSQL instances are compromised daily because of this one misconfiguration.

⚠️ NEVER expose PostgreSQL to the internet!

listen_addresses should be 'localhost' for production. If Django and PostgreSQL are on the same server (which they should be for small-to-medium deployments), PostgreSQL should only listen on 127.0.0.1. External access opens you to brute-force attacks. If you need remote access, use an SSH tunnel: ssh -L 5432:localhost:5432 user@server.

28.4 Backup & Restore

CommandWhat It DoesOutput Format
pg_dump anihpj_db > backup.sqlFull database backup as SQL textPlain SQL (editable, human-readable)
pg_dump -Fc anihpj_db > backup.dumpCustom format (compressed, flexible)Binary (smaller, supports selective restore)
pg_dumpall > all_databases.sqlBackup ALL databases + rolesPlain SQL (global objects included)
psql anihpj_db < backup.sqlRestore from SQL dumpMust specify target database
pg_restore -d anihpj_db backup.dumpRestore from custom formatCan restore selective tables
pg_restore -l backup.dumpList contents of custom dumpSee what's inside before restoring
Automated Nightly Backup Script for Anihpj
  #!/bin/bash
  # /usr/local/bin/anihpj-backup.sh — Nightly PostgreSQL backup
  # Cron: 0 2 * * * /usr/local/bin/anihpj-backup.sh

  BACKUP_DIR="/backups/anihpj"
  DB_NAME="anihpj_db"
  RETENTION_DAYS=14   # Keep 2 weeks of daily backups
  TIMESTAMP=$(date +%Y%m%d_%H%M%S)

  mkdir -p "$BACKUP_DIR"

  # Create backup
  sudo -u postgres pg_dump -Fc "$DB_NAME" > "$BACKUP_DIR/${DB_NAME}_${TIMESTAMP}.dump"

  # Compress (custom format is already compressed, but SQL dumps benefit)
  # gzip "$BACKUP_DIR/${DB_NAME}_${TIMESTAMP}.sql"

  # Delete backups older than retention period
  find "$BACKUP_DIR" -name "*.dump" -mtime +$RETENTION_DAYS -delete

  # Optional: rsync to offsite location
  # rsync -av "$BACKUP_DIR/" backup-server:/backups/anihpj/

  echo "[$(date)] Backup complete: ${DB_NAME}_${TIMESTAMP}.dump"

28.5 Performance Basics

PostgreSQL Memory Architecture — How RAM Is Used
  ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │                    TOTAL SYSTEM RAM (4GB)                    │
  │                                                              │
  │  ┌──────────────────────────────────────┐                   │
  │  │  shared_buffers = 1GB (25%)          │ ← PG's own cache │
  │  │  ┌────┬────┬────┬────┬────┬────┐    │   Data pages     │
  │  │  │ 📄 │ 📄 │ 📄 │ 📄 │ 📄 │ 📄 │... │   read from disk  │
  │  │  └────┴────┴────┴────┴────┴────┘    │   cached here     │
  │  └──────────────────────────────────────┘                   │
  │                                                              │
  │  ┌──────────────────────────────────────┐                   │
  │  │  OS Page Cache ~2.5GB (the rest)     │ ← Linux caches   │
  │  │  (effective_cache_size = 3GB hint)   │   files in RAM.  │
  │  │  PostgreSQL reads through this —     │   "Double buffering"│
  │  │  data cached TWICE if not tuned!    │   is wasteful.    │
  │  └──────────────────────────────────────┘                   │
  │                                                              │
  │  ┌──────────┐  ┌──────────┐  ┌──────────┐                 │
  │  │work_mem  │  │work_mem  │  │work_mem  │  ← Per-operation │
  │  │ 16MB     │  │ 16MB     │  │ 16MB     │     NOT per-     │
  │  │ Sort Q1  │  │ Sort Q2  │  │ Hash Q3  │     connection!  │
  │  └──────────┘  └──────────┘  └──────────┘                 │
  │                                                              │
  │  ⚠️ 10 connections × 4 sorts each × 16MB = 640MB possible!  │
  │     total work_mem usage can spike dramatically.            │
  │                                                              │
  │  ┌──────────────────────┐                                   │
  │  │ maintenance_work_mem │  ← Used by VACUUM, CREATE INDEX  │
  │  │ 256MB                │     Only ONE operation at a time │
  │  └──────────────────────┘                                   │
  └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

  TUNING RULE OF THUMB:
  shared_buffers = 25% RAM (start here, max 8GB)
  effective_cache_size = 75% RAM (just a hint, not an allocation)
  work_mem = (RAM - shared_buffers) / (max_connections × 4)
  maintenance_work_mem = 10% RAM (but max 2GB)
ParameterWhat It DoesRecommended (4GB Server)
shared_buffersPostgreSQL's internal cache — the single most important setting1GB (25% of RAM)
effective_cache_sizeHint: how much OS cache is available (doesn't allocate, just estimates)3GB (75% of RAM)
work_memMemory per sort/hash operation PER QUERY (not per connection!)16MB (start conservative)
maintenance_work_memMemory for VACUUM, CREATE INDEX, ALTER TABLE256MB
random_page_costCost of random disk I/O (lower for SSDs!)1.1 (SSD) / 4.0 (HDD default)
autovacuumAutomatically reclaim dead rows and update statisticson (DEFAULT — never turn off!)
🔬 Why VACUUM Matters — PostgreSQL's Garbage Collector

PostgreSQL uses MVCC (Multi-Version Concurrency Control): when you UPDATE or DELETE a row, the OLD version stays on disk until VACUUM reclaims it. Without autovacuum: (1) tables bloat (dead rows accumulate), (2) queries slow down scanning dead rows, (3) transaction ID wraparound can SHUT DOWN the database. Check: SELECT relname, n_dead_tup FROM pg_stat_user_tables;. Run manual VACUUM: VACUUM ANALYZE anihpj_jobpost;. Never turn autovacuum off — just tune it if needed.

🔬 How MVCC Works — Why Readers Never Block Writers

PostgreSQL's secret sauce: every row has hidden columns xmin (transaction ID that CREATED this version) and xmax (transaction ID that DELETED/UPDATED this version). When you UPDATE a row: (1) PostgreSQL doesn't modify the existing row — it marks it with xmax = current transaction ID, (2) It inserts a NEW version of the row with xmin = current transaction ID, (3) Other transactions still see the OLD version (their snapshot only shows rows where xmin < their transaction start). Result: READERS never block WRITERS and WRITERS never block READERS. No read locks needed! The cost: old row versions accumulate. That's what VACUUM cleans up. This is fundamentally different from MySQL/InnoDB's undo-log approach. Concrete example: If you run a 1-hour analytics query on the jobs table, and simultaneously 50 users are posting new jobs or editing existing ones — both operations work concurrently without blocking each other. The analytics query sees a consistent snapshot from when it started. The new posts create new row versions invisible to the analytics query. All without a single lock.

🔬 WAL — Write-Ahead Log: PostgreSQL's Safety Net

Before PostgreSQL modifies ANY data file, it FIRST writes the change to the WAL (Write-Ahead Log) in pg_wal/. This is a sequential, append-only log of every database change. Why: If the server crashes mid-operation, on restart PostgreSQL replays the WAL — redoing any changes that were logged but not yet written to data files. This guarantees NO data loss from crashes (Durability in ACID). WAL also enables: (1) Point-in-Time Recovery (PITR) — replay WAL to any moment in time, (2) Streaming Replication — standby servers continuously apply the primary's WAL, (3) Logical Replication — decode WAL changes into SQL for selective replication. Monitoring: SELECT pg_current_wal_lsn(); shows current WAL position. pg_waldump reads WAL files for debugging. The WAL is why PostgreSQL can survive a power outage without data corruption — it's the ultimate safety net.

Q4
What's the difference between postgresql.conf and pg_hba.conf?
Click to reveal answer
✅ Answer

postgresql.conf controls HOW PostgreSQL runs: port, memory (shared_buffers, work_mem), max connections, logging, SSL. pg_hba.conf controls WHO can connect and HOW they authenticate: which users, from which IPs, using which auth method (peer, md5, scram-sha-256). Think of postgresql.conf as engine settings and pg_hba.conf as the security guard at the door.

Q6
What authentication method does PostgreSQL use when you run "sudo -u postgres psql"? Why no password?
Click to reveal answer
✅ Answer

It uses peer authentication (the default for local connections in pg_hba.conf). Peer auth checks: "Is the Linux username the SAME as the PostgreSQL role name?" Since you're running as Linux user postgres (via sudo), and there's a PostgreSQL role called postgres, the names match → access granted with NO password. This is secure because only root (via sudo) can become the postgres Linux user.

How do you check which queries are currently running on PostgreSQL? What about slow queries?
Click to reveal answer
✅ Answer
-- Active queries:
SELECT pid, now() - query_start AS duration, query, state
FROM pg_stat_activity
WHERE state != 'idle'
ORDER BY duration DESC;

-- Kill a runaway query:
SELECT pg_terminate_backend(pid);

-- Enable slow query logging (postgresql.conf):
log_min_duration_statement = 1000   -- log queries > 1 second

Q9
What is autovacuum and why must it never be disabled in production?
Click to reveal answer
✅ Answer

autovacuum is PostgreSQL's automatic garbage collector. It: (1) Reclaims dead rows from UPDATE/DELETE (prevents table bloat), (2) Updates query planner statistics (so queries use optimal plans), (3) Prevents transaction ID wraparound (which would FORCE a database shutdown). Disabling autovacuum leads to: slow queries, bloated tables, and eventually a database that refuses to start. Check it's running: SELECT name, setting FROM pg_settings WHERE name LIKE '%vacuum%';

Chapter 29: Email, Time Services & FTP

Beyond the core web stack, every anihpj server needs accurate time (for SSL certs, log correlation, and cron jobs), email delivery (for password resets and notifications), and optionally file transfer. This chapter covers Chrony (NTP time sync), Postfix (mail transfer agent basics), and vsftpd (FTP server — though SFTP is preferred).

🔴 Advanced⏱️ ~1 hour📧 Services

🎯 What You'll Learn

  • ✅ Synchronize system time with Chrony/NTP
  • ✅ Configure Postfix for sending email notifications
  • ✅ Set up vsftpd (and understand why SFTP is better)
🧠 Core Understanding — Chapter 29

Accurate time is critical for logs, SSL certificates, and distributed systems. NTP synchronizes clocks over the network with millisecond precision. Chrony is the modern NTP implementation — faster sync, better on VMs and intermittent connections. timedatectl shows/sets timezone and NTP status. Postfix is a mail transfer agent — it delivers system emails (cron output, alerts) and can relay to external SMTP servers. Even if you don't run a mail server, the system needs to send administrative emails.

29.1 Chrony & NTP — Time Synchronization

CommandWhat It DoesExample Output
timedatectlView timezone, NTP status, system clockTime zone: Africa/Lagos (WAT, +0100)
timedatectl list-timezonesList all available timezonesgrep for your city: | grep Lagos
timedatectl set-timezone Africa/LagosSet system timezone permanentlyAffects all users and services
timedatectl set-ntp trueEnable automatic time sync via NTPUses systemd-timesyncd or chrony
chronyc trackingDetailed Chrony sync statusShows offset, drift, last update
chronyc sources -vList NTP servers and their status^* = currently synced source
🔬 Why Accurate Time is CRITICAL for Anihpj

(1) SSL/TLS certificates: Browsers reject certs if system clock is wrong — users see scary warnings. (2) Log correlation: When debugging, you need logs from Nginx, Gunicorn, and PostgreSQL to agree on timestamps. (3) Cron jobs: Nightly backup at 2 AM must actually run at 2 AM. (4) Database replication: PostgreSQL streaming replication requires synchronized clocks. (5) Authentication: TOTP 2FA and Kerberos require time within ~30 seconds. Install chrony: apt install chrony. Config: /etc/chrony/chrony.conf — pool entries like pool 2.ubuntu.pool.ntp.org iburst.

🔬 NTP Stratum Levels — The Hierarchy of Time

NTP organizes time sources into a hierarchy: Stratum 0: Atomic clocks, GPS receivers — the ABSOLUTE reference (you can't connect to these directly). Stratum 1: Servers directly connected to stratum 0 hardware (few hundred exist globally). Stratum 2: Servers synced to stratum 1 (these are what most organizations use — like pool.ntp.org). Stratum 3+: Servers synced to stratum 2, and so on. Each level adds microseconds of drift. Your anihpj server is probably stratum 3 or 4. Why it matters: chrony selects the BEST source among configured servers — lower stratum, lower jitter, lower delay. chronyc sources -v shows stratum for each source. The ^* marker indicates the currently selected best source. Best practice: Use at least 4 NTP servers from the pool — chrony will detect and reject outliers ("falsetickers").

29.2 Postfix — Basic Mail Transfer Agent

Command / PathWhat It Does
apt install postfix mailutilsInstall Postfix + mail command
/etc/postfix/main.cfMain Postfix configuration
postconf -e "myhostname = anihpj.com"Set config value from command line
postfix reloadApply config changes
echo "Test body" | mail -s "Test Subject" admin@anihpj.comSend a test email
mailqView mail queue (undelivered messages)
Postfix Config for Anihpj — Send-Only (Relay via External SMTP)
  # /etc/postfix/main.cf — Send-only configuration for anihpj
  # Purpose: Send password reset emails, notifications, error alerts

  myhostname = anihpj.com
  myorigin = /etc/mailname          # Domain emails appear to come from
  inet_interfaces = loopback-only   # Only listen on localhost (not a public mail server!)

  # Relay all outbound mail through your email provider
  relayhost = [smtp.gmail.com]:587

  # SASL authentication for the relay
  smtp_sasl_auth_enable = yes
  smtp_sasl_password_maps = hash:/etc/postfix/sasl_passwd
  smtp_sasl_security_options = noanonymous
  smtp_tls_security_level = encrypt
  smtp_use_tls = yes

  # /etc/postfix/sasl_passwd (chmod 600!):
  # [smtp.gmail.com]:587    anihpj@gmail.com:app-specific-password
  # Then: sudo postmap /etc/postfix/sasl_passwd

  # Test:
  echo "Anihpj backup completed successfully" | mail -s "Daily Backup Report" admin@anihpj.com
Mail Flow Diagram — How Anihpj Sends a Password Reset Email
  ┌────────────────────┐
  │  Django (anihpj)    │
  │  User clicks        │
  │  "Forgot Password"  │
  └────────┬───────────┘
           │ ① Django calls send_mail()
           ▼
  ┌────────────────────┐
  │  Postfix (localhost)│  ← MTA (Mail Transfer Agent)
  │  Accepts email      │
  │  Queues for delivery│
  └────────┬───────────┘
           │ ② Postfix authenticates
           │    with SASL (smtp_sasl)
           ▼
  ┌────────────────────┐
  │  Gmail SMTP Relay   │  ← Upstream MTA
  │  smtp.gmail.com:587│
  │  (App Password auth)│
  └────────┬───────────┘
           │ ③ DNS MX lookup:
           │    recipient@company.com
           │    → MX: mail.company.com
           ▼
  ┌────────────────────┐
  │  Recipient's MTA    │
  │  mail.company.com   │
  │  (e.g., Office 365, │
  │   Gmail, Exchange)  │
  └────────┬───────────┘
           │ ④ Deliver to mailbox
           ▼
  ┌────────────────────┐
  │  Recipient's Inbox  │
  │  "Anihpj Password   │
  │   Reset Link"       │
  └────────────────────┘

  IMPORTANT CONCEPTS:
  MUA (Mail User Agent)  = Thunderbird, Outlook, Gmail web — what user sees
  MTA (Mail Transfer)    = Postfix, Sendmail — routes mail between servers
  MDA (Mail Delivery)    = Dovecot, procmail — puts mail in user's mailbox
  SMTP (Simple Mail)     = The protocol MTAs speak to each other (port 25/587)
🔬 How Email Actually Travels — SMTP Protocol Flow

When your Django app sends a password reset email: (1) Django connects to Postfix on localhost:25, (2) Postfix accepts the email and queues it, (3) Postfix connects to the relay (smtp.gmail.com:587), authenticates, and forwards, (4) Gmail's servers look up the MX record of the recipient's domain, (5) Gmail delivers to the recipient's mail server. Key terms: MUA (Mail User Agent — Thunderbird, Gmail web), MTA (Mail Transfer Agent — Postfix, Sendmail, Gmail's servers), MDA (Mail Delivery Agent — dovecot, places mail in user's mailbox). Postfix can be: (a) a full mail server (receives AND sends), (b) a relay (sends only, like anihpj), (c) a smarthost (forwards everything to one upstream). Anihpj uses relay mode — sends notifications but doesn't receive email. Check logs: tail -f /var/log/mail.log shows the full SMTP conversation including delivery status. SPF/DKIM/DMARC: If your emails go to spam, you need these DNS records to prove your server is authorized to send from @anihpj.com.

29.3 vsftpd — FTP Server Basics

🔴 FTP (vsftpd) — Plaintext Legacy

Username and password sent in CLEAR TEXT. Anyone on the network (WiFi, ISP, VPN) can sniff credentials. Separate port range for data (passive mode nightmare with firewalls). No encryption whatsoever.

🟢 SFTP (SSH-based) — Encrypted Modern

Runs over SSH port 22. Same encryption as your SSH connection. Same keys, same authentication. No additional daemon. Firewall-friendly (single port). Supported by every FTP client since 2005.

DirectiveRecommendedWhy
anonymous_enableNONever allow anonymous uploads
local_enableYESAllow local user accounts to login
write_enableYESAllow file uploads (if needed)
chroot_local_userYESJail users to their home directory
Active vs Passive FTP — The Firewall Nightmare Explained
  ACTIVE FTP (the OLD way — firewall unfriendly)
  ┌──────────┐                    ┌──────────┐
  │ CLIENT   │                    │ SERVER   │
  │ Port 21──┼───────────────────▶│ Port 21  │ ← Control (commands)
  │           │                    │          │
  │ Port 20◀─┼────────────────────│ Port 20  │ ← DATA (server connects BACK!)
  └──────────┘                    └──────────┘
  ⚠️  PROBLEM: Server initiates connection TO client.
      Client firewalls BLOCK this! NAT breaks it!

  PASSIVE FTP (the NEW way — firewall friendly)
  ┌──────────┐                    ┌──────────┐
  │ CLIENT   │                    │ SERVER   │
  │ Port 21──┼───────────────────▶│ Port 21  │ ← Control (commands)
  │           │  "Enter Passive"    │          │
  │ Port ? ──┼───────────────────▶│ Port 30xx│ ← DATA (client connects out)
  └──────────┘                    └──────────┘
  ✅ Client initiates BOTH connections → firewalls allow outgoing traffic

  🎯 SFTP (SSH-based, port 22) eliminates this ENTIRE problem:
      ONE port, ONE connection, FULL encryption. No active/passive drama.
⚠️ Use SFTP, Not FTP!

FTP sends usernames and passwords in plaintext over the network. Anyone on the same network can sniff credentials. SFTP (SSH File Transfer Protocol) encrypts everything and uses the same SSH key infrastructure you already have. It runs over port 22 — no additional daemon needed. Modern tools (FileZilla, WinSCP, scp, rsync) all support SFTP. sftp user@anihpj-server is the secure alternative. vsftpd is included on the LFCS exam, but in real production, always use SFTP.

🔬 /etc/aliases — Redirect System Mail to Real Addresses

Linux system daemons (cron, at, sudo) send mail to the local root user for errors and reports. Since you (hopefully) never log in as root, these messages pile up unseen. /etc/aliases lets you redirect them: root: admin@anihpj.com. After editing, run sudo newaliases to update the alias database. Other useful aliases: postmaster: root (RFC requirement), www-data: /dev/null (discard web server mail). Test: echo "test" | mail -s "Alias Test" root → should arrive at admin@anihpj.com.

✅ Answer

1. SSL/TLS certificates — browsers reject certs if clock is wrong (invalid date errors). 2. Log correlation — debugging requires matching timestamps across Nginx, Gunicorn, PostgreSQL logs. 3. Cron jobs — nightly backups at 2 AM must run at the correct time. Also: database replication, 2FA (TOTP requires ±30 sec accuracy), and Kerberos authentication.

📖 Explanation

Cron is the original Unix task scheduler. Five time fields define when a job runs. Cron's minimal environment (no .bashrc, stripped PATH) is the #1 reason scripts fail in cron but work interactively. ✅ is the key tool here. Q7
Why is SFTP preferred over FTP for production file transfers?
Click to reveal answer
✅ Answer

FTP sends credentials (username + password) in PLAINTEXT — anyone on the network can sniff them. SFTP runs over SSH, which encrypts ALL traffic including authentication. SFTP uses the same SSH keys you already manage. No additional daemon, no additional port, no additional attack surface. FTP should only be used for legacy systems that don't support SFTP.

📖 Explanation

sed is a stream editor: it reads one line, applies your transformation, prints the result, and moves to the next. This streaming design means it never needs to hold the entire file in memory. ✅ is the key tool here. Its man page (man ✅) is available during the exam if you need to check less common options. Verify by viewing the file after editing: cat file or head -20 file. If you used -i, check the file wasn't corrupted. Flag hard tasks and return later. Q9
What's the difference between chronyd and systemd-timesyncd? Which should anihpj use?
Click to reveal answer
✅ Answer

systemd-timesyncd is a minimal SNTP client — it only queries time, doesn't adjust clock gradually (can cause jumps). Good for desktop/laptop. chronyd is a full NTP implementation — it slews the clock gradually (no jumps), supports multiple servers with error detection, and handles intermittent networks. Anihpj should use chrony for production. Install: apt install chrony. It automatically disables systemd-timesyncd.

📖 Explanation

Package managers solve dependency hell — they calculate which packages you need, download them, and install them in the correct order. Always use the package manager rather than compiling from source for system stability. apt is the key tool here. Its man page (man apt) is available during the exam if you need to check less common options. The exam is distribution-neutral. This command works on both Ubuntu and Rocky — know which package manager to use for installation.

Chapter 30: Anihpj in Production — The Complete Stack

This is where everything comes together. All the services you've learned — SSH, Nginx, Gunicorn, PostgreSQL, systemd, firewalls, logging — combine into a single, secure, production-ready anihpj deployment. This chapter provides the complete architecture diagram and a step-by-step deployment checklist you can follow to build a real server from scratch.

🔴 Advanced⏱️ ~1 hour🚀 Production

🎯 What You'll Learn

  • ✅ Understand the complete anihpj production architecture
  • ✅ Follow a 13-step deployment checklist to build a server from scratch
🧠 Core Understanding — Chapter 30

Deploying anihpj combines every LFCS skill: SSH (remote access), Nginx (web server), PostgreSQL (database), Gunicorn (application server), systemd (service management), UFW (firewall), logrotate (log management), and cron (scheduling). The architecture: Browser → Nginx:443 → proxy_pass → Gunicorn:8000 → Django → PostgreSQL:5432. Each component runs as a non-root user with minimal permissions. SSL termination happens at Nginx — Gunicorn only talks to localhost. This is the standard production pattern for Python web applications.

30.2 Step-by-Step Production Deployment Checklist

13 Steps to a Production Anihpj Server
  ☐ 1. OS INSTALL
     Ubuntu 22.04 LTS. Set hostname, timezone (Africa/Lagos),
     create admin user with sudo. apt update && apt upgrade -y.

  ☐ 2. SECURITY BASICS
     ufw allow 22/tcp && ufw allow 80/tcp && ufw allow 443/tcp && ufw enable
     sshd_config: PermitRootLogin no, PasswordAuthentication no
     Install fail2ban: apt install fail2ban

  ☐ 3. CREATE ANIHPJ SERVICE USER
     sudo useradd -r -s /usr/sbin/nologin -d /var/www/anihpj anihpj
     # -r = system account, -s = no login shell, -d = home directory

  ☐ 4. INSTALL PYTHON & VENV
     apt install python3 python3-venv python3-pip
     python3 -m venv /var/www/anihpj/venv
     source /var/www/anihpj/venv/bin/activate
     pip install django gunicorn psycopg2-binary

  ☐ 5. CONFIGURE POSTGRESQL
     apt install postgresql postgresql-contrib
     sudo -u postgres psql
       CREATE DATABASE anihpj_db;
       CREATE USER anihpj_user WITH PASSWORD 'STRONG_RANDOM_PASSWORD';
       GRANT ALL PRIVILEGES ON DATABASE anihpj_db TO anihpj_user;
       ALTER DATABASE anihpj_db OWNER TO anihpj_user;

  ☐ 6. SET ENVIRONMENT VARIABLES
     nano /var/www/anihpj/.env  (chmod 600!)
       DEBUG=False
       SECRET_KEY=django-insecure-GENERATE_RANDOM_50_CHARS
       DATABASE_URL=postgres://anihpj_user:PASS@localhost:5432/anihpj_db
       ALLOWED_HOSTS=anihpj.com,www.anihpj.com

  ☐ 7. DEPLOY DJANGO CODE
     cd /var/www/anihpj/
     source venv/bin/activate
     python manage.py migrate
     python manage.py collectstatic --noinput
     python manage.py createsuperuser

  ☐ 8. CREATE GUNICORN SYSTEMD SERVICE
     nano /etc/systemd/system/anihpj.service
       [Unit] Description=Anihpj Gunicorn / After=network.target postgresql.service
       [Service] User=anihpj / Group=www-data
       WorkingDirectory=/var/www/anihpj
       ExecStart=/var/www/anihpj/venv/bin/gunicorn anihpj.wsgi:application \
         --workers 3 --bind unix:/run/anihpj/anihpj.sock
       Restart=on-failure / RestartSec=5s
       [Install] WantedBy=multi-user.target
     systemctl daemon-reload && systemctl enable --now anihpj

  ☐ 9. INSTALL & CONFIGURE NGINX
     apt install nginx
     Create /etc/nginx/sites-available/anihpj (see Ch 27.3)
     ln -s /etc/nginx/sites-available/anihpj /etc/nginx/sites-enabled/
     rm /etc/nginx/sites-enabled/default
     nginx -t && systemctl reload nginx

  ☐ 10. GET SSL CERTIFICATE
     apt install certbot python3-certbot-nginx
     certbot --nginx -d anihpj.com -d www.anihpj.com

  ☐ 11. SETUP NIGHTLY BACKUPS
     Create /usr/local/bin/anihpj-backup.sh (see Ch 28.4)
     sudo crontab -e: 0 2 * * * /usr/local/bin/anihpj-backup.sh

  ☐ 12. VERIFY EVERYTHING
     systemctl status nginx postgresql anihpj
     curl -I https://anihpj.com  → HTTP/2 200
     sudo -u postgres psql -c "SELECT 1"  → 1
     journalctl -u anihpj --no-pager | tail -20

  ☐ 13. ENABLE ALL SERVICES ON BOOT
     systemctl enable nginx postgresql anihpj fail2ban chrony
     reboot (test that everything comes back automatically)
🔧 Pro Tip: Build a "Golden Image"

After completing this checklist ONCE, take a snapshot/image of your VM. For your NEXT project (another Django app, a staging server, a client deployment), clone the image and skip steps 1-5. Docker takes this concept even further — the Dockerfile encodes ALL these steps as code (see Appendix H for Docker fundamentals).

🔬 Production Monitoring — Is Anihpj Actually Working?

Deploying is step 1. Knowing it STAYS working is the real challenge. What to monitor: (1) Uptime — curl -o /dev/null -s -w '%{http_code}' https://anihpj.com should return 200. Cron this every minute. (2) Disk space — df -h / /var/lib/postgresql /var/www/anihpj/media. Alert at 80%. (3) PostgreSQL — SELECT count(*), now() - MAX(created_at) AS latest_post FROM jobpost_jobpost;. If latest post is >1 hour old during business hours, something's wrong. (4) SSL expiry — certbot certificates or echo | openssl s_client -connect anihpj.com:443 2>/dev/null | openssl x509 -noout -enddate. (5) System load — uptime / top -bn1 | head. Tools evolution: cron + mail (LFCS level) → Monit/Nagios → Prometheus + Grafana → Datadog/New Relic. Start with cron alerts — they're free and you already know how to set them up.

🔬 Rate Limiting with Nginx — Protect Anihpj from Abuse

A single malicious user can overwhelm your job board with thousands of requests. Nginx rate limiting protects you: limit_req_zone $binary_remote_addr zone=anihpj:10m rate=10r/s; in the http block creates a shared memory zone tracking requests per IP. Then limit_req zone=anihpj burst=20 nodelay; in the location block allows 10 req/sec with a burst of 20. Beyond that: HTTP 429 "Too Many Requests." Why it matters: Without rate limiting, a simple script can scrape all your job listings, overload the database with fake applications, or brute-force login forms. Rate limiting is your first line of defense — before fail2ban, before WAF, before anything else. It's configured in Nginx with 3 lines.

🚀 Complete Bash Deployment Script — One Command to Production
  #!/bin/bash
  # deploy-anihpj.sh — Complete production deployment
  # Usage: sudo bash deploy-anihpj.sh
  set -e  # Exit on any error

  echo "=== Step 1: System Update ==="
  apt update && apt upgrade -y
  timedatectl set-timezone Africa/Lagos
  hostnamectl set-hostname anihpj-prod

  echo "=== Step 2: Create Service User ==="
  useradd -r -s /usr/sbin/nologin -d /var/www/anihpj anihpj

  echo "=== Step 3: Install Packages ==="
  apt install -y python3 python3-venv python3-pip nginx postgresql postgresql-contrib certbot python3-certbot-nginx fail2ban chrony

  echo "=== Step 4: Setup PostgreSQL ==="
  systemctl enable --now postgresql
  sudo -u postgres psql < /etc/systemd/system/anihpj.service <

Q4
Why does the anihpj system user have /usr/sbin/nologin as its shell? What's the security benefit?
Click to reveal answer
✅ Answer

Setting the shell to /usr/sbin/nologin prevents ANYONE from logging in as the anihpj user via SSH or console. Even if someone steals the anihpj user's password (which it doesn't have — it's locked), they can't get a shell. This implements least privilege: the service account can run Gunicorn (via systemd) but can never be used for interactive login. Service accounts should NEVER have real shells.

📖 Explanation

This Production Stack task mirrors real production scenarios. The LFCS exam is 100% hands-on performance-based — knowing the command is only half the battle; you must execute it correctly under time pressure. /usr/sbin/nologin is the key tool here. Its man page (man /usr/sbin/nologin) is available during the exam if you need to check less common options. Reboot once before submitting (last 5 minutes). This catches non-persistent configs and broken fstab entries before the grader sees them.

What's the purpose of "collectstatic" in Django deployment? Where do the files end up?
Click to reveal answer
✅ Answer
python manage.py collectstatic --noinput
# Collectstatic gathers ALL static files (CSS, JS, images) from
# all Django apps and STATICFILES_DIRS into STATIC_ROOT
# (e.g., /var/www/anihpj/staticfiles/).
# Nginx then serves these files DIRECTLY (not through Django/Gunicorn),
# which is MUCH faster — no Python overhead for static assets.
📖 Explanation

Every running program is a process with a PID. The kernel schedules processes using the Completely Fair Scheduler (CFS). Signals (TERM, KILL, HUP) control process lifecycle — SIGTERM asks politely, SIGKILL forces termination. The flags --noinput control how this command behaves. Understanding what each flag does — not just memorizing the combination — lets you adapt when the exam presents a variation. The exam is distribution-neutral. This command works on both Ubuntu and Rocky — know which package manager to use for installation.

📖 Explanation

systemd manages every service on modern Linux. systemctl start activates a unit now; systemctl enable creates the symlink for auto-start at boot. You need both for a persistent service. The flags -active control how this command behaves. Understanding what each flag does — not just memorizing the combination — lets you adapt when the exam presents a variation. Verify with systemctl status unit-name. Look for "Active: active (running)" and check the PID. If it failed, journalctl -xeu unit-name shows why. Practice this in your lab VM until you can type it from memory. The 2-hour timer is unforgiving if you're looking up every command.

Q7
Why is the .env file permission set to 600? What's inside it that needs protection?
Click to reveal answer
✅ Answer

chmod 600 .env ensures ONLY the owner (anihpj) can read the file. It contains SECRETS: Django SECRET_KEY (used for cryptographic signing — if leaked, attackers can forge sessions), DATABASE_URL with the PostgreSQL password, API keys, and email credentials. Anyone who can read .env can steal the database password. 600 = owner read/write only — no group, no others.

📖 Explanation

Linux permissions are the first line of defense. Every file access is checked against the owner-group-others permission bits. ACLs extend this model, letting you grant specific users specific permissions beyond the basic rwx scheme. chmod is the key tool here. Its man page (man chmod) is available during the exam if you need to check less common options. Practice this in your lab VM until you can type it from memory. The 2-hour timer is unforgiving if you're looking up every command.

Q8
What's the minimum UFW firewall rules needed for anihpj production? Write the commands.
Click to reveal answer
✅ Answer
sudo ufw default deny incoming
sudo ufw default allow outgoing
sudo ufw allow 22/tcp    # SSH
sudo ufw allow 80/tcp    # HTTP (redirects to HTTPS)
sudo ufw allow 443/tcp   # HTTPS
sudo ufw enable
sudo ufw status verbose   # verify
📖 Explanation

Firewall rules process from top to bottom — the first match wins. Rules are evaluated in the kernel's netfilter framework for every packet. Unprotected, a Linux server on the public internet will be scanned within minutes. sudo is the key tool here. Its man page (man sudo) is available during the exam if you need to check less common options. Verify by connecting: ssh user@host. Use ssh -v for verbose debugging. Check /var/log/auth.log for authentication failures. Flag hard tasks and return later. Spending 15 minutes on one task guarantees you'll run out of time for 3-4 easier ones.

Q9
What does the Nginx "proxy_set_header X-Forwarded-For" do? Why does Django need it?
Click to reveal answer
✅ Answer

When Nginx proxies a request to Gunicorn, Gunicorn sees the connection coming from localhost (127.0.0.1) — it doesn't know the REAL client IP. proxy_set_header X-Forwarded-For $proxy_add_x_forwarded_for passes the original client IP in a header. Django reads this header to: log real IPs in access logs, apply IP-based rate limiting, and show accurate IPs in the admin panel. Without it, all requests appear to come from 127.0.0.1.

📖 Explanation

This Production Stack task mirrors real production scenarios. The LFCS exam is 100% hands-on performance-based — knowing the command is only half the battle; you must execute it correctly under time pressure. The flags -Forwarded, -For control how this command behaves. Understanding what each flag does — not just memorizing the combination — lets you adapt when the exam presents a variation. The exam is distribution-neutral. This command works on both Ubuntu and Rocky — know which package manager to use for installation.

Chapter 31: SELinux & AppArmor — Mandatory Access Control

Standard Linux permissions (DAC) let the file owner decide who accesses it. But what if a hacker compromises your anihpj web app and runs code as the www-data user? DAC can't stop them from reading everything www-data can read. Mandatory Access Control (MAC) adds a second, system-enforced security layer that even root can't bypass. This chapter covers both MAC systems tested on the LFCS: SELinux (Rocky/RHEL) and AppArmor (Ubuntu).

Security 10%
🎯 MAC on the LFCS Exam

The LFCS exam gives you BOTH an Ubuntu VM and a Rocky VM. On Ubuntu: use AppArmor commands. On Rocky: use SELinux commands. The #1 exam scenario: "Service X can't access files" — check the MAC system FIRST before debugging permissions. Know how to temporarily disable (for testing) and re-enable.

31.1 DAC vs MAC — Why Linux Permissions Aren't Enough

🔴 DAC — Discretionary Access Control

Owner decides who accesses. rwx bits + owner/group. The PROBLEM: if a process runs as user "anihpj", it has ALL of anihpj's permissions. A compromised Django app can read .env, SSH keys, everything anihpj owns.

🟢 MAC — Mandatory Access Control

System enforces policy BEYOND rwx. Even if you're root, the MAC policy can block you. A compromised nginx process can only access files labeled httpd_sys_content_t — your .env and SSH keys are off-limits.

🔬 Analogy: DAC vs MAC

DAC = Apartment key. If you have the key (correct rwx permissions), you can enter any room. MAC = Security guard with a clipboard. Even if you have the key, the guard checks your ID against the list. If you're not on the list for that room, you don't enter — even if you're the building owner (root). SELinux/AppArmor is that security guard. Every process and file gets a label, and the kernel enforces which labels can interact.

🔬 Where MAC Fits in the Linux Kernel — The LSM Hook Architecture

Linux doesn't have SELinux or AppArmor hardcoded into it. Instead, the kernel has LSM (Linux Security Modules) — a framework of hook points placed at every security-critical code path. When a process tries to open a file, the kernel: (1) Checks DAC (rwx permissions) — if denied, stop here. (2) Calls EVERY loaded LSM hook — SELinux, AppArmor, Yama, etc. — each can independently DENY the action. (3) If ALL hooks pass AND DAC passed, access is GRANTED. This is critical: DAC is checked FIRST, then LSMs. If DAC denies access, LSMs are never consulted. If DAC allows but an LSM denies, the action is blocked. This means MAC can only RESTRICT what DAC allows — it can never GRANT access that DAC denies. You can have both SELinux AND AppArmor loaded simultaneously (though rarely done — Ubuntu uses AppArmor, Rocky uses SELinux). Other LSMs: Yama (ptrace restrictions), Lockdown (kernel integrity), BPF (eBPF-based MAC). The LSM framework is why you never need to "choose" between SELinux and AppArmor at the kernel level — they're pluggable modules.

1
Service Fails with "Permission Denied"

Your web app or daemon can't access a file even though ls -l shows correct rwx permissions. First clue that MAC is blocking.

2
Check the MAC System

Ubuntu: sudo dmesg | grep apparmor. Rocky: sudo ausearch -m avc -ts recent. Look for "DENIED" entries with the process name.

3
Fix the Policy (Not Disable It)

Ubuntu: Edit AppArmor profile or aa-complain for testing. Rocky: restorecon -Rv /path/ or semanage fcontext. NEVER permanently disable MAC!

31.2 SELinux — Security-Enhanced Linux (Rocky/RHEL)

CommandWhat It Does
getenforceShow current mode: Enforcing / Permissive / Disabled
setenforce 0Temporarily switch to Permissive (log but don't block)
/etc/selinux/configPersistent SELinux mode setting
ls -Z /var/www/anihpj/Show SELinux context (user:role:type:level)
ps -ZShow SELinux context of running processes
restorecon -Rv /var/www/anihpj/Restore default file contexts (fixes most SELinux issues!)
semanage fcontext -a -t httpd_sys_content_t "/var/www/anihpj(/.*)?"Set persistent file context for a directory
ausearch -m avc -ts recentSearch audit log for recent SELinux denials
ausearch -c nginxSearch denials for a specific command (quick filter)
sealert -l \*Show human-readable explanations for all recent denials
audit2allow -a -M anihpj_policyGenerate SELinux policy from denial logs
🔬 SELinux Booleans — Toggle Features Without Rewriting Policy

SELinux booleans are on/off switches that modify policy behavior WITHOUT creating custom policies. getsebool -a lists all booleans. getsebool httpd_can_network_connect checks one. setsebool -P httpd_can_network_connect on enables it permanently (-P = persistent across reboots). Common booleans for web servers: httpd_can_network_connect (allow nginx/apache to make outbound connections — needed for reverse proxy), httpd_can_sendmail (allow web app to send email), httpd_enable_cgi (allow CGI scripts). Anihpj use case: If Django needs to connect to an external API (e.g., payment gateway), and SELinux blocks it: sudo setsebool -P httpd_can_network_connect on. This is safer than disabling SELinux entirely!

🔬 SELinux MCS and MLS — Multi-Level Security for Containers and Classified Systems

The :s0 at the end of SELinux contexts is the sensitivity level. MCS (Multi-Category Security): Adds categories like :s0:c0,c1. Two processes can only interact if they share ALL categories. This is how OpenShift and virtlib isolate containers/VMs — each container gets a unique random category pair (s0:c123,c456) that no other container has. Even if a container process somehow escapes to the host, it can't access other containers' files because the categories don't match. MLS (Multi-Level Security): Used by military/intelligence. Levels like s0 (unclassified), s1 (confidential), s2 (secret), s3 (top secret). Bell-LaPadula model: "no read up, no write down" — a Secret process can read Confidential but can't read Top Secret. You will NOT encounter MLS on the LFCS exam, but MCS is used extensively by container platforms. To see MCS in action: ls -Z /var/lib/docker/ on a system with SELinux enabled — every container layer has unique MCS categories.

🔬 How SELinux Type Enforcement Actually Works — The TE Model

SELinux uses Type Enforcement (TE) — the majority of SELinux policy. Every process has a domain (a type ending in _t, like httpd_t). Every file has a type (like httpd_sys_content_t). The policy contains ALLOW rules: "Processes in domain httpd_t MAY read files of type httpd_sys_content_t." If there's no explicit ALLOW rule, access is DENIED — even if rwx permissions say yes. How contexts are assigned: (1) Inheritance: New files inherit the context of their parent directory. (2) Transition rules: When a process exec()s another program, SELinux can transition to a NEW domain (e.g., init_t → httpd_t when starting nginx). (3) Default rules: File contexts stored in /etc/selinux/targeted/contexts/files/file_contexts — restorecon applies these. The context string system_u:object_r:httpd_sys_content_t:s0 breaks down as: user (system_u) : role (object_r) : type (httpd_sys_content_t) : level (s0). The TYPE is what matters for TE — the user and role are mostly for RBAC which is rarely used in targeted policy. For LFCS: Focus on types — they're 95% of what you'll encounter in denials and fixes.

🔬 Targeted vs Strict vs MLS — Which SELinux Policy Are You Running?

SELinux has three policy types. Targeted (default on RHEL/Rocky): Only specific "targeted" processes are confined — everything else runs in unconfined_t (unrestricted). Targeted processes include: httpd_t, mysqld_t, sshd_t, named_t. Strict: EVERY process is confined by policy. Much harder to configure — rarely used outside military/defense. MLS (Multi-Level Security): Bell-LaPadula model — data has classification levels (Top Secret, Secret, Confidential). Processes can only read DOWN and write UP. Used by intelligence agencies. Check yours: sestatus | grep "Loaded policy" → shows targeted. The LFCS exam uses targeted policy — you need to manage confined services, not create policy from scratch. If a service isn't working, check: (1) Is SELinux enforcing? (2) Are file contexts correct? (3) Is there a boolean that needs enabling? In that order.

🔧 Real-World: "SELinux Is Blocking Nginx from Serving Anihpj"

Situation: You deployed anihpj code to /var/www/anihpj. Nginx returns 403 Forbidden for all requests.

  1. Check SELinux: getenforce → Enforcing. ausearch -m avc -ts recent | grep nginx → "denied { read } for pid=1234 comm="nginx" name="index.html" dev="sda1" ino=45678 scontext=system_u:system_r:httpd_t:s0 tcontext=unconfined_u:object_r:default_t:s0"
  2. Diagnosis: Files have context default_t (wrong!). Nginx needs httpd_sys_content_t.
  3. Fix: sudo semanage fcontext -a -t httpd_sys_content_t "/var/www/anihpj(/.*)?" && sudo restorecon -Rv /var/www/anihpj/
  4. Verify: ls -Z /var/www/anihpj/ → httpd_sys_content_t. Nginx now serves files!

Key lesson: 90% of SELinux problems are wrong file contexts. restorecon fixes most of them.

31.3 AppArmor — Application Armor (Ubuntu)

CommandWhat It Does
aa-statusShow AppArmor status: loaded profiles, modes, processes in complain
/etc/apparmor.d/Profile directory — one profile per application
aa-enforce /etc/apparmor.d/usr.sbin.nginxEnforce a profile (block violations)
aa-complain /etc/apparmor.d/usr.sbin.nginxComplain mode (log but don't block — for debugging)
aa-disable /etc/apparmor.d/usr.sbin.nginxDisable a profile entirely
dmesg | grep apparmorView AppArmor denial messages in kernel log
apparmor_parser -r /etc/apparmor.d/profileReload a profile after editing
🔧 Real-World: "AppArmor Blocks Gunicorn from Writing Logs"

Situation: Gunicorn can't write to /var/log/anihpj/. dmesg | grep apparmor shows: apparmor="DENIED" operation="mknod" profile="/usr/bin/gunicorn" name="/var/log/anihpj/gunicorn-error.log".

  1. Diagnose: The gunicorn AppArmor profile doesn't allow writing to /var/log/anihpj/.
  2. Fix (temporary): sudo aa-complain /etc/apparmor.d/usr.bin.gunicorn — puts profile in complain mode.
  3. Fix (permanent): Edit /etc/apparmor.d/local/usr.bin.gunicorn and add: /var/log/anihpj/* rw,. Reload: sudo apparmor_parser -r /etc/apparmor.d/usr.bin.gunicorn. Set back to enforce: sudo aa-enforce /etc/apparmor.d/usr.bin.gunicorn.
🔬 Inside an AppArmor Profile — What the Rules Actually Look Like

AppArmor profiles live in /etc/apparmor.d/ and are named after the executable path (slashes become dots: usr.sbin.nginx). Each profile declares what the program CAN do — everything else is denied. Key sections: #include <tunables/global> (variables like @{HOME}), capability net_bind_service, (Linux capabilities), /var/www/anihpj/staticfiles/** r, (file access: r=read, w=write, m=memory-map, k=lock), network inet tcp, (allow TCP networking). Local overrides: /etc/apparmor.d/local/usr.sbin.nginx — add custom rules here (not in main profile) so package updates don't overwrite them. Syntax: glob patterns use * (one directory level) and ** (recursive). deny /etc/shadow r, explicitly blocks access even if a broader rule would allow it. Debugging: aa-logprof scans logs for denials and interactively suggests profile updates — the easiest way to fix a broken profile!

🔬 Generating AppArmor Profiles with aa-genprof — Don't Write from Scratch

Writing an AppArmor profile from scratch is error-prone and dangerous — too restrictive and your app breaks, too permissive and there's no security benefit. aa-genprof automates profile creation by observing actual application behavior: (1) sudo aa-genprof /usr/bin/myapp starts profiling mode. (2) In another terminal, exercise the application thoroughly — access all files, make network connections, handle every feature it has. (3) Back in aa-genprof, type S (scan) — it reads the audit logs and presents interactive suggestions for every denied action. (4) For each suggestion, choose: Allow (add the exact path), Deny (explicitly block), Glob (generalize the path pattern). (5) Type F (finish) — aa-genprof writes the complete profile and sets it to enforce mode. The key insight: aa-genprof starts with an EMPTY profile (deny everything) and builds up permissions based on what the application ACTUALLY does, not what you THINK it does. This catches things you'd never think to add manually — like an application reading /etc/nsswitch.conf or /proc/sys/kernel/hostname. For anihpj: If you create a custom monitoring daemon at /usr/local/bin/anihpj-monitor and AppArmor blocks it, run sudo aa-genprof /usr/local/bin/anihpj-monitor, exercise all monitoring features, and let aa-genprof build the profile. Much safer and more thorough than manually editing profiles.

🔬 Complain vs Enforce — Why Per-Profile Modes Make AppArmor Production-Safe

AppArmor's two modes are fundamentally different from SELinux's global mode switch. Enforce: Policy is active. Violations are logged AND blocked. The application receives "Permission denied." Equivalent to SELinux Enforcing. Complain: Policy is NOT enforced for THIS profile only. Violations are LOGGED but ALLOWED. The application works normally. Other profiles remain in enforce mode. This is the critical difference from SELinux: In SELinux, to debug an nginx issue you must set the ENTIRE system to permissive (setenforce 0), which temporarily disables protection for ALL services — a massive security gap. In AppArmor, you put ONLY nginx in complain mode (aa-complain /etc/apparmor.d/usr.sbin.nginx) — every other service (sshd, postgresql, mysql, etc.) remains fully protected. Typical workflow: (1) Deploy new app, set to complain. (2) Exercise the app while aa-logprof captures violations. (3) Generate/update profile with aa-logprof. (4) Switch back to enforce. (5) Verify app still works. This per-profile granularity is why many sysadmins prefer AppArmor for production debugging. Warning: A profile left in complain mode indefinitely is a security vulnerability. Always switch back to enforce after debugging.

Q9
What's the fundamental difference between SELinux and AppArmor? Which distro uses which?
Click to reveal answer
✅ Answer

SELinux: Label-based — every file and process has a security context (user:role:type:level). Policies define which contexts can interact. Used by RHEL/Rocky/Fedora. AppArmor: Path-based — profiles attached to executable file paths. Simpler syntax. Used by Ubuntu/Debian. On the LFCS exam: Ubuntu VM = AppArmor, Rocky VM = SELinux.

Chapter 32: System Hardening — Defense in Depth

Security isn't one tool — it's layers. This chapter covers the practical hardening techniques every anihpj server needs: least privilege (giving users/services only what they need), auditd (tracking who accessed what), fail2ban (automatic IP banning), AIDE (detecting changed files), and a comprehensive hardening checklist you can apply to any production server.

The exam may ask you to configure fail2ban, set up audit rules, or implement least privilege.
