Know the philosophy: every open port, every running service, every user with a shell is an attack surface.

32.1 The Principle of Least Privilege

Least Privilege Applied to Anihpj
  PRINCIPLE: Every entity should have the MINIMUM permissions
  needed to do its job — and NO MORE.

  ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │  ANIHPJ USER (anihpj)                                       │
  │  ✅ Can: run Gunicorn, read .env, write to /var/log/anihpj │
  │  ❌ Cannot: sudo, SSH in (nologin shell), read other homes  │
  │  Implementation: useradd -r -s /usr/sbin/nologin            │
  └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

  ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │  DATABASE USER (anihpj_user)                                │
  │  ✅ Can: SELECT/INSERT/UPDATE/DELETE on anihpj_db           │
  │  ❌ Cannot: CREATE DATABASE, DROP DATABASE, see other DBs   │
  │  Implementation: GRANT ALL ON DATABASE anihpj_db (only!)    │
  └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

  ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │  NGINX WORKERS (www-data)                                   │
  │  ✅ Can: read /var/www/anihpj/static/, connect to socket    │
  │  ❌ Cannot: read .env, write to code, execute binaries      │
  │  Implementation: chown anihpj:www-data; chmod 750 static/   │
  └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

  ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │  NETWORK                                                   │
  │  ✅ Open: 22 (SSH), 80 (HTTP), 443 (HTTPS)                 │
  │  ❌ Closed: 5432 (PostgreSQL), 8000 (Gunicorn), 3306 (MySQL)│
  │  Implementation: ufw default deny; ufw allow 22,80,443     │
  └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
🔬 Linux Capabilities — Breaking Root into 40 Separate Powers

Traditionally, Linux has a binary privilege model: you're either root (UID 0, can do ANYTHING) or you're not. Capabilities split root's power into 40+ discrete permissions. A process can have CAP_NET_BIND_SERVICE (bind to ports <1024) without having CAP_SYS_ADMIN (mount filesystems, load kernel modules). Key capabilities: CAP_NET_BIND_SERVICE — bind to privileged ports (<1024). CAP_NET_RAW — use raw sockets (ping). CAP_SYS_TIME — set system clock. CAP_SYS_PTRACE — trace other processes (debugging). Anihpj example: Instead of running Gunicorn as root to bind to port 80, give the gunicorn binary CAP_NET_BIND_SERVICE: sudo setcap cap_net_bind_service=+ep /usr/bin/python3. Now Gunicorn can bind to port 80 as a non-root user. Check process capabilities: getpcaps $(pgrep gunicorn). Check file capabilities: getcap /usr/bin/ping (ping needs CAP_NET_RAW). This is how modern container runtimes work — they drop ALL capabilities except the few the container actually needs.

🔬 PAM — Pluggable Authentication Modules: The Gatekeeper of Linux Authentication

Every time you log in via SSH, sudo, or the console, PAM (Pluggable Authentication Modules) is what ACTUALLY authenticates you. PAM is a stackable authentication framework — you can chain multiple modules together for complex auth logic. Config location: /etc/pam.d/ — one file per service (sshd, sudo, login, passwd). Module types: auth (verify identity — password, fingerprint), account (check account validity — not expired, time restrictions), session (setup/teardown — create home dir, mount shares), password (update authentication token — change password). Control flags: required (must pass, but continue checking others — delays revealing which module failed), requisite (must pass, immediately fail if not), sufficient (if this passes, skip remaining modules), optional (ignored if it fails). Common modules: pam_unix.so (traditional /etc/shadow auth), pam_tally2.so (account lockout after N failures), pam_google_authenticator.so (TOTP 2FA), pam_ldap.so (LDAP/AD integration). Anihpj example: /etc/pam.d/sshd typically includes auth required pam_unix.so (password check) and account required pam_nologin.so (block users with nologin shell). Adding 2FA: add auth required pam_google_authenticator.so BEFORE pam_unix.so. PAM is the reason you can integrate Linux with Active Directory, enforce password complexity, or add hardware token auth — all without modifying SSH, sudo, or login code.

1
Service Accounts

Create with useradd -r -s /usr/sbin/nologin. No interactive login possible. Each service gets its own user — never share accounts.

2
File Permissions

.env = 600. Static files = 644. Application code = 640 for owner:group. find / -perm -o+w -type f to audit world-writable files.

3
sudo Control

Grant specific commands: deploy ALL=(root) /usr/bin/systemctl reload nginx — NOT ALL=(ALL) NOPASSWD: ALL. Audit sudo usage: journalctl -xe | grep sudo.

4
Network Restriction

UFW default deny incoming. Open only needed ports. PostgreSQL on localhost. Internal services on private IPs only. Audit: ss -tlnp weekly.

32.2 auditd — Auditing File Access

CommandWhat It Does
apt install auditdInstall the audit daemon
auditctl -w /etc/passwd -p rwxa -k passwd_changesWatch /etc/passwd for read/write/execute/attr changes
auditctl -w /etc/shadow -p rwa -k shadow_accessWatch /etc/shadow for any access
auditctl -lList all active audit rules
ausearch -f /etc/shadowSearch audit log for /etc/shadow access
ausearch -k passwd_changes -iSearch by key name, interpret timestamps/UIDs
aureport --summarySummary report of all audit events
augenrules --loadLoad rules from /etc/audit/rules.d/ (persistent)
🔬 Make Audit Rules Persistent

Rules added with auditctl -w are LOST on reboot. For persistent rules, add them to /etc/audit/rules.d/audit.rules: -w /etc/passwd -p rwxa -k passwd_changes. Then sudo augenrules --load && sudo systemctl restart auditd. Audit logs are at /var/log/audit/audit.log — search with ausearch, not grep (the log is binary-optimized).

🔬 auditd Rule Syntax Deep-Dive

Audit rules use flags to specify what to monitor. File watches (-w): -p rwxa = watch for (r)ead, (w)rite, e(x)ecute, (a)ttribute changes. Syscall rules (-a): -a always,exit -S unlink -S rename -k file_deletion logs every file deletion and rename. Key (-k): Tags all events from a rule with a searchable key — ausearch -k passwd_changes finds them all. Performance: Too many rules can slow the system. Be selective: watch /etc/, /var/www/anihpj/, ~/.ssh/authorized_keys — not /var/log/ (excessive noise). View loaded rules: auditctl -l. Delete a rule: auditctl -W /etc/passwd -p rwxa (same syntax but uppercase -W). Anihpj example: -w /var/www/anihpj/ -p wa -k anihpj_code_changes — alerts on any code modification.

32.3 fail2ban — Automatic IP Banning

How fail2ban Protects Anihpj
  ATTACKER                          ANIHPJ SERVER
  ─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
  ① SSH attempt (wrong password)
     ─────────────────────────────────▶  /var/log/auth.log:
                                          "Failed password for root"

  ② SSH attempt (wrong password)
     ─────────────────────────────────▶  Failed again (2nd attempt)

  ③ SSH attempt (wrong password)
     ─────────────────────────────────▶  Failed again (3rd attempt)

  ④ SSH attempt (wrong password)
     ─────────────────────────────────▶  Failed again (4th attempt)

  ⑤ SSH attempt (wrong password)
     ─────────────────────────────────▶  Failed again (5th attempt!)
                                          🔴 fail2ban TRIGGERS:
                                          iptables -A INPUT -s IP -j DROP

  ⑥ SSH attempt (any password)
     ──────── ✗ BLOCKED ✗ ─────────────  iptables DROPS connection
                                          (Banned for 1 hour)

  CONFIG (/etc/fail2ban/jail.local):
  [sshd]
  enabled = true
  port = 22
  maxretry = 5
  bantime = 3600        # 1 hour
  findtime = 600        # 10 minute window for counting failures

  CHECK STATUS:
  sudo fail2ban-client status sshd     → list banned IPs
  sudo fail2ban-client set sshd unbanip 1.2.3.4  → manual unban
🔬 fail2ban for Nginx — Protect Your Web App Too

SSH isn't the only attack vector. fail2ban can protect Nginx against: (1) 4xx floods: Ban IPs generating excessive 404/403 errors (vulnerability scanners). (2) Login brute-force: Django admin or WordPress wp-login.php attacks. (3) Rate-limit abuse: IPs hitting your API too fast. Setup: Create /etc/fail2ban/filter.d/nginx-4xx.conf with regex matching 4xx errors in access.log. Create /etc/fail2ban/jail.local entry: [nginx-4xx]
enabled = true
port = http,https
filter = nginx-4xx
logpath = /var/log/nginx/anihpj-access.log
maxretry = 100
findtime = 300
bantime = 3600. This bans IPs generating 100+ 4xx errors in 5 minutes. Check: sudo fail2ban-client status nginx-4xx.

Creating a Custom fail2ban Filter — Step by Step
  # 1. Create the filter definition
  sudo nano /etc/fail2ban/filter.d/nginx-4xx.conf

  [Definition]
  # Regex to match 4xx errors in Nginx access log
  failregex = ^ -.* "(GET|POST|HEAD).*" (404|403|400|405) .*$
  # Ignore legitimate 404s (e.g., favicon.ico, robots.txt)
  ignoreregex = .*(favicon.ico|robots.txt|apple-touch-icon).*

  # 2. Create the jail configuration
  sudo nano /etc/fail2ban/jail.local

  [nginx-4xx]
  enabled  = true
  port     = http,https
  filter   = nginx-4xx
  logpath  = /var/log/nginx/anihpj-access.log
  maxretry = 100        # 100+ 4xx errors = scanning
  findtime = 300        # within 5 minutes
  bantime  = 3600       # ban for 1 hour

  # 3. Test the regex before deploying
  sudo fail2ban-regex /var/log/nginx/anihpj-access.log /etc/fail2ban/filter.d/nginx-4xx.conf
  # Shows: Lines matched: X / Lines total: Y

  # 4. Reload fail2ban and check
  sudo systemctl reload fail2ban
  sudo fail2ban-client status nginx-4xx

  # 5. Simulate attack to verify (from another machine):
  for i in {1..150}; do curl -s -o /dev/null -w "%{http_code}" https://anihpj.com/nonexistent; done
  # After 5 min: sudo fail2ban-client status nginx-4xx → "Currently banned: 1"

32.4 AIDE — File Integrity Monitoring

CommandWhat It Does
apt install aideInstall AIDE
aideinitInitialize AIDE database (baseline snapshot of system files)
aide --checkCompare current state against baseline — report changes
aide --updateUpdate baseline after legitimate changes (apt upgrade, deploy)
/etc/aide/aide.confConfig: which directories to monitor, what attributes to check
🔬 What AIDE Detects

AIDE creates a cryptographic hash of every monitored file. On each check, it recomputes hashes and compares. It detects: modified files (hacker changed your code), new files (hacker uploaded a backdoor), deleted files (hacker removed logs), changed permissions (hacker made a file SUID root). Anihpj use case: Monitor /var/www/anihpj/, /etc/nginx/, /etc/postgresql/, /etc/ssh/sshd_config, /etc/passwd, /etc/shadow. Run aide --check daily via cron and email the diff. If source code changes unexpectedly — investigate immediately.

🔬 AIDE Configuration Deep-Dive — What to Monitor and How

AIDE's config (/etc/aide/aide.conf) defines WHAT to monitor and HOW. Permission flags: p (permissions), i (inode), n (number of links), u (user), g (group), s (size), m (mtime), a (atime), c (ctime). Checksum flags: md5 (fast, adequate), sha256 (strong, recommended), sha512 (strongest, slower). Combine into rules: NORMAL = p+i+n+u+g+s+m+c+sha256 (standard file monitoring). DIR = p+i+n+u+g (directory metadata only — directories change size constantly). LOG = p+u+g (log files — size and mtime change normally, only watch permissions/owner). Selective monitoring strategy: /etc NORMAL (everything in /etc). /var/www/anihpj NORMAL (application code). /var/log DIR (don't hash logs — they change too much). !/var/log/lastlog (exclude volatile files — changes on every login). Performance: AIDE reads and hashes every monitored file — on first run with many files, it can take minutes and use significant I/O. Schedule checks during low-traffic hours. After legitimate changes (apt upgrade, code deploy), update the database: aide --update then replace the old database. Never keep checking against a stale baseline.

32.5 Hardening Checklist

🔐
SSH Hardening

PermitRootLogin no, PasswordAuthentication no, AllowUsers whitelist, non-default port. sshd -t before reload.

🛡️
Firewall

UFW default deny incoming. Only 22, 80, 443 open. PostgreSQL on localhost only. Verify weekly with ufw status verbose.

👤
User Security

Service accounts: nologin shell. .env: chmod 600. sudo: specific commands only. umask 027 for services.

📦
Updates & Patches

unattended-upgrades for security patches. Weekly apt update. Remove unused services. Kernel hardening via sysctl.

📋
Auditing

auditd watching /etc/passwd, /etc/shadow. AIDE daily integrity checks. fail2ban active on SSH and Nginx.

💾
Backups & Recovery

Nightly pg_dump. GPG encrypted offsite copy. Tested restore procedure. 3-2-1 backup rule enforced.

Complete 30-Point Production Hardening Checklist
  ☐  1. SSH: PermitRootLogin no
  ☐  2. SSH: PasswordAuthentication no (key-only)
  ☐  3. SSH: AllowUsers whitelist
  ☐  4. SSH: non-default port (>1024 reduces scan noise)
  ☐  5. UFW: default deny incoming, allow 22/80/443
  ☐  6. PostgreSQL: listen_addresses = 'localhost'
  ☐  7. PostgreSQL: strong password for anihpj_user
  ☐  8. anihpj user: nologin shell, no sudo
  ☐  9. .env file: chmod 600, NOT in Git
  ☐ 10. Django: DEBUG=False in production
  ☐ 11. Django: ALLOWED_HOSTS restricted
  ☐ 12. Django: SECRET_KEY not in settings.py (use env var)
  ☐ 13. unattended-upgrades: auto-install security patches
  ☐ 14. fail2ban: active on SSH (maxretry=5, bantime=1h)
  ☐ 15. fail2ban: active on Nginx (rate-limit abuse)
  ☐ 16. AppArmor: enforce profiles on nginx, gunicorn
  ☐ 17. auditd: watch /etc/passwd, /etc/shadow, /etc/sudoers
  ☐ 18. AIDE: monitor /var/www/anihpj/, key configs
  ☐ 19. File permissions: find / -perm -4000 (audit SUID)
  ☐ 20. No default passwords: change all vendor defaults
  ☐ 21. Chrony: time synced (SSL certs need correct time)
  ☐ 22. logrotate: logs rotated (prevent disk full)
  ☐ 23. /tmp mounted with noexec,nosuid,nodev
  ☐ 24. Remove unused services: telnet, rsh, ftp, nfs if not needed
  ☐ 25. Kernel: sysctl net.ipv4.tcp_syncookies=1 (SYN flood protection)
  ☐ 26. Kernel: sysctl net.ipv4.ip_forward=0 (unless router)
  ☐ 27. SSL: certbot auto-renewal verified
  ☐ 28. Backups: nightly, tested restore, offsite copy
  ☐ 29. Monitoring: disk space, CPU, memory alerts
  ☐ 30. Documentation: server build log, config backups in Git

Q1
Set up auditd to monitor /etc/passwd for any write or attribute changes.
Click to reveal answer

User management is security fundamentals. UIDs (not usernames) are what the kernel checks. 🎯 Crypto on the LFCS Exam

LFCS may ask you to generate a self-signed certificate with OpenSSL, check cert expiry, or use GPG to encrypt a file. Key commands: openssl req -x509, openssl x509 -enddate, gpg -e, gpg -d. Know the difference between .pem (text), .der (binary), .p12 (PKCS#12 bundle with private key).

33.1 Symmetric vs Asymmetric Encryption

🔑 Symmetric (AES)

ONE key for both encrypt AND decrypt. Like a physical key that locks AND unlocks. Fast — good for bulk data. Problem: how do you share the key securely? Used in HTTPS for the actual data transfer (AES-256-GCM).

🔐 Asymmetric (RSA/Ed25519)

TWO keys: public (encrypt) and private (decrypt). Like a mailbox — anyone can drop mail in (public key), only you can read it (private key). Slower but solves key distribution. Used in HTTPS for the initial key exchange.

🔬 Cipher Suites Demystified — What "TLS_AES_256_GCM_SHA384" Actually Means

When your browser connects to anihpj.com, it and Nginx negotiate a cipher suite — a specific combination of algorithms: (1) Key Exchange: ECDHE (Elliptic Curve Diffie-Hellman Ephemeral) — how the session key is agreed upon. "Ephemeral" means a NEW key pair is generated for every session (Perfect Forward Secrecy — compromising one session doesn't compromise others). (2) Authentication: RSA/ECDSA — verifies the server's identity via its certificate. (3) Bulk Encryption: AES-256-GCM — encrypts the actual data. GCM (Galois/Counter Mode) provides BOTH encryption AND integrity checking (authenticated encryption). (4) Hash: SHA384 — used in the TLS PRF (Pseudo-Random Function) for deriving keys. Modern recommended: TLS 1.3 with AES-256-GCM or ChaCha20-Poly1305. Weak/avoid: RC4, 3DES, CBC-mode ciphers, anything with NULL or EXPORT. Check your server: nmap --script ssl-enum-ciphers -p 443 anihpj.com or sslscan anihpj.com.

Hybrid Encryption — How HTTPS Actually Works
  BROWSER                                          SERVER
  ────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
  ① Browser gets server's PUBLIC KEY (from certificate)

  ② Browser generates random SESSION KEY (symmetric)
     ┌──────────────────────────────────────┐
     │  🔑 Session Key: a8f3b2c1... (256bit)│
     └──────────────────────────────────────┘

  ③ Browser ENCRYPTS session key with server's PUBLIC KEY
     ┌──────────────────────────────────────┐
     │  🔒 Encrypted Session Key            │
     │  (can only be decrypted with          │
     │   server's PRIVATE key)              │
     └──────────────────────────────────────┘
     ────────────────────────────────────▶  Sent to server

  ④ Server decrypts session key with PRIVATE KEY
     Now BOTH sides have the same session key!

  ⑤ 🔒 ALL SUBSEQUENT DATA encrypted with AES-256 + session key
     ┌──────────────────────────────────────┐
     │  GET /jobs/  →  AES-256 encrypt  →   │
     │  [encrypted bytes]  ──────────────▶  │
     │              ←  AES-256 decrypt  ←   │
     │                 [encrypted bytes]    │
     └──────────────────────────────────────┘

  💡 Asymmetric (slow) used ONCE for key exchange.
     Symmetric (fast) used for EVERYTHING after.
     Best of both worlds: security + performance.

33.2 OpenSSL — Working with Certificates

CommandWhat It Does
openssl genrsa -out anihpj.key 4096Generate 4096-bit RSA private key
openssl req -x509 -new -key anihpj.key -days 365 -out anihpj.crtGenerate self-signed cert (dev/testing only!)
openssl x509 -in anihpj.crt -text -nooutView all certificate details
openssl x509 -in anihpj.crt -enddate -nooutCheck certificate expiry date only
openssl s_client -connect anihpj.com:443 -servername anihpj.comTest TLS connection (shows full chain and cipher)
openssl s_client -connect anihpj.com:443 2>/dev/null | openssl x509 -noout -datesCheck remote cert expiry (one-liner)
openssl req -new -key anihpj.key -out anihpj.csrGenerate CSR (Certificate Signing Request)
🔧 Real-World: Self-Signed Cert for Anihpj Dev Server

Situation: Internal staging server at staging.anihpj.local needs HTTPS but can't get Let's Encrypt (no public DNS).

  1. Generate key + cert: openssl req -x509 -newkey rsa:4096 -keyout staging.key -out staging.crt -days 365 -nodes -subj "/CN=staging.anihpj.local"
  2. Configure Nginx: point ssl_certificate and ssl_certificate_key to the files.
  3. Trust on dev machines: Add staging.crt to browser/system trust store. Or just click through the browser warning — it's only dev.
  4. Verify: openssl s_client -connect staging.anihpj.local:443 → shows your self-signed cert.
🔬 Certificate Formats Explained — PEM, DER, PKCS#12, and When to Use Each

Certificates come in different file formats — the SAME certificate data, just different encodings. PEM (Privacy Enhanced Mail): Base64-encoded text with -----BEGIN CERTIFICATE----- headers. The universal format on Linux. Files: .pem, .crt, .cer, .key. Can contain just the certificate, just the private key, or both concatenated. DER (Distinguished Encoding Rules): Binary format — same data as PEM but not Base64-encoded. Used by Java and some Windows tools. Files: .der, .cer. Convert: openssl x509 -in cert.pem -outform der -out cert.der. PKCS#12 (.p12 / .pfx): Binary archive format — contains certificate + private key + intermediate CAs, all protected by a password. Used for importing/exporting to Windows, browsers, and Java keystores. Convert PEM to PKCS12: openssl pkcs12 -export -in cert.pem -inkey key.pem -out bundle.p12. When to use each: Linux/Nginx/Apache → PEM. Windows/IIS → PKCS#12. Java → DER or PKCS#12 (JKS). Browser import → PKCS#12. Quick check: If you can cat the file and see readable text with BEGIN/END markers, it's PEM. If it's binary gibberish, it's DER or PKCS#12 — use openssl to inspect it.

🔬 Certificate Chain Verification — How Your Browser Knows to Trust Anihpj.com

When you connect to anihpj.com, you don't just get one certificate — you get the ENTIRE chain. The chain: (1) Your server's certificate (anihpj.com — the "leaf" or "end-entity" cert). (2) The intermediate CA certificate (Let's Encrypt R3). (3) The root CA certificate (ISRG Root X1) — this is NOT sent by the server; it's already in your browser's trust store. Verification process: Browser gets (1) and (2) from the server. Browser already has (3) pre-installed. Browser verifies: (2) was signed by (3) — check signature with R3's public key. (1) was signed by (2) — check signature with anihpj.com's public key. If both checks pass AND the root is trusted AND no certificate is expired AND the hostname matches → TLS handshake succeeds. Manual verification: openssl verify -CAfile root.pem -untrusted intermediate.pem anihpj.crt. Online check: openssl s_client -connect anihpj.com:443 -showcerts shows every cert the server sends. Chain issues (common): (1) Missing intermediate — server didn't send it, browser can't build the chain. Fix: include fullchain.pem (cert + intermediate), not just cert.pem. (2) Wrong intermediate — cert signed by R3 but you're sending R4 intermediate. (3) Expired intermediate — Let's Encrypt intermediates also expire. certbot handles all of this automatically — but knowing how to debug chain issues saves hours of confusion.

🔬 OCSP Stapling — Check Certificate Revocation Without Privacy Leaks

Certificates can be REVOKED before they expire (private key compromised, domain ownership lost). How does a browser know if a cert is revoked? CRL (Certificate Revocation List): A massive downloadable list of ALL revoked certificates. Impractical — CRLs can be megabytes and grow infinitely. OCSP (Online Certificate Status Protocol): Browser asks the CA's OCSP server: "Is certificate serial #12345 still valid?" CA responds: "Good" / "Revoked" / "Unknown." Problem: The CA now knows EVERY website you visit (privacy nightmare). OCSP Stapling (the solution): The SERVER (Nginx) periodically asks the CA about its OWN certificate and caches the signed response ("staple"). During TLS handshake, the server sends the OCSP response ALONG with its certificate — the browser verifies it without ever contacting the CA. Benefits: (1) Privacy — the CA never knows which clients are visiting anihpj.com. (2) Speed — no extra round trip to the OCSP server. (3) Reliability — works even if the OCSP server is down (stapled response is valid for hours). Enable in Nginx: ssl_stapling on; and ssl_stapling_verify on; in the server block. Check: openssl s_client -connect anihpj.com:443 -status — look for "OCSP Response Status: successful."

33.3 GPG — Encrypting Files and Emails

CommandWhat It Does
gpg --gen-keyGenerate GPG key pair (interactive, prompts for name/email/passphrase)
gpg --list-keysList your public keys
gpg -e -r admin@anihpj.com backup.sqlEncrypt file for specific recipient (creates backup.sql.gpg)
gpg -d backup.sql.gpg > backup.sqlDecrypt file (prompts for your private key passphrase)
gpg --sign anihpj-v1.0.tar.gzSign a file (proves it came from YOU, not tampered with)
gpg --verify anihpj-v1.0.tar.gz.sigVerify a signature
🔬 How RSA Encryption Actually Works — The Math Behind Your Keys

RSA's security relies on one simple mathematical fact: multiplying two large primes is EASY, but factoring the product back into the two original primes is HARD. Key generation (simplified): (1) Pick two large random primes p and q. (2) Compute n = p × q (the modulus — this is part of BOTH public and private keys). (3) Compute φ(n) = (p-1)(q-1). (4) Choose public exponent e (typically 65537). (5) Compute private exponent d where (e × d) mod φ(n) = 1. Result: Public key = (n, e). Private key = (n, d). Encryption: ciphertext = message^e mod n. Decryption: message = ciphertext^d mod n. Why it's secure: To find d from (n, e), you need φ(n), which requires factoring n into p×q. Factoring a 2048-bit number would take billions of years with current technology. Ed25519 uses elliptic curves instead: faster, smaller keys, equally secure. The underlying math is different (discrete logarithm on elliptic curves vs integer factorization), but the concept is the same: easy to compute, practically impossible to reverse.

🔬 Use Case: Encrypt Anihpj Backups Before Offsite Transfer

You're sending nightly database dumps to an offsite NAS or S3 bucket. If that storage is compromised, your raw SQL dumps expose ALL user data. Encrypt before transfer: pg_dump anihpj_db | gzip | gpg -e -r backup@anihpj.com > /backups/anihpj-$(date +%F).sql.gz.gpg. Now even if someone steals the backup file, they can't read it without the backup@anihpj.com private key and passphrase. The private key lives ONLY on a secure admin machine — never on the server itself.

🔬 GPG Web of Trust — How You Know a Public Key Really Belongs to Someone

With SSL/TLS, Certificate Authorities (CAs) verify domain ownership and sign certificates — centralized trust. GPG uses a DECENTRALIZED model: the Web of Trust. Instead of trusting a central authority, you decide which keys to trust and to what degree. How it works: (1) Alice generates a key pair. (2) Bob meets Alice in person, verifies her ID, and signs her public key: gpg --sign-key alice@anihpj.com. (3) Carol trusts Bob and sees that Bob signed Alice's key — Carol can now trust Alice's key too (transitive trust). (4) The more signatures a key has from people you trust, the more confident you can be it's genuine. Trust levels: gpg --edit-key alice@anihpj.com then trust — set to: Unknown (1), Never (2), Marginal (3), Full (4), Ultimate (5, your own keys). Keyservers: Public key repositories — gpg --keyserver keys.openpgp.org --send-keys KEYID uploads, gpg --recv-keys KEYID downloads. Key signing parties: Events where developers meet physically, verify IDs, and sign each other's keys — building the web of trust. For anihpj: Your team's GPG keys should be cross-signed. When the backup encryption key (backup@anihpj.com) is signed by all team members, everyone can verify the backup was encrypted with the correct key — not a substituted one. The web of trust prevents key substitution attacks that centralized PKI handles via CAs.

33.4 SSH Keys — Deep Dive

Key TypeSizeSecurityRecommendation
Ed25519256-bitExcellent (128-bit equivalent)⭐ USE THIS — modern, fast, compact
RSA2048-4096 bitGood (3072+ recommended)Use only for legacy compatibility
ECDSA256/384/521 bitGood but NIST curvesUse Ed25519 instead
DSA1024 bitDEPRECATEDNEVER use — not supported since OpenSSH 7.0
SSH Key Workflow — From Generation to Authentication
  YOUR LAPTOP                              ANIHPJ SERVER
  ─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
  ① ssh-keygen -t ed25519 -C "anihpj-deploy"
     Creates: ~/.ssh/id_ed25519       (PRIVATE — never share!)
              ~/.ssh/id_ed25519.pub   (PUBLIC — safe to share)

  ② ssh-copy-id deploy@anihpj-server
     Copies id_ed25519.pub → server's ~/.ssh/authorized_keys

  ③ ssh deploy@anihpj-server
     ─────────────────────────────────────▶
     "I want to authenticate as 'deploy'"

     ◀───────────────────────────────────
     "Prove it. Here's a random challenge."

     ─────────────────────────────────────▶
     "I signed the challenge with my
      private key. Here's the signature."

     ◀───────────────────────────────────
     Server checks: signature + public key
     in authorized_keys → MATCH! ✅
     "Welcome, deploy!"

  CERTS (for teams): Instead of copying individual keys to every
  server, sign user keys with a CA: ssh-keygen -s ca_key -I user_id
  -n deploy -V +52w user_key.pub. Servers trust the CA — any key
  signed by the CA can log in. Expiry is enforced. Revoke by
  listing in revoked_keys file. No more authorized_keys management!
🔬 SSH Agent — Store Passphrases So You Don't Type Them 100 Times

If your SSH private key has a passphrase (and it should!), you'd normally type it on every connection. ssh-agent solves this: it runs in the background, holds your decrypted keys in memory, and provides them to SSH clients on demand. Workflow: (1) Start agent: eval $(ssh-agent) — sets environment variables so SSH knows where the agent socket is. (2) Add key: ssh-add ~/.ssh/id_ed25519 — you type the passphrase ONCE. (3) Now ssh anihpj-prod works without prompting. Commands: ssh-add -l lists loaded keys. ssh-add -D removes all keys (logout cleanup). Security: ForwardAgent no in ~/.ssh/config prevents remote servers from using your agent (if the remote server is compromised, attacker can authenticate as you to other servers). Modern alternative: macOS Keychain and GNOME Keyring integrate with ssh-agent automatically. On Linux: ssh-add -c requires confirmation for each use.

1
Generate Private Key

openssl genrsa -out anihpj.key 4096 — Creates a 4096-bit RSA private key. This is the MOST sensitive file — protect it with chmod 600.

2
Create CSR (Certificate Signing Request)

openssl req -new -key anihpj.key -out anihpj.csr — CSR contains your public key + identity info. Send this to a CA (or certbot).

3
Get Certificate Signed

Production: certbot sends CSR to Let's Encrypt, returns signed cert. Dev: openssl req -x509 self-signs. Cert proves your identity to browsers.

4
Install & Verify

Install cert in Nginx. Test: openssl s_client -connect anihpj.com:443. Monitor expiry: openssl x509 -enddate. Auto-renew with certbot.

Q3
What's the difference between symmetric and asymmetric encryption? When is each used in HTTPS?
Click to reveal answer
✅ Answer

Symmetric (AES): ONE key encrypts and decrypts. FAST. Used for the actual data transfer in HTTPS — the session key encrypts all HTTP traffic. Asymmetric (RSA/Ed25519): TWO keys — public encrypts, private decrypts. SLOW but solves key distribution. Used ONCE in HTTPS: the browser encrypts the random session key with the server's public key, and the server decrypts it with its private key. The session key is then used for symmetric encryption of all subsequent data.

📖 Explanation

sed is a stream editor: it reads one line, applies your transformation, prints the result, and moves to the next. This streaming design means it never needs to hold the entire file in memory. ✅ is the key tool here. Its man page (man ✅) is available during the exam if you need to check less common options. Verify by viewing the file after editing: cat file or head -20 file. If you used -i, check the file wasn't corrupted. The exam is distribution-neutral. This command works on both Ubuntu and Rocky — know which package manager to use for installation.

Q8
Which SSH key types are recommended and which are deprecated? Why?
Click to reveal answer
✅ Answer

Recommended: Ed25519 (fast, compact, secure, modern). Acceptable: RSA 3072+ bit (compatible but slower, larger keys). Deprecated: DSA (removed in OpenSSH 7.0), RSA <2048 bit (brute-forceable). Q9
How does SSH certificate-based authentication differ from regular key authentication?
Click to reveal answer
✅ Answer

Regular keys: Each user's public key must be copied to EVERY server's authorized_keys file. When someone leaves, you must remove their key from ALL servers. Certificate-based: A Certificate Authority (CA) signs user keys. Servers trust the CA, not individual keys. Benefits: (1) Users can have expiring certs (no cleanup needed), (2) Revoke by listing in revoked_keys — one place, (3) No more copying keys — sign once, access all servers. Generate CA: ssh-keygen -t ed25519 -f ca_key. Sign user key: ssh-keygen -s ca_key -I user@anihpj -n deploy -V +52w user_key.pub.

📖 Explanation

SSH encrypts every byte between client and server using ephemeral session keys negotiated via Diffie-Hellman. The server authenticates first (host key), then the client (password or key) — preventing man-in-the-middle attacks. The flags -keygen, -t, -f control how this command behaves. Understanding what each flag does — not just memorizing the combination — lets you adapt when the exam presents a variation. Verify by connecting: ssh user@host. Use ssh -v for verbose debugging. Q10
Create a one-liner to check if anihpj.com's SSL certificate expires within 30 days.
Click to reveal answer
✅ Answer
# Check expiry date:
EXPIRY=$(echo | openssl s_client -connect anihpj.com:443 -servername anihpj.com 2>/dev/null | openssl x509 -noout -enddate | cut -d= -f2)
# Convert to epoch and compare (30 days = 2592000 seconds):
EXPIRY_EPOCH=$(date -d "$EXPIRY" +%s)
NOW_EPOCH=$(date +%s)
if [ $((EXPIRY_EPOCH - NOW_EPOCH)) -lt 2592000 ]; then
    echo "⚠️  Certificate expires in less than 30 days!"
fi
📖 Explanation

TLS certificates use X.509 format with a trust chain: Root CA signs Intermediate CA signs your certificate. openssl is the Swiss Army knife for certificate generation, inspection, and debugging. 🧩 Part 9 Consolidation — Defense in Depth: SELinux/AppArmor (Ch31) is your last line of defense — even if an attacker compromises the application, MAC policies limit the damage. auditd and AIDE (Ch32) are your surveillance cameras — they record who accessed what and alert you when files change. fail2ban (Ch32) is your automated bouncer — too many failed attempts and you're banned. OpenSSL and GPG (Ch33) secure your data in transit and at rest — certs for HTTPS, encryption for backups. Security isn't a product — it's a process. These tools are how you implement that process.

Measure First

Monitoring & Performance 20%
🎯 Monitoring on the LFCS Exam

You'll need to diagnose performance issues in a live terminal. Key commands: top, free -h, iostat, ss. The exam may present a "slow server" scenario — you must identify whether the bottleneck is CPU, RAM, disk I/O, or network. Practice the decision tree above until it's second nature.

34.1 CPU Monitoring

CommandWhat It ShowsKey Insight
topReal-time process list with CPU%, MEM%, loadPress 1 to see per-CPU stats. Press P to sort by CPU.
htopColorful, scrollable top with mouse supportF6 to sort, F9 to kill, F5 for tree view.
mpstat -P ALL 1Per-CPU statistics every secondShows which cores are busy. %iowait = disk bottleneck.
sar -u 1 5CPU utilization, 5 samples, 1s intervalHistorical data in /var/log/sysstat/. %idle is key.
uptimeLoad averages: 1 min, 5 min, 15 minLoad > CPU count = processes waiting for CPU!
🔬 %iowait — The Silent Performance Killer

In top and mpstat, the %iowait column shows the percentage of time the CPU was idle BUT there was at least one outstanding disk I/O request. In other words: the CPU is waiting for the disk. Normal: 0-5%. Concerning: 10-20% — disk is a bottleneck. Critical: >20% — your CPU is idle because your disk can't keep up. Common causes: (1) HDD instead of SSD for database workloads, (2) Backup job saturating disk I/O during business hours, (3) Misconfigured PostgreSQL (random_page_cost too high on SSD, causing unnecessary full table scans), (4) Memory pressure causing swap thrashing. Fix: Identify the process with iotop, then either optimize the queries, ionice the backup, or upgrade to SSD. %iowait is the #1 overlooked metric — sysadmins see low CPU usage and think everything's fine, but high %iowait means the disk is the real bottleneck.

Load Average Explained — The Most Misunderstood Metric
  $ uptime
  14:23:01 up 45 days, 2 users, load average: 1.50, 0.80, 0.60
                                    │        │       │
                                    │        │       └─ 15 min average
                                    │        └────────── 5 min average
                                    └─────────────────── 1 min average

  WHAT DO THESE NUMBERS MEAN?
  They represent the AVERAGE number of processes that were:
  1) Running on CPU  OR  2) Waiting for CPU (R state in ps output)

  On a 4-CORE server:
  Load 0.00 → 100% idle
  Load 1.00 → 1 core fully utilized (25% capacity)
  Load 2.00 → 2 cores fully utilized (50% capacity)
  Load 4.00 → ALL 4 cores at 100% — SATURATED!
  Load 8.00 → 2x oversubscribed! Processes WAITING! 😰

  RULE OF THUMB: Load < #CPUs = OK
                 Load = #CPUs = fully utilized
                 Load > #CPUs = investigate NOW!

  ANIHPJ EXAMPLE: 4-core server, load = 4.50
  → top shows 3 gunicorn workers @ 100% + postgres @ 80%
  → Action: Increase gunicorn workers or add CPU cores
🔬 CPU Time States — What Each Percentage in top Actually Means

When top shows CPU percentages, each one tells a different story: us (user): Time spent running application code (gunicorn, postgres, python). High us = CPU-bound application — you need more cores or optimized code. sy (system): Time spent in kernel code (system calls, I/O scheduling, context switching). High sy (>20%) = your app is making too many system calls — check for excessive file operations, fork bombs, or network syscalls. id (idle): CPU doing nothing. High idle on a slow server = bottleneck is elsewhere (disk, network, locks). wa (iowait): CPU idle but waiting for disk I/O. High wa = disk bottleneck — your CPU is bored because the disk can't keep up. st (steal): Virtualized environment only — your VM wants to run but the hypervisor gave CPU time to another VM. High st (>5%) = noisy neighbor on your cloud host — migrate to a different physical machine. ni (nice): Time running low-priority (niced) processes. hi/si (hardware/software interrupts): Time handling hardware interrupts and softirqs — high si often means heavy network traffic. Anihpj diagnosis example: top shows us=15%, sy=5%, wa=40%, id=40%. The CPU is NOT the bottleneck — 40% iowait means the disk is the problem. Don't add CPU cores — upgrade to SSD or tune PostgreSQL queries.

34.2 Memory Monitoring

CommandWhat It ShowsKey Insight
free -hRAM and swap in human-readable format"available" > "free". Linux uses free RAM for cache — that's GOOD.
vmstat 1Virtual memory stats every secondsi/so columns = swap in/out. Non-zero = memory pressure.
sar -r 1 5Memory utilization reportkbmemfree, kbmemused, %memused over time.
cat /proc/meminfoDetailed kernel memory breakdownSlab, PageTables, Cached, Buffers, AnonPages.
smem -tkPer-process memory with shared libs accountedMore accurate than RSS — shows PSS (proportional share).
🔬 Linux Memory Demystified — Why "free -h" Shows Low Free RAM (And Why That's GOOD)

New sysadmins panic when free -h shows "free" memory near zero. This is normal and desired! Linux aggressively uses "free" RAM as disk cache — every file read from disk stays in RAM until that RAM is needed for something else. The available column is what matters: it's free + reclaimable cache = what applications can actually allocate. Example: Server has 4GB RAM. free -h shows: total=4.0G, used=3.6G, free=400M, available=2.8G. The 3.6G "used" includes ~3.2G of disk cache. If an application needs 2GB, Linux instantly drops 2GB of cache and hands it over — no swapping needed. When to worry: (1) available is low (<10% of total), (2) Swap usage is growing (check vmstat 1 — si/so columns non-zero), (3) OOM killer appears in dmesg. Until then, "low free RAM" just means Linux is using your hardware efficiently.

🔧 Real-World: Gunicorn Workers Using Too Much RAM

Situation: Server has 4GB RAM. free -h shows only 200MB available. Swap usage growing.

  1. Identify: smem -tk | head -20 → 3 gunicorn workers each using 800MB PSS = 2.4GB total.
  2. Root cause: Django loaded a large dataset into memory on startup. Each worker fork inherits it.
  3. Fix: Reduce workers from 3 to 2. Add --preload to gunicorn (loads app once, workers share via copy-on-write). Or add more RAM.
  4. Verify: free -h → 1.2GB available. Swap usage stops growing.
🔬 The OOM Killer — When Linux Runs Out of RAM

When memory is critically low and swap is exhausted, the kernel invokes the OOM (Out-Of-Memory) Killer — it selects a process to terminate to free RAM. How it selects victims: Each process has an oom_score (0-1000, higher = more likely to be killed). The score is based on: percentage of RAM used, how long it's been running, and whether it's a privileged process. Check scores: cat /proc/PID/oom_score and cat /proc/PID/oom_score_adj (adjustment — lower = protect). Protect critical processes: echo -1000 > /proc/$(pgrep gunicorn)/oom_score_adj makes gunicorn virtually unkillable by OOM. View OOM history: dmesg | grep -i "killed process" or grep -i "invoked oom-killer" /var/log/syslog. The OOM message includes: which process was killed, its PID, how much RAM it was using, and the total memory state at the time. Anihpj production: Always protect PostgreSQL (oom_score_adj = -900) and gunicorn (-500). Let less critical processes (backup scripts, monitoring agents) be the OOM victims. If OOM kills postgres, your database could be corrupted.

34.3 Disk I/O Monitoring

CommandWhat It ShowsKey Insight
iostat -x 1Extended disk I/O stats every second%util near 100% = disk saturated. await = latency. r/s + w/s = IOPS.
iotopTop-like view for disk I/O per processShows WHO is reading/writing. Requires root.
sar -d 1 5Disk activity reporttps (transfers/sec), rd_sec/s, wr_sec/s per device.
hdparm -t /dev/sdaRaw disk read speed benchmarkSSD: ~500MB/s. HDD: ~100MB/s. Compare actual vs expected.
lsblk -o NAME,SIZE,TYPE,MOUNTPOINT,ROTAList block devices with ROTA flagROTA=1 = HDD (rotational). ROTA=0 = SSD.
🔧 Real-World: "PostgreSQL Queries Suddenly Slow" — Disk I/O Bottleneck

Situation: Database queries that took 50ms now take 2 seconds. iostat -x 1 shows %util=98%, await=45ms.

  1. Check: iotop → postgres is reading heavily from /dev/sdb (the data disk).
  2. Root cause: Nightly pg_dump is still running at 9 AM — disk I/O saturated by backup.
  3. Fix: Use ionice -c 2 -n 7 pg_dump to run backup with lowest I/O priority. Or move backup to a different physical disk.
  4. Prevent: Schedule backups at 2 AM with a timeout. Monitor with iostat -x 1 | tee /var/log/disk-io.log.

34.4 Network Monitoring

📡 iftop — Per-Connection View

Shows bandwidth between YOUR server and each REMOTE IP. Like top but for network flows. Great for finding which client/host is consuming bandwidth. Requires root: sudo iftop -i eth0.

🔍 nethogs — Per-Process View

Shows bandwidth BY PROCESS — which application is using the network. "Oh, the backup script is scp-ing 50Mbps to the NAS." Much more actionable. Requires root: sudo nethogs eth0.

📡 iftop — Per-Connection

Shows bandwidth between YOUR server and each REMOTE IP. Like top but for network flows. Great for finding which client/host is consuming bandwidth. Requires root.

🔍 nethogs — Per-Process

Shows bandwidth BY PROCESS — which application is using the network. "Oh, it's the backup script scp-ing to the NAS." Much more actionable than iftop.

CommandWhat It Shows
iftop -i eth0Bandwidth per connection (like top for network)
nethogs eth0Bandwidth per PROCESS — which app is using the network
sar -n DEV 1 5Network interface stats: rxkB/s, txkB/s per interface
ss -iSocket statistics with TCP internals (RTT, CWND, retransmissions)
tcpdump -i eth0 -c 100 -w capture.pcapCapture 100 packets for analysis (use Wireshark to view .pcap)
ss -tulnpAll listening TCP/UDP sockets with process names

Chapter 35: Performance Tuning & Kernel Parameters

Monitoring tells you WHAT is slow. Tuning fixes it. This chapter covers Linux kernel tuning with sysctl (runtime kernel parameters), ulimits (per-process resource caps), and a complete tuning profile for anihpj in production — from TCP backlog to file descriptor limits to swap behavior.

  • ✅ Apply a complete production tuning profile for anihpj

🎯 Tuning on the LFCS Exam

You may need to change kernel parameters via sysctl and set resource limits. Know: sysctl -w (temporary), /etc/sysctl.conf (persistent), ulimit -n (file descriptors), LimitNOFILE= in systemd units. The exam tests practical tuning — not theoretical kernel internals.

35.1 sysctl — Kernel Runtime Parameters

CommandWhat It Does
sysctl -aList ALL kernel parameters (~1,000+)
sysctl net.ipv4.ip_forwardView a single parameter
sysctl -w net.ipv4.ip_forward=1Change a parameter (LOST on reboot!)
/etc/sysctl.confPersistent config file (applied at boot)
/etc/sysctl.d/99-anihpj.confDrop-in config (preferred — doesn't modify main file)
sysctl -pApply all settings from /etc/sysctl.conf NOW
sysctl -p /etc/sysctl.d/99-anihpj.confApply specific drop-in file
Key Kernel Parameters for Web Servers
ParameterDefaultRecommendedWhy
net.core.somaxconn1281024More queued connections before kernel rejects. Critical for high-traffic nginx.
net.ipv4.tcp_syncookies11Protect against SYN flood attacks. KEEP enabled.
net.ipv4.ip_forward00Disable IP forwarding unless this is a router/NAT gateway.
vm.swappiness6010Prefer RAM over swap. Database servers need this LOW.
fs.file-max~100K200000System-wide file descriptor max. Needed for many connections.
kernel.pid_max3276865536Max process IDs. Needed for container-heavy systems.

35.2 ulimits — Resource Limits for Processes

Command / PathWhat It Does
ulimit -aShow all current limits for your shell
ulimit -n 65536Increase open file limit for current session
/etc/security/limits.confPersistent per-user/group limits
LimitNOFILE=65536In systemd service unit: [Service] directive
cat /proc/PID/limitsCheck limits of a running process
🔬 Why File Descriptor Limits Matter for Web Servers

Every TCP connection, every open file, every UNIX socket consumes a file descriptor. Nginx serving 1,000 concurrent clients needs at least 2,000 FDs (client socket + upstream socket per connection). The default limit of 1024 will cause "Too many open files" errors under moderate load. Anihpj setup: /etc/security/limits.conf: anihpj soft nofile 65536 and anihpj hard nofile 65536. In gunicorn systemd unit: [Service] LimitNOFILE=65536. Check: cat /proc/$(pgrep gunicorn | head -1)/limits | grep "open files".

🔬 Soft vs Hard Limits — The Two-Tier ulimit System

Every resource has TWO limits: Soft limit: The currently enforced limit. Any process can raise its soft limit up to the hard limit. Hard limit: The absolute ceiling — only root can raise this. Why two tiers: It lets applications raise their own limits if needed (e.g., a database that needs more file descriptors after startup) while preventing them from going beyond the hard cap. Check: ulimit -Sn (soft file limit) and ulimit -Hn (hard file limit). Set in limits.conf: anihpj soft nofile 32768 (initial limit) and anihpj hard nofile 65536 (max allowed). For systemd services: LimitNOFILE=65536 sets BOTH soft and hard to the same value. Common mistake: Setting only the soft limit in limits.conf — if PAM doesn't apply it (common with systemd services), the limit stays at default. Always use LimitNOFILE= in the systemd unit for services.

🔬 cgroups v2 — Modern Resource Control Beyond ulimits

ulimits are the traditional per-process limits. cgroups (Control Groups) are the modern, hierarchical approach — limiting resources for entire groups of processes. cgroups v2 (default on Ubuntu 22.04+) is managed by systemd. How systemd uses cgroups: Every service unit gets its own cgroup under /sys/fs/cgroup/system.slice/. You can set resource limits directly in the unit file: MemoryMax=512M caps total RAM for the service, CPUQuota=200% limits to 2 CPU cores worth of time, IOWeight=100 sets relative I/O priority. Check cgroup assignment: systemctl status anihpj shows CGroup: /system.slice/anihpj.service. Check current usage: systemd-cgtop — like top for cgroups. cgroups vs ulimits: ulimits are per-process, cgroups are per-group. If Gunicorn spawns 3 workers, ulimits apply to each individually (each can open 65536 files). cgroups apply to ALL workers combined (total 512MB RAM for the entire service). Anihpj: Add MemoryMax=3G and MemoryHigh=2.5G to anihpj.service — the service gets throttled at 2.5G (memory pressure) and hard-killed at 3G. Much more robust than hoping OOM killer picks the right process.

35.3 Tuning for Anihpj in Production

1
Benchmark Baseline

Before tuning, measure: ab -n 1000 -c 10 https://anihpj.com/ (Apache Bench) or wrk -t4 -c100 -d30s https://anihpj.com/. Record requests/sec, latency p50/p99.

2
Apply Tuning Profile

Drop the 99-anihpj.conf sysctl file. Set limits.conf for anihpj and www-data. Configure LimitNOFILE in systemd units. Tune nginx worker_processes and connections.

3
Re-Benchmark

Run the same benchmark again. Compare requests/sec. Did latency improve? Is CPU/memory usage more efficient? Document the delta.

4
Monitor in Production

Deploy to production. Watch sar logs for 24 hours. Check for regressions. Tuning isn't one-and-done — it's iterative based on real traffic patterns.

Complete Tuning Profile for Anihpj Django Web Server
  # /etc/sysctl.d/99-anihpj.conf
  # NETWORK — handle more concurrent connections
  net.core.somaxconn = 1024              # Queue up to 1024 connections
  net.ipv4.tcp_syncookies = 1           # SYN flood protection
  net.ipv4.tcp_fin_timeout = 30         # Close half-open connections faster
  net.ipv4.tcp_tw_reuse = 1             # Reuse TIME_WAIT sockets

  # MEMORY — prefer RAM over swap (database server!)
  vm.swappiness = 10                     # Only swap under extreme pressure
  vm.dirty_ratio = 15                    # Start writing dirty pages at 15% RAM
  vm.dirty_background_ratio = 5          # Background write at 5% RAM

  # FILE HANDLES — handle many connections + files
  fs.file-max = 200000                   # System-wide file descriptor maximum
  fs.inotify.max_user_watches = 524288  # For Django auto-reload in dev

  # Apply: sudo sysctl -p /etc/sysctl.d/99-anihpj.conf

  # /etc/security/limits.conf
  anihpj    soft    nofile    65536
  anihpj    hard    nofile    65536
  www-data  soft    nofile    65536
  www-data  hard    nofile    65536

  # NGINX TUNING (/etc/nginx/nginx.conf)
  worker_processes auto;                # One worker per CPU core
  worker_connections 1024;              # Connections per worker
  # Total capacity = worker_processes × worker_connections
  # Example: 4 workers × 1024 = 4096 concurrent connections

  # GUNICORN TUNING (anihpj.service)
  # Workers = (2 × CPU cores) + 1
  # On a 4-core server: --workers 9
  # But watch memory! Each worker loads the full Django app.
  # Start with 3, monitor RAM, increase if CPU-bound.

  # POSTGRESQL TUNING (/etc/postgresql/15/main/postgresql.conf)
  shared_buffers = 1GB                   # 25% of 4GB RAM
  effective_cache_size = 3GB             # 75% of 4GB RAM
  random_page_cost = 1.1                 # SSD-optimized (HDD default is 4.0)
  work_mem = 16MB                        # Per-operation sort memory

✅ Answer
sysctl net.ipv4.tcp_syncookies
# Should return 1 (enabled). If 0:
sudo sysctl -w net.ipv4.tcp_syncookies=1
📖 Explanation

LVM abstracts physical disks into flexible storage pools. You can extend volumes online, create snapshots, and add storage without downtime. The PV→VG→LV→mkfs→mount workflow is one of the most-tested topics on LFCS. sysctl is the key tool here. Its man page (man sysctl) is available during the exam if you need to check less common options. Persistent changes require editing config files (/etc/fstab, /etc/sysctl.conf). Runtime commands alone earn zero points for persistence.

Q6
Increase the TCP connection backlog to 1024 and make it persistent.
Click to reveal answer
✅ Answer
sudo sysctl -w net.core.somaxconn=1024
echo "net.core.somaxconn=1024" | sudo tee /etc/sysctl.d/99-somaxconn.conf
📖 Explanation

This pipeline demonstrates the Unix philosophy: small, focused tools connected by pipes to solve complex problems. All commands run concurrently — data streams through kernel buffers without being fully loaded into memory. The flags -w control how this command behaves. Understanding what each flag does — not just memorizing the combination — lets you adapt when the exam presents a variation. Reboot once before submitting (last 5 minutes). This catches non-persistent configs and broken fstab entries before the grader sees them.

Q7
How do you set resource limits for a systemd service? Write the directive for Gunicorn.
Click to reveal answer
✅ Answer
# In /etc/systemd/system/anihpj.service [Service] section:
LimitNOFILE=65536
LimitNPROC=4096
# Then: sudo systemctl daemon-reload && sudo systemctl restart anihpj
📖 Explanation

systemd manages every service on modern Linux. systemctl start activates a unit now; systemctl enable creates the symlink for auto-start at boot. You need both for a persistent service. LimitNOFILE=65536 is the key tool here. Its man page (man LimitNOFILE=65536) is available during the exam if you need to check less common options. Verify with systemctl status unit-name. Look for "Active: active (running)" and check the PID. If it failed, journalctl -xeu unit-name shows why. The exam is distribution-neutral. This command works on both Ubuntu and Rocky — know which package manager to use for installation.

Q10
Why does a database server need vm.swappiness=10 instead of the default 60?
Click to reveal answer
✅ Answer

Default swappiness=60 means the kernel will swap out memory pages fairly aggressively — even when there's available RAM. For a database server like PostgreSQL, this is disastrous: database pages that should be in RAM get swapped to disk, causing queries to become 100-1000x slower. Setting swappiness=10 tells the kernel: "Only swap when you absolutely must — keep data in RAM as long as possible." PostgreSQL relies on the OS page cache for efficient reads; swapping defeats that purpose entirely. Production database servers often run swappiness=1 or even 0 (though 0 is now "never swap unless OOM" in newer kernels).

📖 Explanation

Disk space monitoring prevents outages. df shows filesystem-level usage; du shows directory-level usage. A full /var/log or /tmp can crash services even if the disk isn't full. The flags -1000x control how this command behaves. Understanding what each flag does — not just memorizing the combination — lets you adapt when the exam presents a variation. Practice this in your lab VM until you can type it from memory. The 2-hour timer is unforgiving if you're looking up every command.

Chapter 36: Troubleshooting — Finding and Fixing Problems

Everything breaks eventually. The difference between a junior and senior sysadmin isn't preventing problems — it's how fast they diagnose and fix them. This chapter covers a systematic troubleshooting methodology, boot recovery (GRUB rescue, emergency mode, kernel panic), service failures, disk-full emergencies, network debugging, and the dreaded "Permission denied" — including when it's actually SELinux/AppArmor blocking you.

🔴 Advanced⏱️ ~2 hours🔍 Troubleshooting

🎯 What You'll Learn

  • ✅ Apply a systematic 5-step troubleshooting methodology
  • ✅ Recover from boot failures: GRUB rescue, emergency mode, kernel panic
  • ✅ Diagnose and fix services that won't start
  • ✅ Handle disk-full emergencies and network issues
  • ✅ Debug "Permission denied" including MAC interference

🎓 LFCS Relevance
Troubleshooting 20%
🎯 Troubleshooting on the LFCS Exam

The LFCS exam may give you a BROKEN VM that won't boot, a service that won't start, or a "disk full" emergency. You have 2 hours to fix everything. Key skills: boot recovery (GRUB, emergency mode, Live ISO), reading logs (journalctl, dmesg, /var/log/), and systematic diagnosis (change ONE thing at a time, verify each fix).

36.1 The Troubleshooting Methodology

1
Define

What is the EXACT symptom? "The site is down" isn't helpful. "curl https://anihpj.com returns 'connection refused'" IS. Be precise.

2
Isolate

Which LAYER is broken? Network (can't ping)? Service (nginx down)? Application (Gunicorn crashed)? Database (PostgreSQL not responding)? Test each layer independently.

3
Test

Change ONE thing at a time. Restart ONE service. Check logs after each action. If you change three things and it works, you don't know which fixed it.

4
Fix

Apply the MINIMAL change that resolves the issue. Don't reinstall the OS because a config file had a typo. Understand WHY the fix works.

5
Verify

Confirm the fix works. Test the exact symptom from step 1. Check related functionality didn't break. Document what happened and why.

36.2 Boot Problems

Boot Failure Recovery — Decision Flow
  SERVER WON'T BOOT — What do you see?

  ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │  BLACK SCREEN (no GRUB menu)                                 │
  │  → Boot from Ubuntu Live ISO/USB                             │
  │  → mount /dev/sda1 /mnt                                      │
  │  → grub-install --boot-directory=/mnt/boot /dev/sda          │
  │  → update-grub (from chroot)                                 │
  └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

  ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │  GRUB RESCUE PROMPT (grub>)                                  │
  │  → ls (find partitions)                                      │
  │  → set root=(hd0,gpt2)                                       │
  │  → linux /vmlinuz root=/dev/sda2                             │
  │  → initrd /initrd.img                                        │
  │  → boot                                                      │
  │  After boot: update-grub && grub-install /dev/sda            │
  └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

  ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │  KERNEL PANIC (scrolling error messages)                     │
  │  → Reboot, hold SHIFT at GRUB                                │
  │  → Select "Advanced options" → previous kernel version      │
  │  → Boot old kernel → apt update && apt upgrade               │
  └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

  ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │  EMERGENCY MODE (root password prompt)                       │
  │  → Enter root password                                       │
  │  → journalctl -xb (see boot errors)                          │
  │  → mount -o remount,rw /  (make root writable)              │
  │  → Fix the issue (broken fstab? bad systemd unit?)          │
  │  → systemctl reboot                                          │
  └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

  ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │  FILESYSTEM ERRORS (fsck required)                           │
  │  → Boot to recovery/emergency mode                           │
  │  → umount /dev/sda1  (must be unmounted!)                   │
  │  → fsck -y /dev/sda1 (auto-repair)                          │
  │  → reboot                                                    │
  └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

36.3 Service Won't Start

"nginx won't start" — Step-by-Step Diagnosis
  ① systemctl status nginx
     → Active: failed (Result: exit-code)
     → "nginx: [emerg] bind() to 0.0.0.0:80 failed (98: Address already in use)"

  ② Check what's using port 80:
     ss -tlnp | grep :80
     → LISTEN  0.0.0.0:80  (apache2 is running!)

  ③ Fix: stop apache2, start nginx
     sudo systemctl stop apache2
     sudo systemctl disable apache2    # prevent auto-start
     sudo systemctl start nginx

  ④ Verify:
     systemctl status nginx → active (running) ✅

  OTHER COMMON SERVICE FAILURES:
  ─────────────────────────────────────────────
  Config syntax error → nginx -t / sshd -t / apache2ctl -t
  Port conflict       → ss -tlnp | grep PORT
  Permission denied   → check file perms + SELinux/AppArmor logs
  Dependency failed   → systemctl list-dependencies service
  Missing binary      → which command / apt install package

36.4 Disk Full / Out of Space

🔧 Real-World: "Anihpj Server Runs Out of Disk Space at 3 AM"

Situation: Monitoring alert: /var partition at 98%. Website throws 500 errors (can't write session data).

  1. Find what's full: df -hT → /var at 98% (18GB/20GB).
  2. Find largest dirs: du -sh /var/* | sort -rh | head -5 → /var/log = 12GB!
  3. Find largest files: find /var/log -type f -size +100M -exec ls -lh {} \; → nginx access.log = 8GB.
  4. Quick fix: sudo truncate -s 0 /var/log/nginx/access.log (zero the file without deleting).
  5. Root cause: Log rotation wasn't configured. Fix: sudo logrotate -f /etc/logrotate.d/nginx. Then configure daily rotation.
  6. Other cleanup: sudo journalctl --vacuum-size=500M (shrink journal). sudo apt clean (clear package cache).

36.5 Network Troubleshooting

Network Troubleshooting Ladder — Layer 1 to Layer 7
  LAYER 1: PHYSICAL
  ─────────────────
  ip link show          → Is the interface UP?
  ethtool eth0          → Link detected? Speed? Duplex?
  dmesg | grep eth0     → Driver loaded? Errors?

  LAYER 2: DATA LINK
  ─────────────────
  ip neigh              → ARP table — can we see the gateway?
  Check switch/VLAN configuration

  LAYER 3: NETWORK
  ─────────────────
  ip addr show          → IP assigned?
  ping 8.8.8.8          → Can we reach the internet?
  ip route show         → Default gateway correct?
  traceroute 8.8.8.8     → Where does traffic stop?

  LAYER 4: TRANSPORT
  ─────────────────
  ss -tlnp              → Is the service LISTENING?
  nc -zv localhost 5432 → Can we connect to PostgreSQL?
  ufw status            → Firewall blocking?

  LAYER 7: APPLICATION
  ─────────────────
  curl -I https://anihpj.com  → HTTP response?
  journalctl -u nginx         → Application errors?
  tail -f /var/log/nginx/error.log

  COMMON NETWORK ISSUES:
  "No route to host"     → Wrong gateway or interface down
  "Connection refused"    → Service not listening or firewall
  "Name resolution failed"→ DNS broken — check /etc/resolv.conf
  "Connection timed out"  → Firewall dropping packets silently

36.6 Permission Denied Errors

"Permission Denied" — Root Cause Decision Tree
  "Permission denied" when accessing a file or directory
      │
      ├─ ① Check basic permissions: ls -la file
      │     Owner/group/other rwx correct?
      │     → chmod / chown to fix
      │
      ├─ ② Check directory permissions: ls -la /path/to/dir
      │     You need +x on ALL parent directories to traverse!
      │     → chmod +x /path/to/missing/dir
      │
      ├─ ③ Check if user is in the right group: id username
      │     → usermod -aG groupname username
      │
      ├─ ④ Check ACLs (if enabled): getfacl file
      │     Extended ACLs can override basic permissions!
      │     → setfacl -m u:user:rwx file
      │
      ├─ ⑤ Check MAC (Ubuntu): sudo dmesg | grep apparmor
      │     AppArmor profile blocking? → aa-complain / aa-logprof
      │
      ├─ ⑥ Check MAC (Rocky): sudo ausearch -m avc -ts recent
      │     SELinux context wrong? → restorecon -Rv /path/
      │
      └─ ⑦ Check mount options: mount | grep /mountpoint
            Mounted with noexec, nosuid, or read-only?
            → mount -o remount,rw /mountpoint

🔄
Boot RecoveryGRUB rescue, old kernel, emergency mode, Live ISO + chroot. Five failure types, five fixes.
💾

  daemon-reload (after editing units!)
  systemctl status → check state
Q10
What's the first step in any troubleshooting process? Why is it the most important?
Click to reveal answer
✅ Answer

DEFINE the exact symptom. "The website is down" is useless because it could mean: DNS failure, network outage, firewall block, nginx crash, Gunicorn crash, database failure, disk full, or just your own internet being down. Reproduce the error precisely: "curl https://anihpj.com returns '502 Bad Gateway' — the HTML body says 'nginx' — so nginx IS running but can't reach Gunicorn." Now you've isolated the problem to the nginx→Gunicorn connection. Defining precisely saves hours of checking the wrong layer.

📖 Explanation

Every running program is a process with a PID. The kernel schedules processes using the Completely Fair Scheduler (CFS). Signals (TERM, KILL, HUP) control process lifecycle — SIGTERM asks politely, SIGKILL forces termination. ✅ is the key tool here. Its man page (man ✅) is available during the exam if you need to check less common options. On the exam, verify your result immediately — a single unverified typo can cascade into multiple failed tasks.

37.1 cron — The Standard Task Scheduler

Command / PathWhat It Does
crontab -eEdit your user's crontab
crontab -lList current crontab entries
crontab -rRemove ALL cron jobs ⚠️ IRREVERSIBLE — backup first!
/etc/crontabSystem-wide crontab (includes user column)
/etc/cron.d/Drop-in crontab files (package-managed)
/etc/cron.daily/Scripts run daily by run-parts
/etc/cron.hourly/Scripts run hourly
/etc/cron.weekly/Scripts run weekly
Cron Time Format — The 5 Fields
  * * * * *  /path/to/command
  │ │ │ │ │
  │ │ │ │ └── Day of week (0=Sun, 1=Mon ... 6=Sat)
  │ │ │ └──── Month (1-12)
  │ │ └────── Day of month (1-31)
  │ └──────── Hour (0-23)
  └────────── Minute (0-59)

  EXAMPLES for anihpj:
  0  2  *  *  *   /scripts/backup-anihpj.sh    → 2 AM daily backup
  */5 *  *  *  *   /scripts/health-check.sh     → every 5 minutes
  0  0  *  *  0    /scripts/rotate-logs.sh      → Sundays midnight
  30 6  1  *  *    /scripts/monthly-report.sh   → 1st of month 6:30 AM
  0  3  *  *  1-5  /scripts/weekday-cleanup.sh  → 3 AM Mon-Fri

  💡 Use crontab.guru to visualize and verify cron expressions
  ⚠️ cron uses the server's LOCAL timezone — check with timedatectl
🔬 How cron Actually Works Internally

The cron daemon (crond) wakes up EVERY MINUTE, scans all crontab files (/var/spool/cron/crontabs/ for users, /etc/crontab and /etc/cron.d/ for system), and checks if any job's time fields match the current minute. If they do, cron forks a child process, sets up a minimal environment (HOME=/home/user, LOGNAME=user, PATH=/usr/bin:/bin, SHELL=/bin/sh), and executes the command. Key implications: (1) The minimum granularity is 1 minute — you cannot schedule a job every 30 seconds with cron. (2) If a job takes longer than its interval, multiple instances can stack up — use a lock file: flock -n /tmp/backup.lock /scripts/backup.sh. (3) cron does NOT track job status — if a job fails silently, cron won't retry. Always add logging/alerting. (4) Day-of-week vs day-of-month: When BOTH are specified (e.g., 0 0 1 * 1 = "midnight on the 1st AND Mondays"), cron runs on BOTH conditions (OR logic, not AND) — this catches people off guard. (5) cron reads crontabs into memory at startup and when files change — you never need to restart crond after crontab -e. Check cron's own logs: grep CRON /var/log/syslog shows every job execution with timestamp, user, and command.

📅
System Tasks (root crontab)

0 2 * * * /scripts/backup.sh — backups, updates, cleanup. Use /etc/cron.d/ for package-managed cron jobs. Never edit /etc/crontab directly.

👤
User Tasks (user crontab)

0 8 * * 1-5 echo "standup" | mail -s "Reminder" user@anihpj.com — personal reminders, reports. Managed via crontab -e.

📂
Drop-in Tasks (/etc/cron.d/)

Package-installed cron jobs (certbot, logrotate). Format includes the USER column: 0 */12 * * * root certbot renew. Preferred for automated deployments.

📁
Script Directories (cron.daily)

Drop executable scripts in /etc/cron.daily/ — run by run-parts. No time syntax needed. Good for simple daily tasks managed by configuration management tools.

🔬 The Cron Environment — Why Your Script Works in Terminal but Fails in Cron

The #1 cron troubleshooting issue: cron runs with a MINIMAL environment. No $PATH (default is just /usr/bin:/bin), no $HOME aliases, no virtualenv activation, no user environment variables. Fix: (1) Always use FULL paths: /usr/bin/pg_dump not pg_dump. (2) Set PATH at the top of your crontab: PATH=/usr/local/bin:/usr/bin:/bin. (3) For Django/virtualenv: 0 2 * * * /var/www/anihpj/venv/bin/python /var/www/anihpj/manage.py clearsessions. (4) Source your environment: 0 2 * * * . /var/www/anihpj/.envrc && /scripts/backup.sh. (5) Redirect stderr to a log file to catch errors: /scripts/backup.sh 2>> /var/log/backup-errors.log. Debug: Add env > /tmp/cron-env.txt as a one-time cron job to see exactly what environment cron provides.

37.2 anacron — Run Missed Jobs

Featurecronanacron
PrecisionExact time (2:00 AM)Period-based (daily, weekly)
Server off at scheduled time?Job SKIPPEDJob RUNS on next boot
Best forAlways-on serversLaptops, servers that reboot often
Config filecrontab -e/etc/anacrontab
Format5 time fieldsPERIOD DELAY JOB-ID COMMAND

Example /etc/anacrontab: 1 5 cron.daily run-parts /etc/cron.daily — runs daily jobs, 5 minutes after boot if missed. When to use: On anihpj dev servers that developers frequently reboot — anacron ensures daily log rotation and cleanup still happen.

🔬 Migrating from Cron to systemd Timers — A Practical Strategy

Most production servers accumulate cron jobs over years. Migrating to systemd timers gives you better logging, dependency management, and centralized visibility. Migration strategy: (1) Inventory all cron jobs: for user in $(cut -d: -f1 /etc/passwd); do echo "=== $user ==="; sudo crontab -u $user -l 2>/dev/null; done plus cat /etc/crontab /etc/cron.d/*. (2) Categorize: Simple periodic tasks (every 5 min, hourly) → systemd timers with OnCalendar=. Complex schedules (every 2nd Tuesday) → keep in cron. (3) Convert one at a time: For each cron job, create a oneshot .service file with the command, then a .timer file with the schedule. Enable the timer, DISABLE the cron job (comment it out — don't delete yet). (4) Monitor for a week: systemctl list-timers and journalctl -u job-name.service — verify the timer fires and the job succeeds. (5) Remove the old cron entry only after confirming the timer works reliably. Example conversion: Cron: */5 * * * * /scripts/health-check.sh becomes a health-check.service (Type=oneshot, ExecStart=/scripts/health-check.sh) + health-check.timer (OnCalendar=*:0/5, Persistent=true). Benefits after migration: systemctl list-timers shows ALL scheduled tasks in one place. journalctl -u health-check.service shows all output with timestamps. Failed jobs can trigger OnFailure=notify@%i.service to send alerts. Do NOT migrate jobs that use complex cron syntax (like 0 0 1-7 * 1 for "first Monday") — systemd timers can't express all cron patterns. Keep ~10% of jobs in cron for edge cases, move 90% to timers for visibility.

37.3 systemd Timers — Modern Alternative to Cron

⏰ cron — Simple & Universal

Every Linux admin knows it. 5-field syntax. Works everywhere. No dependencies — fire and forget. Best for simple recurring tasks that don't need complex dependencies.

⚡ systemd Timer — Powerful & Integrated

Second-precision. Journald logging. Service dependencies. Randomized delays. Persistent catch-up. systemctl list-timers shows everything. Best for service-integrated health checks.

Complete systemd Timer for Anihpj Health Check
  # /etc/systemd/system/anihpj-healthcheck.service
  [Unit]
  Description=Anihpj Health Check
  After=network.target

  [Service]
  Type=oneshot
  ExecStart=/usr/local/bin/anihpj-healthcheck.sh
  User=anihpj

  # /etc/systemd/system/anihpj-healthcheck.timer
  [Unit]
  Description=Run Anihpj health check every 5 minutes

  [Timer]
  OnCalendar=*:0/5           # Every 5 minutes
  Persistent=true              # Catch up if server was off
  RandomizedDelaySec=30        # Stagger ±30s to avoid thundering herd

  [Install]
  WantedBy=timers.target

  # Enable and start:
  sudo systemctl enable --now anihpj-healthcheck.timer

  # Check status:
  systemctl list-timers
  # NEXT                        LEFT       LAST
  # Mon 2026-06-11 14:25:00     3min ago   Mon 2026-06-11 14:20:00

  # Key advantages over cron:
  # ✅ Second-level precision (OnUnitActiveSec=30s)
  # ✅ Logging in journalctl (journalctl -u anihpj-healthcheck)
  # ✅ Dependencies (After=postgresql.service)
  # ✅ Random delay (RandomizedDelaySec=) — no thundering herd
  # ✅ Missed job catchup (Persistent=true)

37.4 at — One-Time Scheduled Commands

CommandWhat It Does
at 14:30Schedule command for 2:30 PM today (interactive prompt)
echo "systemctl restart nginx" | at 03:00Pipe command directly — restart nginx at 3 AM
at now + 30 minutesRun 30 minutes from now
at 02:00 tomorrowRun tomorrow at 2 AM
atqList pending at jobs with job numbers
atrm 3Remove job #3 from the queue
at -f script.sh 22:00Schedule a script file to run at 10 PM

Anihpj use case: echo "systemctl restart anihpj" | at 03:00 Sun — schedule a maintenance restart for 3 AM Sunday. Check with atq. Cancel with atrm if maintenance is postponed.

🔬 How the at Daemon (atd) Works — One-Shot Scheduling Internals

The at daemon (atd) maintains a queue of pending jobs in /var/spool/atjobs/ — each job is stored as a file containing the command, environment variables, and execution time. atd checks the queue periodically (typically every 60 seconds) and executes jobs whose time has arrived. Key behaviors: (1) at jobs inherit the CURRENT environment (working directory, environment variables, umask) at the time of scheduling — unlike cron's minimal environment. (2) Output is EMAILED to the user (via sendmail/postfix) — if mail isn't configured, output is lost. Redirect to a file: echo "/scripts/backup.sh > /var/log/backup.log 2>&1" | at 02:00. (3) at jobs run ONCE and are deleted — they don't repeat. (4) at.allow and at.deny: Like cron, at has access control files in /etc/at.allow and /etc/at.deny. Default: only root and users in at.allow can use at. (5) batch command: A variant of at that runs jobs when system load drops below a threshold (default 1.5) — useful for CPU-intensive maintenance tasks: echo "pg_dump anihpj_db" | batch. Check atd: systemctl status atd — must be running for at jobs to execute. If atd is stopped, all pending jobs are saved and will execute when atd starts again.

Q5
What's the difference between cron and anacron? When would you use anacron for anihpj?
Click to reveal answer
✅ Answer

cron runs jobs at EXACT times — if the server is off at 2 AM, the backup is SKIPPED until tomorrow. anacron runs jobs based on PERIOD — if the server was off for 24 hours, anacron runs missed daily jobs on next boot. Use anacron for anihpj dev/staging servers that developers frequently reboot — ensures log rotation and cleanup still happen even if the server was off during the scheduled window.

Q10

✅ Answer

/var/spool/cron/crontabs/  # per-user crontabs (managed by crontab -e)
📖 Explanation

Cron is the original Unix task scheduler. Five time fields define when a job runs. Cron's minimal environment (no .bashrc, stripped PATH) is the #1 reason scripts fail in cron but work interactively. The flags -wide control how this command behaves. Understanding what each flag does — not just memorizing the combination — lets you adapt when the exam presents a variation. Verify with crontab -l. Test the command manually first. Check /var/log/syslog for cron execution logs. Flag hard tasks and return later. Spending 15 minutes on one task guarantees you'll run out of time for 3-4 easier ones.

38.1 Complete Server Build — Step by Step

1
Base System

Ubuntu 22.04 LTS. Update, set hostname & timezone, create admin user, SSH key-only, disable root login, UFW allow 22/80/443.

2
Dependencies

Python 3.11 + venv + pip. PostgreSQL 15. Nginx + Certbot. Redis (optional). All installed and running via systemctl.

3
Application Setup

Create anihpj user (nologin). Clone/deploy code. Virtualenv + pip install. .env (chmod 600). Create PostgreSQL DB + user. Migrate + collectstatic.

4
Services

Gunicorn systemd unit. Nginx reverse proxy config. SSL via certbot. UFW verify. All services enabled on boot.

5
Maintenance

Log rotation (logrotate). Nightly backup cron. fail2ban SSH+Nginx. Health check timer. Monitoring baseline.

Anihpj Deployment Pipeline — From Code to Production

  └────────────┘ └──────────┘ └──────────┘ └─────────────┘

  IF DEPLOYMENT FAILS:
