44.1 Why SysAdmins Need Git

Git is a distributed version control system that tracks every change to every file. For sysadmins, this is a superpower: every configuration change becomes traceable, reversible, and auditable.

📝
Track Config Changes

Every change to /etc/nginx/nginx.conf, /etc/ssh/sshd_config, or systemd unit files is recorded with who changed it, when, and why.

⏪
Instant Rollback

Bad config change broke something? git checkout -- file restores the last good version instantly. No backup tape, no manual copy-paste.

🚀
Deploy Code

git pull origin main on production deploys the latest application code in seconds. Combined with systemctl restart, you have a complete deployment pipeline.

🤝
Collaborate on IaC

Ansible playbooks, Terraform configs, Dockerfiles — all stored in Git. Multiple admins can work on infrastructure code without stepping on each other.

😰 Managing Configs WITHOUT Git
  • 🔴 "Who changed the SSH port?" — Nobody knows, no audit trail
  • 🔴 "The nginx config broke everything — what was the old version?" — Hope you made a backup!
  • 🔴 "I need to deploy the new code to production" — SCP files manually, pray nothing is missing
  • 🔴 "Two admins edited the same config file" — Changes overwrite each other silently
🎉 Managing Configs WITH Git
  • ✅ git log /etc/nginx/nginx.conf — Full history: who, when, what, why
  • ✅ git checkout HEAD~1 /etc/nginx/nginx.conf — Instant rollback to yesterday's config
  • ✅ git pull && systemctl restart — One-command deployment
  • ✅ Git merge handles conflicts — nobody's changes are silently lost

44.2 Essential Git Commands

CommandWhat It DoesLFCS Context
git clone URLDownload repository to local directoryClone anihpj repo to /opt/anihpj
git statusWhat changed since last commit?Check if config files were modified
git diffShow unstaged changes line by lineSee exactly what changed in nginx.conf
git diff --stagedShow staged (ready to commit) changesReview before commit
git add fileStage specific file for commitgit add /etc/nginx/nginx.conf
git add .Stage ALL changed files in current directoryQuick — be sure you want everything!
git commit -m "message"Create a commit with messageAlways descriptive: "Fix: DB connection timeout 30s→60s"
git push origin mainUpload commits to remote repositoryPush to GitHub/GitLab
git pull origin mainDownload + merge remote changesDeploy latest code on production
git log --oneline -5Last 5 commits in compact formatQuick history check
git branchList all local branches* marks current branch
git checkout -b feature-xCreate and switch to new branchBranch before making risky changes
git merge feature-xMerge branch into current branchBring feature into main
git checkout -- fileUndo uncommitted change (restore from last commit)⚠️ Destroys changes permanently!
git remote -vShow remote repository URLsVerify you're pushing to the right place
🧬 Git Internals — How Git Stores Your Data (Objects)
┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│  GIT IS A CONTENT-ADDRESSABLE FILESYSTEM — everything is an object   │
│                                                                      │
│  THE 4 OBJECT TYPES (stored in .git/objects/XX/XXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXX) │
│                                                                      │
│  ┌──────────┬────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐  │
│  │  BLOB    │ Compressed file content (NO filename, NO metadata) │  │
│  │          │ Hash = SHA1(file content) — same content = same hash│  │
│  │          │ Example: echo "hello" | git hash-object --stdin    │  │
│  │          │          → ce013625030ba8dba906f756967f9e9ca394464a│  │
│  ├──────────┼────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤  │
│  │  TREE    │ Directory listing: maps filenames → blobs + trees  │  │
│  │          │ Stores: mode (100644=file, 040000=dir), type, hash,│  │
│  │          │ name. A tree = a snapshot of a directory.          │  │
│  │          │ git ls-tree HEAD   → see the root tree             │  │
│  ├──────────┼────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤  │
│  │  COMMIT  │ Points to a tree (snapshot) + parent commit(s)     │  │
│  │          │ Contains: tree hash, parent hash(es), author,      │  │
│  │          │ committer, timestamp, message.                     │  │
│  │          │ git cat-file -p HEAD  → see commit object contents │  │
│  ├──────────┼────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤  │
│  │  TAG     │ Human-readable name pointing to a commit           │  │
│  │          │ Annotated tags: full object with message.          │  │
│  │          │ Lightweight tags: just a file with commit hash.    │  │
│  └──────────┴────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘  │
│                                                                      │
│  HOW A COMMIT WORKS (the DAG — Directed Acyclic Graph):              │
│                                                                      │
│  commit A  ←── commit B  ←── commit C  (main branch)                │
│       │            │            │                                     │
│       └── tree X   └── tree Y   └── tree Z  (each tree = snapshot)  │
│                                                                      │
│  • Every commit points to its parent(s) → forms a chain              │
│  • Branch = a movable pointer to a commit (refs/heads/main)          │
│  • HEAD = pointer to current branch (ref: refs/heads/main)           │
│  • Detached HEAD = HEAD points directly to a commit (no branch)      │
│                                                                      │
│  EXPLORE YOUR REPO:                                                  │
│  git log --graph --oneline --all  → visual DAG of all branches      │
│  git cat-file -t HEAD             → "commit"                        │
│  git cat-file -p HEAD             → see what HEAD contains           │
│  find .git/objects -type f | wc -l → how many objects in your repo  │
└──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
📝 Git Workflow for Anihpj Deployment
┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│                                                                      │
│  DEV MACHINE (your laptop)              PRODUCTION SERVER            │
│  ┌────────────────────────────┐         ┌─────────────────────────┐ │
│  │ $ git clone anihpj repo    │         │ $ cd /opt/anihpj        │ │
│  │ $ vim settings.py          │         │ $ git pull origin main  │ │
│  │ $ git diff                 │         │   → downloads latest    │ │
│  │ $ git add settings.py      │         │ $ sudo systemctl restart│ │
│  │ $ git commit -m            │         │   anihpj                │ │
│  │   "fix: DB pool=50"        │         │                         │ │
│  │ $ git push origin main ────┼────────▶│ Deployed in seconds!    │ │
│  └────────────────────────────┘         └─────────────────────────┘ │
│                                                                      │
│  ROLLBACK (if deployment breaks something):                          │
│  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐   │
│  │ $ git log --oneline -5           # find last good commit     │   │
│  │   a1b2c3d fix: DB pool=50       # ← THIS is latest (broken) │   │
│  │   e4f5g6h feat: cache layer     # ← LAST GOOD               │   │
│  │   i7j8k9l fix: nginx timeout                                 │   │
│  │                                                              │   │
│  │ $ git checkout e4f5g6h           # go back to last good      │   │
│  │ $ sudo systemctl restart anihpj  # restart with old code     │   │
│  │ → Instant rollback! No backup tape, no manual copy-paste.   │   │
│  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘   │
└──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

44.3 etckeeper — Automatic Git for /etc

etckeeper is a brilliant tool that automatically tracks your entire /etc directory in Git. Every time APT installs, removes, or upgrades a package, etckeeper automatically creates a commit showing exactly what changed. This gives you a complete, searchable history of every system configuration change.

📂 etckeeper Workflow — Automatic /etc Version Control
# Install etckeeper
$ sudo apt install etckeeper
→ etckeeper initializes a git repo in /etc automatically
→ Hooks are installed: pre-install, post-install for apt

# Every apt operation creates a commit:
$ sudo apt install nginx
→ etckeeper: committing changes to /etc before apt runs
→ apt installs nginx (adds /etc/nginx/* files)
→ etckeeper: committing changes to /etc after apt finishes

# View the history:
$ cd /etc && git log --oneline -5
a1b2c3d daily autocommit (apt changes)
e4f5g6h saving uncommitted changes before apt run
i7j8k9l daily autocommit (apt changes)
k0l1m2n initial commit — /etc as of installation

# See what a specific package changed:
$ git log -p -- etc/ssh/sshd_config
→ Shows every line added/removed in SSH config over time

# Find who changed a config (via sudo):
$ git log -- etc/nginx/nginx.conf
→ Commits show which sudo user made the change

# Roll back a bad change:
$ git diff HEAD~1 etc/ssh/sshd_config  # What changed last time?
$ git checkout HEAD~1 -- etc/ssh/sshd_config  # Restore previous version
$ sudo systemctl restart sshd  # Apply the restored config
💡 etckeeper Pro Tips: (1) It works with Bazaar, Mercurial, and Darcs too — but Git is the default. (2) The daily autocommit catches any changes made outside of apt (manual edits). (3) Combine with a remote Git repo (git remote add origin git@github.com:team/server-configs.git) for off-server backups and team collaboration. (4) Use git log -S 'search-term' to find when a specific string was added/removed across all of /etc.

44.4 LFCS Git Scenarios — What You'll Actually Do

The LFCS exam tests Git in a practical, terminal-only context. You won't be asked theory — you'll be given a task like "clone this repo, make a change, commit, and push" and expected to execute it in the terminal. Here are the key scenarios:

ScenarioCommandsWhat LFCS Tests
Clone a repogit clone URL /opt/anihpjCan you download code to the right directory?
Check statuscd /opt/anihpj && git statusDo you know how to see what changed?
View changesgit diff or git diff --stagedCan you inspect before committing?
Stage + commitgit add . && git commit -m "msg"Can you create a meaningful commit?
Undo changesgit checkout -- fileCan you revert an uncommitted mistake?
Push changesgit push origin mainCan you share your work with the team?
Pull updatesgit pull origin mainCan you deploy the latest code?
View historygit log --oneline -5Can you see what's been done recently?
Branchgit checkout -b featureCan you isolate work on a branch?
⚠️ LFCS Gotcha: The exam environment may have Git pre-installed but NOT configured. If you get "Please tell me who you are" errors, run: git config --global user.email "exam@example.com" && git config --global user.name "Exam Candidate". This is one of the most common reasons candidates lose time on Git tasks!

Chapter 45: ACLs Deep Dive & LDAP Integration

Standard Linux permissions (owner-group-other) only support 3 levels. ACLs (Access Control Lists) let you grant specific permissions to specific users and groups — beyond what rwx alone can do. LDAP centralizes user accounts so one user database serves all your servers. The LFCS exam tests both: setfacl/getfacl for ACLs and basic LDAP client configuration via SSSD.

🆕 2026 Topic⏱️ ~1.5 hours🔐 Access

🎯 What You'll Learn

  • ✅ Set per-user and per-group ACLs with setfacl
  • ✅ Understand ACL mask and default ACLs
  • ✅ Configure LDAP client authentication with SSSD

45.1 Why ACLs? — Beyond Traditional rwx

Standard Linux permissions follow the owner-group-other model: exactly three levels of access. This works for simple cases but breaks down in real-world scenarios:

❌ Standard Perms Can't Do This

"Alice needs read-write, Bob needs read-only, Carol needs no access, and the developers group needs read-execute — ALL on the same file." With standard permissions, you can only assign ONE group — everyone else falls to "other." Impossible.

✅ ACLs Make It Easy

setfacl -m u:alice:rw,u:bob:r,u:carol:-,g:devs:rx file — done! Each user and group gets their own specific permissions, independent of everyone else. No more compromising security because of permission model limitations.

Files with ACLs show a + at the end of the permission string in ls -l output: -rwxrwx---+. This is your visual cue that there are extended permissions beyond the standard rwx. The + is critical — always look for it when troubleshooting permission issues.

🔍 Real-World ACL Scenario: anihpj Shared Directory
  • 🔴 Without ACLs: /projects/anihpj/ is owned by root:developers with 770. Alice (in developers) has full access, but Bob (a contractor in the "contractors" group) can't even read the code. You'd have to add Bob to the developers group — giving him more access than intended.
  • ✅ With ACLs: setfacl -m u:bob:rx /projects/anihpj/ — Bob gets read+execute only, without being added to the developers group. His access is precisely limited to what he needs.

45.2 setfacl & getfacl

CommandWhat It Does
getfacl fileView ACL entries
setfacl -m u:alice:rw fileGive alice read+write
setfacl -m g:devs:r fileGive devs group read
setfacl -x u:alice fileRemove alice's ACL
setfacl -b fileRemove ALL ACLs (reset to standard perms)
setfacl -R -m g:devs:rwx dir/Recursive application
setfacl -d -m g:devs:rw dir/Default ACL — new files inherit
🗄️ How ACLs Are Stored — Extended Attributes (xattrs) Deep Dive
┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│  ACLs ARE STORED AS EXTENDED ATTRIBUTES on the inode                 │
│                                                                      │
│  STANDARD PERMISSIONS (always present in the inode):                 │
│  ┌────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐     │
│  │  Inode stores: mode (rwx bits) + UID + GID                 │     │
│  │  These are the standard chmod/chown-able permissions       │     │
│  │  Limited to: owner (1 user) + group (1 group) + other      │     │
│  └────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘     │
│                                                                      │
│  ACLs (stored in the 'system.posix_acl_access' xattr):               │
│  ┌────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐     │
│  │  Each inode can have additional xattr key-value pairs:      │     │
│  │                                                              │     │
│  │  system.posix_acl_access  →  access ACL (read/write/exec)   │     │
│  │  system.posix_acl_default →  default ACL (inheritance)      │     │
│  │                                                              │     │
│  │  SEE THE RAW DATA:                                          │     │
│  │  getfattr -n system.posix_acl_access file                   │     │
│  │  getfattr -d file              → all xattrs on file         │     │
│  │  attr -l file                  → list xattr names           │     │
│  │                                                              │     │
│  │  FILESYSTEM REQUIREMENTS:                                    │     │
│  │  ext4, XFS, btrfs → ✅ Native xattr support                 │     │
│  │  NFS → ⚠️ Depends on server-side config                     │     │
│  │  tmpfs, FAT32 → ❌ No xattr support                         │     │
│  │  Mount check: mount | grep 'acl' or tune2fs -l /dev/sda1    │     │
│  │  (Usually enabled by default on modern distros!)            │     │
│  └────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘     │
│                                                                      │
│  WHY ls -l SHOWS '+': The kernel checks for the                     │
│  system.posix_acl_access xattr on every ls -l call. If present,     │
│  it appends '+' to the permission string. This is a cheap check     │
│  — the kernel doesn't read the whole ACL, just checks if the        │
│  xattr exists.                                                       │
└──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
🔐 ACL In Action — Anihpj Shared Directory
$ ls -la /projects/anihpj/
drwxrwx---+ 2 root developers 4096 May 24 anihpj/
           ^── '+' means ACLs are set!

$ getfacl /projects/anihpj/
# file: /projects/anihpj/
# owner: root
# group: developers
user::rwx                                ← owner (root) has full access
user:alice:rwx                           ← alice gets FULL access (ACL!)
user:bob:r-x                             ← bob gets read+execute only (ACL!)
group::rwx                               ← developers group has full access
group:interns:r-x                        ← interns group: read+execute (ACL!)
mask::rwx                                ← effective ceiling = rwx
other::---                               ← NOBODY else gets anything

🎯 With standard permissions (owner-group-other), this is IMPOSSIBLE.
   Only ONE group can have group permissions — with ACLs, you can give
   Alice rwx, Bob rx, interns rx, developers rwx — ALL on the same file.

45.3 ACL Mask — The Silent Permission Ceiling

The ACL mask is the maximum permission ceiling for all named users (except the file owner) and all named groups. Think of it as a "cap" — even if you give Alice rwx, if the mask is r-x, Alice cannot write. The mask does NOT affect the file owner or the "other" permissions.

🔐 How the ACL Mask Works — Permission Calculation
$ setfacl -m u:alice:rwx file
$ setfacl -m m::r-x file      # Set mask to read+execute only
$ getfacl file
user::rwx                       # Owner (root) — mask does NOT apply
user:alice:rwx       #effective:r-x   ← Mask capped alice's write!
group::r-x
group:devs:rwx        #effective:r-x   ← Mask capped devs' write!
mask::r-x                       # This is the ceiling
other::---

CALCULATION: Effective = Requested AND Mask
  alice wants rwx, mask is r-x → effective = r-x (write stripped!)
  devs wants rwx, mask is r-x  → effective = r-x (write stripped!)

KEY RULES:
  • Mask limits ALL named users (except owner) and named groups
  • Owner permissions (user::) are NEVER affected by the mask
  • Other permissions (other::) are NEVER affected by the mask
  • Default mask = union of all group + named user permissions
  • setfacl -m m::rwx file   → explicitly set mask
  • setfacl -b file          → remove all ACLs including mask
⚠️ The Mask Trap: The most common ACL confusion: "I gave Alice rwx with setfacl, but she can't write!" The culprit is almost always the mask. Always check getfacl output for #effective: annotations — they tell you the real permissions after the mask is applied. If you see #effective:r-x when you expected rwx, the mask is restricting access.

45.4 LDAP — Enterprise Identity Management

Centralized user database. Instead of /etc/passwd on each server → single LDAP server. Add user once → available everywhere. Common: OpenLDAP, Active Directory, FreeIPA. LFCS tests configuring a Linux client to use LDAP.

🏢 LDAP Architecture — Centralized vs Local Users
┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│                                                                      │
│  WITHOUT LDAP (Local Users — ❌ Painful):                            │
│  ┌──────────┐  ┌──────────┐  ┌──────────┐                          │
│  │Server A  │  │Server B  │  │Server C  │                          │
│  │/etc/passwd│  │/etc/passwd│  │/etc/passwd│                          │
│  │/etc/shadow│  │/etc/shadow│  │/etc/shadow│                          │
│  │alice:x:1001│  │alice:x:1002│  │alice:x:1003│  ← Different UIDs!   │
│  └──────────┘  └──────────┘  └──────────┘                          │
│  ❌ Add user → update ALL 3 servers manually                        │
│  ❌ Change password → update ALL 3 servers                          │
│  ❌ Decommission user → delete from ALL 3 servers                   │
│                                                                      │
│  WITH LDAP (Centralized — ✅ Efficient):                             │
│  ┌──────────┐  ┌──────────┐  ┌──────────┐                          │
│  │Server A  │  │Server B  │  │Server C  │                          │
│  │sssd.conf │  │sssd.conf │  │sssd.conf │                          │
│  └────┬─────┘  └────┬─────┘  └────┬─────┘                          │
│       │             │             │                                  │
│       └─────────────┼─────────────┘                                  │
│                     │                                                │
│              ┌──────┴──────┐                                         │
│              │ LDAP SERVER │                                         │
│              │ (OpenLDAP   │                                         │
│              │  or FreeIPA)│                                         │
│              │             │                                         │
│              │ uid=alice   │  ← ONE record for alice                │
│              │ uid=1001    │  ← Same UID everywhere                 │
│              │ passwd: *** │  ← ONE password                        │
│              └─────────────┘                                         │
│  ✅ Add user ONCE → available on ALL servers                        │
│  ✅ Change password ONCE → changed everywhere                      │
│  ✅ Disable user ONCE → locked out of ALL servers                   │
└──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
📋 LDAP Schema Deep Dive — How User Data Is Organized (DIT)
┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│  LDAP DIRECTORY TREE (DIT — Directory Information Tree)              │
│                                                                      │
│  dc=company,dc=com                          ← Root suffix (domain)   │
│  ├── ou=People,dc=company,dc=com            ← Users branch           │
│  │   ├── uid=alice,ou=People,dc=company,dc=com                      │
│  │   │   objectClass: inetOrgPerson, posixAccount, shadowAccount    │
│  │   │   uid: alice          cn: Alice Smith                        │
│  │   │   uidNumber: 1001     gidNumber: 1001                        │
│  │   │   homeDirectory: /home/alice                                 │
│  │   │   loginShell: /bin/bash                                      │
│  │   │   userPassword: {SSHA}encrypted_hash...                      │
│  │   └── uid=bob,ou=People,dc=company,dc=com  (same schema)         │
│  ├── ou=Groups,dc=company,dc=com           ← Groups branch          │
│  │   ├── cn=anihpj-devs,ou=Groups,dc=company,dc=com                 │
│  │   │   objectClass: posixGroup                                    │
│  │   │   gidNumber: 2001                                            │
│  │   │   memberUid: alice, bob, carol                               │
│  │   └── cn=anihpj-admins,ou=Groups,dc=company,dc=com               │
│  └── ou=Services,dc=company,dc=com         ← Service accounts       │
│      └── uid=anihpj-svc,ou=Services,dc=company,dc=com               │
│                                                                      │
│  LDAP SEARCH FILTERS (the query language — RFC 4515):                │
│  ┌────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐     │
│  │  ldapsearch -x -b "dc=company,dc=com" "(uid=alice)"        │     │
│  │    → Find user alice anywhere in the tree                   │     │
│  │                                                              │     │
│  │  ldapsearch -x -b "ou=Groups,dc=company,dc=com" \           │     │
│  │    "(&(objectClass=posixGroup)(memberUid=alice))"           │     │
│  │    → Find ALL groups alice belongs to (AND)                 │     │
│  │                                                              │     │
│  │  ldapsearch -x -b "dc=company,dc=com" \                      │     │
│  │    "(|(uid=alice)(uid=bob))" cn mail                         │     │
│  │    → Find alice OR bob, return only cn + mail               │     │
│  │                                                              │     │
│  │  FILTER OPERATORS:  & = AND, | = OR, ! = NOT, * = wildcard  │     │
│  │  (&(objectClass=person)(!(uid=alice)))  → all people NOT alice│    │
│  └────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘     │
│                                                                      │
│  COMMON objectClasses FOR LINUX (POSIX integration):                 │
│  posixAccount   → uid, uidNumber, gidNumber, homeDir, loginShell     │
│  posixGroup     → cn, gidNumber, memberUid (members by username)     │
│  shadowAccount  → userPassword, shadowLastChange, shadowMax, etc.    │
│  inetOrgPerson  → cn, sn, givenName, mail (human-readable identity)  │
│                                                                      │
│  WHY THIS MATTERS: SSSD reads these attributes to populate the       │
│  local cache. getent passwd alice → SSSD queries LDAP, caches result │
│  locally. The mapping: uid→username, uidNumber→UID, gidNumber→GID,   │
│  homeDirectory→home, loginShell→shell. Same as /etc/passwd!          │
└──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

45.5 Configuring LDAP Client (SSSD)

StepCommand / Path
Installapt install sssd libpam-sss libnss-sss sssd-tools
Config/etc/sssd/sssd.conf (chmod 600!)
nsswitchpasswd: files sss in /etc/nsswitch.conf
PAMauth sufficient pam_sss.so in /etc/pam.d/common-auth
Restartsystemctl restart sssd
Testgetent passwd alice — should show LDAP user

45.6 LDAP + anihpj — Enterprise Use Case in Practice

In a real anihpj deployment across multiple servers, LDAP is the backbone of identity management:

🔑
Single Sign-On

Developers use the same LDAP password for SSH, anihpj admin panel, PostgreSQL access, and internal tools. One password change updates everywhere.

👥
Group-Based Access

SSH access controlled by LDAP group membership: cn=anihpj-devs,ou=groups,dc=company,dc=com gets SSH access. Remove from group → SSH access revoked instantly.

🗑️
Instant Decommissioning

Developer leaves the company → disable their LDAP account → access revoked on ALL servers (SSH, DB, app) in seconds. No need to visit each server individually.

📋
Audit Compliance

LDAP logs show every authentication attempt. Combined with sudo logs, you have a complete audit trail: who logged in, from where, and what they did.

🎉 anihpj with LDAP — The Full Picture
  • ✅ New developer hired → Create LDAP account once → instantly can SSH to all dev servers, access anihpj admin, and query the dev database
  • ✅ Password policy enforced centrally → Minimum 12 chars, 90-day rotation, enforced by LDAP server for ALL systems
  • ✅ anihpj service account → Created as a local user (/etc/passwd) for reliability — if LDAP is down, the app still runs
  • ✅ SSH configured with AllowGroups anihpj-devs anihpj-admins — only LDAP groups get SSH, everyone else denied

Q4
How can you tell if a file has ACLs just by looking at ls -l output?
Click to reveal answer
✅ Answer

A + at the end of the permission string indicates ACLs: -rwxrwx---+. Standard permissions show no plus sign.

Check if LDAP user "alice" is recognized by the system.
Click to reveal answer
✅ Answer
getent passwd alice
id alice
📖 Explanation

User management is security fundamentals. UIDs (not usernames) are what the kernel checks. A missing home directory, wrong shell, or incorrect group membership can prevent logins that are otherwise configured correctly. getent is the key tool here. Q6
Give the "developers" group read and execute access to /projects/anihpj/ recursively.
Click to reveal answer
✅ Answer
# Apply to existing files:
setfacl -R -m g:developers:rx /projects/anihpj/
# Set default for NEW files:
setfacl -d -m g:developers:rx /projects/anihpj/
# Verify:
getfacl /projects/anihpj/
📖 Explanation

Linux permissions are the first line of defense. Every file access is checked against the owner-group-others permission bits. ACLs extend this model, letting you grant specific users specific permissions beyond the basic rwx scheme. The flags -R, -m control how this command behaves. Understanding what each flag does — not just memorizing the combination — lets you adapt when the exam presents a variation. Persistent changes require editing config files (/etc/fstab, /etc/sysctl.conf). Runtime commands alone earn zero points for persistence.

Q7
What is the ACL mask and why does it matter?
Click to reveal answer
✅ Answer

The mask is the maximum permission ceiling for all named users and the owning group. Even if you set u:alice:rwx, if the mask is r-x, alice effectively gets only r-x. This is a safety mechanism — you can temporarily lower everyone's permissions without changing individual ACLs. setfacl -m m::rx file sets the mask. The effective permissions shown by getfacl account for the mask (e.g., user:alice:rwx #effective:r-x).

📖 Explanation

Linux permissions are the first line of defense. Every file access is checked against the owner-group-others permission bits. ACLs extend this model, letting you grant specific users specific permissions beyond the basic rwx scheme. The flags -x, -x, -m control how this command behaves. Understanding what each flag does — not just memorizing the combination — lets you adapt when the exam presents a variation. Man pages are available but cost time. Know the common flags by heart; use man only for esoteric options.

Q8
Configure the system to use LDAP for user authentication via SSSD.
Click to reveal answer
✅ Answer
# Step 1: Install
sudo apt install sssd libpam-sss libnss-sss sssd-tools

# Step 2: Configure /etc/sssd/sssd.conf (chmod 600!)
sudo chmod 600 /etc/sssd/sssd.conf

# Step 3: Update /etc/nsswitch.conf
# passwd: files sss
# group: files sss
# shadow: files sss

# Step 4: Configure PAM
# Add to /etc/pam.d/common-auth: auth sufficient pam_sss.so

# Step 5: Start SSSD
sudo systemctl enable --now sssd

# Step 6: Test
getent passwd alice   # Should show LDAP user
📖 Explanation

systemd manages every service on modern Linux. systemctl start activates a unit now; systemctl enable creates the symlink for auto-start at boot. You need both for a persistent service. The flags -sss, -sss, -tools control how this command behaves. Understanding what each flag does — not just memorizing the combination — lets you adapt when the exam presents a variation. Verify with systemctl status unit-name. Look for "Active: active (running)" and check the PID. If it failed, journalctl -xeu unit-name shows why. If a task says "make persistent" or "survive reboot," you MUST write to a file in /etc/. This is the #1 reason candidates lose points.

Q9
An ACL-protected file shows effective permissions different from what you set. Why?
Click to reveal answer
✅ Answer

The ACL mask is limiting the permissions. Even if you set u:alice:rwx, the effective permission is mask & acl. If mask is r-x, alice's effective permission is r-x. Fix: setfacl -m m::rwx file to raise the mask. This commonly happens when you use chmod on a file with ACLs — chmod changes the mask, not individual ACL entries!

Q10
Decommission a user from your LDAP-managed infrastructure. What happens?
Click to reveal answer
✅ Answer

Remove the user from the LDAP directory (or disable their account — set loginShell to /sbin/nologin or add them to a "disabled" group). Within seconds (SSSD cache refresh), the user can no longer authenticate to ANY server using LDAP. SSH, sudo, application login — all blocked instantly across the entire infrastructure. This is the power of centralized authentication: one change, everywhere, immediately. Compare to local users — you'd need to log into every server and run userdel.

📖 Explanation

This ACLs & LDAP task mirrors real production scenarios. The LFCS exam is 100% hands-on performance-based — knowing the command is only half the battle; you must execute it correctly under time pressure. loginShell is the key tool here. Its man page (man loginShell) is available during the exam if you need to check less common options. Reboot once before submitting (last 5 minutes). This catches non-persistent configs and broken fstab entries before the grader sees them.

🗓️ Day in the Life: Advanced SysAdmin — Part 12 in Practice

From VM provisioning to Git-tracked configuration — how Chapters 39-45 work together:

🖥️ 9:00
Provision Test VM
Ch 39: virt-install

virt-install --name anihpj-test --memory 2048 --vcpus 2 --disk size=20. VM ready in 2 minutes.

📦 9:30
Containerize App
Ch 40: Podman

podman build -t anihpj:v2 . && podman run -d --name app -p 8000:8000 anihpj:v2.

🌉 10:30
Bridge VM to LAN
Ch 41: Network Bridge

ip link add br0 type bridge && ip link set eth0 master br0. VM now on the LAN.

🔌 13:00
Mount Backup Share
Ch 42: autofs

Access /mnt/backups → autofs auto-mounts the NAS. After backup completes → auto-unmounts.

📝 15:00
Track Config Change
Ch 44: Git/etckeeper

Edited nginx config. git add . && git commit -m "updated rate limiting". Full audit trail.

🔐 16:00
Onboard New Dev
Ch 45: LDAP + ACLs

Added dev to LDAP group. setfacl -m g:developers:rwx /var/www/anihpj/. Instant access.

🧩 Part 12 Consolidation — The 2026 Exam Topics: Virtualization (Ch39) and containers (Ch40) represent the future of deployment — VMs for strong isolation, containers for density and speed. Advanced networking (Ch41) connects them to the world — bridges for VMs, bonding for HA, static routes for complex topologies. autofs (Ch42) and storage monitoring (Ch43) ensure your data is accessible and performant. Git (Ch44) tracks every change — making rollbacks trivial. ACLs and LDAP (Ch45) provide the fine-grained access control that standard permissions can't deliver. These seven chapters represent the skills that differentiate a Linux administrator from a Linux power user.

A Essential Commands Reference

Quick-reference tables for every command category tested on LFCS. Each table includes the command, its purpose, common options, and a practical example using anihpj context where applicable. Bookmark this appendix — it's your last-minute review before the exam.

💡 How to Use This Appendix for Maximum Retention

Don't just read the tables — type every command in your terminal. Muscle memory is critical for the LFCS exam where you have limited time and no autocomplete. For each section, cover the "anihpj Example" column and try to write the command from memory. Check your answer, then move on. Spend 15 minutes daily on a different category in the week before your exam — you'll be amazed how much sticks.

❌ Rookie Mistakes on LFCS

Forgetting -r on cp for directories. Using rm -rf without checking pwd first. Trying grep without -r for recursive search. Forgetting that find -exec needs \; at the end.

✅ Pro Moves

cp -a preserves everything. rm -i prompts before each deletion. grep -rin "pattern" /dir/ does case-insensitive recursive search with line numbers. find . -name "*.log" -mtime +30 -delete cleans old logs safely.

A.8 Command Combinations — Real-World Pipelines

The real power of Linux comes from combining commands with pipes (|). Here are the most useful combinations you'll use daily as a sysadmin:

🧠 How Pipes Actually Work — The Kernel's Role
┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│  A PIPE (|) CREATES A KERNEL BUFFER (typically 64KB)                 │
│                                                                      │
│  $ cmd1 | cmd2 | cmd3                                                │
│                                                                      │
│  ┌─────────┐    pipe buffer    ┌─────────┐    pipe buffer    ┌─────────┐
│  │  cmd1   │ ───────────────▶  │  cmd2   │ ───────────────▶  │  cmd3   │
│  │ stdout  │     (64KB)        │ stdin→  │     (64KB)        │ stdin   │
│  │ (write) │                   │ stdout  │                   │ (read)  │
│  └─────────┘                   └─────────┘                   └─────────┘
│                                                                      │
│  KEY INSIGHTS:                                                        │
│  • ALL commands in a pipeline run CONCURRENTLY (not sequentially!)    │
│  • If cmd2 reads slower than cmd1 writes, cmd1 BLOCKS (backpressure)  │
│  • Exit code of pipeline = exit code of LAST command (use $PIPESTATUS)│
│  • pipefail option: pipeline fails if ANY command fails               │
│  • Kernel handles all synchronization — no temp files needed          │
│                                                                      │
│  WHY THIS IS BRILLIANT FOR LARGE FILES:                              │
│  grep ERROR /var/log/huge.log | sort | uniq -c                        │
│  • Without pipes: grep writes to temp file → sort reads temp →        │
│    uniq reads temp → 3x disk I/O for 1GB log = 3GB written!          │
│  • With pipes: data flows through memory, never touches disk          │
│  • Memory usage: only 64KB buffers, even for terabyte-sized input     │
└──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

Here are the most useful combinations you'll use daily as a sysadmin:

🔗 Essential Command Pipelines — LFCS Must-Know Patterns
# FIND & ACT: Find all Python files modified today and list them
find /opt/anihpj -name "*.py" -mtime 0 -exec ls -lh {} \;

# FIND & DELETE: Remove all __pycache__ directories
find /opt/anihpj -type d -name "__pycache__" -exec rm -rf {} \; 2>/dev/null

# FIND LARGE FILES: Top 10 largest files in /var/log
find /var/log -type f -exec du -h {} \; | sort -rh | head -10

# GREP CHAIN: Find ERROR lines, count per hour
grep ERROR /var/log/anihpj/app.log | cut -d' ' -f2 | cut -d: -f1 | sort | uniq -c | sort -rn

# PROCESS ANALYSIS: Top 5 CPU-consuming processes
ps aux --sort=-%cpu | head -6

# DISK ANALYSIS: What's eating your disk space?
du -sh /* 2>/dev/null | sort -rh | head -10

# PORT ANALYSIS: What's listening on which ports?
ss -tlnp | awk '{print $4, $NF}' | sort -u

# LOG ANALYSIS: Count HTTP status codes from nginx access log
awk '{print $9}' /var/log/nginx/access.log | sort | uniq -c | sort -rn

# KERNEL MESSAGES: Last 20 boots
dmesg -T | grep -i error | tail -20

# SYSTEMD ANALYSIS: Which services take longest to boot?
systemd-analyze blame | head -10

# BULK RENAME: Rename all .txt files to .md
for f in *.txt; do mv "$f" "${f%.txt}.md"; done

# PROCESS CHAIN: Kill all processes matching a pattern
ps aux | grep gunicorn | awk '{print $2}' | xargs kill -TERM
# OR simpler: pkill -f gunicorn

B Common LFCS Exam Scenarios & Solutions

Real LFCS exam tasks with complete solutions. Every scenario follows the pattern: exact question → exact commands → exact verification. These are the most commonly tested scenarios — practice them until they become muscle memory.

🎯 LFCS Exam Strategy — How to Approach Tasks: (1) Read the task TWICE — missing a detail like "UID 1500" means 0 points. (2) Verify EVERY step — after creating a user: id username; after editing fstab: mount -a; after configuring a service: systemctl start then systemctl status. (3) Check persistence — if the task says "persistent across reboots" or "permanent," you MUST write to config files (fstab, netplan, systemctl enable). (4) Backup first — cp file.conf file.conf.bak before editing any config file. (5) SSH carefully — when editing network or SSH config, keep a second terminal open in case you lock yourself out. (6) Skip and return — if a task takes more than 5 minutes, flag it and come back. Don't get stuck!
⚠️ The #1 LFCS Exam Mistake

Candidates lose the most points not because they don't know Linux, but because they don't verify their work. After creating a user, run id username. After editing fstab, run mount -a. After configuring a service, run systemctl start name then systemctl status name. If the task says "persistent," reboot the VM if allowed, or at minimum check that config files are correctly written. The difference between passing (65%) and failing (64%) is often one unverified task.

🎯 LFCS Exam Strategy — How to Approach Tasks: (1) Read the task TWICE — missing a detail like "UID 1500" means 0 points. (2) Verify EVERY step — after creating a user: id username; after editing fstab: mount -a; after configuring a service: systemctl start then systemctl status. (3) Check persistence — if the task says "persistent across reboots" or "permanent," you MUST write to config files (fstab, netplan, systemctl enable). (4) Backup first — cp file.conf file.conf.bak before editing any config file. (5) SSH carefully — when editing network or SSH config, keep a second terminal open in case you lock yourself out. (6) Skip and return — if a task takes more than 5 minutes, flag it and come back. Don't get stuck!

B.1 User Management Scenarios

Scenario 1: Create a developer account

Task: Create user "django-dev" with UID 1500, home directory /home/django-dev, bash shell, and add to groups "developers" and "docker".

Solution
sudo groupadd -g 2001 developers
sudo groupadd docker  # may already exist
sudo useradd -m -u 1500 -s /bin/bash -G developers,docker django-dev
# Verify:
grep django-dev /etc/passwd
id django-dev  # should show uid=1500, groups=2001(docker)
Scenario 2: Password aging policy

Task: Set password to expire every 30 days, with 7 days warning, and lock account after 45 days of inactivity for user "django-dev".

Solution
sudo chage -M 30 -W 7 -I 45 django-dev
# Verify:
sudo chage -l django-dev
# Max password age: 30, Warning: 7, Inactive: 45
Scenario 3: Restricted sudo access

Task: Allow "django-dev" to run ONLY systemctl restart anihpj and journalctl -u anihpj without a password.

Solution
sudo visudo -f /etc/sudoers.d/django-dev
# Add:
django-dev ALL=(ALL) NOPASSWD: /usr/bin/systemctl restart anihpj, /usr/bin/journalctl -u anihpj
# Verify:
sudo -l -U django-dev

B.2 Filesystem & Storage Scenarios

Scenario 4: Add new disk for anihpj data

Task: A new 100GB disk (/dev/sdb) is attached. Partition it, format as ext4, mount at /data/anihpj, and make it persistent across reboots.

Solution
# Step 1: Create partition
sudo fdisk /dev/sdb   # n → p → 1 → Enter → Enter → w
# Step 2: Format
sudo mkfs.ext4 /dev/sdb1
# Step 3: Create mount point
sudo mkdir -p /data/anihpj
# Step 4: Mount
sudo mount /dev/sdb1 /data/anihpj
# Step 5: Get UUID and add to fstab
sudo blkid /dev/sdb1  # copy UUID
sudo echo "UUID=xxxx-xxxx /data/anihpj ext4 defaults 0 2" >> /etc/fstab
# Verify: sudo mount -a && df -h /data/anihpj
Scenario 5: Extend LVM volume online

Task: /data/anihpj (on LVM) is 90% full. Extend the logical volume by 50GB without unmounting.

Solution
# Step 1: Check current state
sudo vgs  # is there free space in VG?
df -h /data/anihpj
# Step 2: Extend LV (adds 50GB)
sudo lvextend -L +50G /dev/vg_data/lv_anihpj
# Step 3: Resize filesystem (online!)
sudo resize2fs /dev/vg_data/lv_anihpj
# Verify: df -h /data/anihpj  → now 50GB larger!

B.3 Service Configuration Scenarios

Scenario 6: Nginx virtual host for anihpj

Task: Configure Nginx to serve anihpj on port 80, proxying to Gunicorn on 127.0.0.1:8000.

Solution
sudo vim /etc/nginx/sites-available/anihpj
# Add:
server {
    listen 80;
    server_name anihpj.com www.anihpj.com;
    root /opt/anihpj/static;
    location / {
        proxy_pass http://127.0.0.1:8000;
        proxy_set_header Host $host;
        proxy_set_header X-Real-IP $remote_addr;
    }
    location /static/ {
        alias /opt/anihpj/static/;
    }
}
sudo ln -s /etc/nginx/sites-available/anihpj /etc/nginx/sites-enabled/
sudo nginx -t && sudo systemctl reload nginx
Scenario 7: SSH key auth only

Task: Disable password authentication for SSH — only allow key-based login.

Solution
sudo vim /etc/ssh/sshd_config
# Change/uncomment:
PasswordAuthentication no
PubkeyAuthentication yes
ChallengeResponseAuthentication no
PermitRootLogin prohibit-password
# Verify and reload:
sudo sshd -t && sudo systemctl reload sshd
# TEST from another terminal BEFORE closing current session!

B.4 Networking Scenarios

Scenario 8: Configure static IP

Task: Set static IP 192.168.1.100/24 with gateway 192.168.1.1 and DNS 8.8.8.8 on eth0 — persistent across reboots.

Solution (Netplan — Ubuntu)
sudo vim /etc/netplan/01-netcfg.yaml
network:
  version: 2
  renderer: networkd
  ethernets:
    eth0:
      addresses: [192.168.1.100/24]
      routes:
        - to: default
          via: 192.168.1.1
      nameservers:
        addresses: [8.8.8.8, 1.1.1.1]
sudo netplan apply
# Verify: ip addr show eth0 && ip route show

B.5 Security Scenarios

Scenario 9: Fix web app permissions

Task: /opt/anihpj/ is owned by root:root with 755. The web server (www-data) needs write access to /opt/anihpj/media/ for uploads, but should NOT be able to modify code.

Solution
# Keep code read-only for www-data
sudo chown -R root:root /opt/anihpj/
sudo find /opt/anihpj/ -type d -exec chmod 755 {} \;
sudo find /opt/anihpj/ -type f -exec chmod 644 {} \;
# Give www-data write access ONLY to media/uploads
sudo chown -R www-data:www-data /opt/anihpj/media/
sudo chmod 775 /opt/anihpj/media/
# Verify: sudo -u www-data touch /opt/anihpj/media/test → should work
#         sudo -u www-data touch /opt/anihpj/settings.py → should FAIL
Scenario 10: Configure fail2ban for SSH

Task: Install and configure fail2ban to block IPs after 3 failed SSH attempts within 10 minutes, ban for 1 hour.

Solution
sudo apt install fail2ban
sudo cp /etc/fail2ban/jail.conf /etc/fail2ban/jail.local
sudo vim /etc/fail2ban/jail.local
# Find [sshd] section, set:
[sshd]
enabled = true
maxretry = 3
bantime = 3600
findtime = 600
sudo systemctl enable --now fail2ban
# Verify: sudo fail2ban-client status sshd

B.6 Additional Critical Scenarios

Scenario 11: Create a systemd timer for anihpj cleanup

Task: Create a systemd timer that runs a cleanup script every day at 3 AM to remove temporary files older than 7 days from /tmp/anihpj/.

Solution
# Step 1: Create the cleanup script
sudo vim /usr/local/bin/anihpj-cleanup.sh
#!/bin/bash
find /tmp/anihpj/ -type f -mtime +7 -delete
echo "$(date): Cleaned $(find /tmp/anihpj/ -type f | wc -l) files remaining"
sudo chmod +x /usr/local/bin/anihpj-cleanup.sh

# Step 2: Create systemd service unit
sudo vim /etc/systemd/system/anihpj-cleanup.service
[Unit]
Description=anihpj Temp File Cleanup
[Service]
Type=oneshot
ExecStart=/usr/local/bin/anihpj-cleanup.sh
User=root

# Step 3: Create timer unit
sudo vim /etc/systemd/system/anihpj-cleanup.timer
[Unit]
Description=Daily anihpj cleanup at 3 AM
[Timer]
OnCalendar=daily
Persistent=true
[Install]
WantedBy=timers.target

sudo systemctl enable --now anihpj-cleanup.timer
# Verify: systemctl list-timers | grep anihpj
Scenario 12: Troubleshoot a service that won't start

Task: The anihpj service fails to start after a configuration change. Diagnose and fix the issue.

Systematic Troubleshooting Approach
# Step 1: Check service status for clues
sudo systemctl status anihpj
# Step 2: View recent logs
sudo journalctl -u anihpj --since "5 min ago" -n 50
# Step 3: Check config syntax (if applicable)
# For Python apps: python -c "import anihpj.settings"
# Step 4: Check if port is already in use
sudo ss -tlnp | grep 8000
# Step 5: Check file permissions
ls -la /opt/anihpj/
sudo -u anihpj test -r /opt/anihpj/settings.py && echo "Readable"
# Step 6: Try running manually to see exact error
sudo -u anihpj /opt/anihpj/venv/bin/gunicorn anihpj.wsgi:application --bind 127.0.0.1:8000
# Step 7: Fix the issue (common: wrong permissions, port conflict, missing env vars)
# Step 8: Restart and verify
sudo systemctl daemon-reload
sudo systemctl restart anihpj
systemctl is-active anihpj && echo "UP!"
Scenario 13: Configure log shipping to a remote server

Task: Forward anihpj application logs to a central syslog server at 10.0.0.100 using rsyslog.

Solution
# Step 1: Create rsyslog config
sudo vim /etc/rsyslog.d/50-anihpj-forward.conf
# Forward all anihpj logs to remote server
if $programname == 'anihpj' then @10.0.0.100:514
# OR: Forward a specific log file
module(load="imfile")
input(type="imfile"
      File="/var/log/anihpj/app.log"
      Tag="anihpj-app:"
      Severity="info"
      Facility="local0")
local0.* @@10.0.0.100:514

# Step 2: Restart rsyslog
sudo systemctl restart rsyslog
# Verify: logger -t anihpj "Test message" && ssh 10.0.0.100 "tail /var/log/syslog"

📊 Appendix B Exam Strategy

🎯
Read TwiceLFCS tasks are specific — read carefully. "Create user with UID 1500" means you MUST use -u 1500, not accept defaults.
✅
Verify EverythingAfter every task, verify it worked: grep /etc/passwd, df -h, systemctl status. This catches mistakes early.
🔄
Check PersistenceDid your change survive a reboot? Mount point in fstab? Service enabled? If the exam spec says "persistent", you MUST make it persistent.

C Shell Scripting Quick Reference

Shell scripting is tested throughout the LFCS exam — you may need to write a script to automate a task, parse logs, or schedule maintenance. This appendix covers all the syntax patterns you need, from basic variables to error handling.

💡 The Golden Rules of Shell Scripting for LFCS

(1) Always start with #!/bin/bash — not sh, not dash. Bash has features (arrays, [[ ]], regex) that POSIX sh doesn't. (2) Always use set -euo pipefail — this one line prevents 90% of scripting bugs. (3) Quote your variables: "$var" not $var — unquoted variables split on spaces and break with filenames containing spaces. (4) Use [[ ]] not [ ] — double brackets are safer (no word splitting) and support regex (=~). (5) Test with shellcheck script.sh — it catches common bugs before they bite you.

❌ Common Scripting Pitfalls

if [ $var = "value" ] — breaks if var is empty (becomes [ = "value" ]). cat file | grep pattern — useless use of cat. for f in $(ls) — breaks on filenames with spaces. No error handling — script continues after failures, causing chaos.

✅ Pro Scripting Patterns

if [[ $var == "value" ]] — safe with empty vars. grep pattern file — no cat needed. for f in *.txt — safe globbing. set -euo pipefail + trap cleanup EXIT — production-grade robustness.

C.1 Variables & Substitution

Variable Syntax — All Patterns
# Basic assignment (NO spaces around =)
name="anihpj"
version=2

# Variable expansion
$name           → anihpj
echo "${name}"   → anihpj (always use {} in strings!)

# Default values
${var:-default}   → use 'default' if var is unset or empty
${var:=default}   → assign 'default' if var is unset + use it
${var:?error}     → print error and exit if var is unset

# String manipulation
file="settings.py"
${file%.py}       → "settings" (remove shortest suffix)
${file%%.*}       → "settings" (remove longest suffix)
${file#*.}        → "py" (remove shortest prefix)
${file/old/new}   → replace first match
${file//old/new}  → replace ALL matches

# Length
${#var}           → length of var

# Command substitution
now=$(date +%Y%m%d)
files=$(ls /opt/anihpj/)
# OLD style (avoid): `date +%Y%m%d`

C.2 Conditionals — if/elif/else & test Operators

Conditional Patterns
# STRING TESTS ([[]] preferred over [])
[[ -z "$var" ]]         # true if var is empty
[[ -n "$var" ]]         # true if var is NOT empty
[[ "$a" == "$b" ]]      # string equality
[[ "$a" != "$b" ]]      # string inequality
[[ "$a" =~ regex ]]     # regex match (bash 3+)

# NUMERIC TESTS
[[ $num -eq 5 ]]        # equal
[[ $num -ne 5 ]]        # not equal
[[ $num -lt 5 ]]        # less than
[[ $num -gt 5 ]]        # greater than
[[ $num -le 5 ]]        # less or equal
[[ $num -ge 5 ]]        # greater or equal

# FILE TESTS
[[ -f "$file" ]]        # is regular file?
[[ -d "$dir" ]]         # is directory?
[[ -x "$script" ]]      # is executable?
[[ -r "$file" ]]        # is readable?
[[ -w "$file" ]]        # is writable?
[[ -s "$file" ]]        # exists and size > 0?
[[ -e "$path" ]]        # exists (any type)?

# LOGICAL OPERATORS
[[ $a && $b ]]          # AND
[[ $a || $b ]]          # OR
[[ ! $a ]]              # NOT

# IF/ELIF/ELSE PATTERN
if [[ -f /opt/anihpj/settings.py ]]; then
    echo "Config found"
elif [[ -f /etc/anihpj/settings.py ]]; then
    echo "Using system config"
else
    echo "ERROR: No config found" >&2
    exit 1
fi

C.3 Loops — for, while, until, read

Loop Patterns
# FOR LOOP (items)
for app in anihpj jobpost celery; do
    echo "Deploying $app..."
    systemctl restart "$app"
done

# FOR LOOP (C-style)
for ((i=1; i<=5; i++)); do
    echo "Attempt $i"
    curl -s http://localhost:8000/health && break
    sleep 2
done

# FOR LOOP (globbing)
for file in /opt/anihpj/*.py; do
    echo "Processing $file"
done

# WHILE LOOP
count=0
while [[ $count -lt 10 ]]; do
    echo "$count"
    ((count++))
done

# WHILE READ (line by line)
while IFS= read -r line; do
    echo "$line"
done < /etc/anihpj/hosts.conf

# UNTIL LOOP (opposite of while)
until systemctl is-active anihpj; do
    echo "Waiting for anihpj..."
    sleep 2
done
echo "anihpj is up!"

C.4 Functions & Return Values

Function Syntax
# Define a function
check_service() {
    local service=$1      # local variable (best practice!)
    if systemctl is-active --quiet "$service"; then
        echo "$service is running"
        return 0           # success
    else
        echo "$service is DOWN!" >&2
        return 1           # failure
    fi
}

# Call function with arguments
check_service anihpj     # $1="anihpj"
check_service nginx      # $1="nginx"

# Check return value
if check_service postgresql; then
    echo "DB is healthy"
fi

# FUNCTION VARIABLES
$0  → script name     $1-$9 → positional args
$#  → number of args   $@   → all args (quoted: "$@")
$*  → all args (unquoted)   $?   → last exit code
$$  → current PID      $!   → PID of last background job

C.5 Error Handling — The Robust Script Pattern

Production-Grade Error Handling
#!/bin/bash
# ALWAYS start scripts with these safety flags:
set -euo pipefail
# -e: exit on any error
# -u: treat unset variables as errors
# -o pipefail: pipeline fails if ANY command fails

# Trap for cleanup (runs even on error)
cleanup() {
    echo "Cleaning up temporary files..."
    rm -f /tmp/anihpj-deploy-*.tmp
}
trap cleanup EXIT

# Log function
log() {
    echo "[$(date +'%Y-%m-%d %H:%M:%S')] $*" | tee -a /var/log/anihpj-deploy.log
}

# Main
log "Starting anihpj deployment..."

if ! command -v python3 &>/dev/null; then
    log "ERROR: python3 not found!"
    exit 1
fi

cd /opt/anihpj || { log "ERROR: /opt/anihpj not found"; exit 1; }
git pull origin main
systemctl restart anihpj

log "Deployment complete!"

C.6 String & Array Operations

String Manipulation & Arrays
# STRING OPERATIONS
s="anihpj-production-v2"
echo ${s#*-}      → "production-v2" (remove shortest prefix)
echo ${s##*-}     → "v2" (remove longest prefix)
echo ${s%-*}      → "anihpj-production" (remove shortest suffix)
echo ${s%%-*}     → "anihpj" (remove longest suffix)
echo ${s/anihpj/APP}  → "APP-production-v2"
echo ${s//-/ }    → "anihpj production v2" (global replace)

# SUBSTRING
echo ${s:0:6}     → "anihpj" (offset:length)
echo ${s: -2}     → "v2" (last 2 chars)

# UPPERCASE / LOWERCASE
echo ${s^^}        → "ANIHPJ-PRODUCTION-V2"
echo ${s,,}        → "anihpj-production-v2"

# ARRAYS
apps=(anihpj jobpost celery nginx postgresql)
echo ${apps[0]}     → "anihpj"
echo ${apps[@]}     → all elements
echo ${#apps[@]}    → 5 (array length)
apps+=("redis")    → append element
for app in "${apps[@]}"; do echo $app; done
unset apps[2]      → remove "celery"

C.8 Debugging Scripts — When Things Go Wrong

🐛 Debugging Techniques Every Scripter Must Know
# 1. TRACE MODE — see every command as it executes
bash -x script.sh          # trace entire script
set -x                      # enable tracing mid-script
set +x                      # disable tracing

# 2. SELECTIVE DEBUGGING — trace only the problematic section
#!/bin/bash
set -euo pipefail
# ... normal code ...
set -x   # START tracing
# ... suspected buggy code ...
set +x   # STOP tracing

# 3. VARIABLE INSPECTION
echo "DEBUG: var='$var' (length=${#var})"  # print variable state
# For arrays: declare -p arrayname           # full array dump

# 4. DRY RUN — see what would happen without doing it
# Prefix dangerous commands with echo:
echo rm -rf "$DIR"  # remove echo when confident

# 5. LOGGING TO FILE (production scripts)
exec 2> /var/log/script-errors.log  # redirect stderr
exec > >(tee -a /var/log/script.log) 2>&1  # log everything

# 6. ASSERTIONS — catch assumptions
[[ -d "$BACKUP_DIR" ]] || { echo "FATAL: $BACKUP_DIR missing" >&2; exit 1; }
[[ $(whoami) == "root" ]] || { echo "Must run as root" >&2; exit 1; }

# 7. INTERACTIVE DEBUGGING
# Add 'bash' at any point to drop into an interactive shell:
cd /opt/anihpj || exit 1
bash  # ← script pauses here, you can inspect variables, then type 'exit'
# Continue with rest of script...

C.7 Common Script Templates

Backup Script Template
#!/bin/bash
set -euo pipefail
BACKUP_DIR="/backups/anihpj"
RETENTION_DAYS=7
TIMESTAMP=$(date +%Y%m%d_%H%M%S)
mkdir -p "$BACKUP_DIR"
tar -czf "$BACKUP_DIR/anihpj_${TIMESTAMP}.tar.gz" \
    /opt/anihpj/ /etc/anihpj/ /etc/nginx/sites-enabled/
# Remove backups older than RETENTION_DAYS
find "$BACKUP_DIR" -name "anihpj_*.tar.gz" -mtime +$RETENTION_DAYS -delete
echo "Backup complete: anihpj_${TIMESTAMP}.tar.gz"
Health Check Script Template
#!/bin/bash
# Checks all anihpj services and reports status
check() {
    if systemctl is-active --quiet "$1"; then
        echo "✅ $1 is running"
    else
        echo "❌ $1 is DOWN!"
        return 1
    fi
}
failed=0
check nginx || ((failed++))
check anihpj-gunicorn || ((failed++))
check postgresql || ((failed++))
curl -sf http://localhost:8000/health >/dev/null || {
    echo "❌ Health endpoint failed"; ((failed++)); }
[[ $failed -eq 0 ]] && echo "🎉 All services healthy!" || echo "⚠️ $failed service(s) down!"

📊 Shell Scripting Quick Tips

🛡️
Always: set -euo pipefailPrevents silent failures. -e exits on error, -u catches unset vars, -o pipefail catches pipeline failures.
🧹
Always: trap cleanup EXITEnsures temp files are deleted even if the script crashes. Professional scripts always clean up after themselves.
📝
LFCS TipScripts must be executable (chmod +x) and have a valid shebang (#!/bin/bash). Test them thoroughly before submitting.

D Configuration Files Reference

Annotated reference for every critical configuration file tested on LFCS. Each section shows the file format, key fields explained, and common exam-ready configurations. Master these — the exam will test your ability to configure systems by editing these files directly.

⚠️ Config File Safety Protocol

Before editing ANY configuration file: (1) cp file.conf file.conf.bak — always make a backup. (2) Test syntax before applying: nginx -t, sshd -t, visudo validates automatically. (3) Reload, don't restart when possible: systemctl reload nginx instead of restart — less downtime. (4) Keep a root shell open in a separate terminal when editing network/SSH configs — if you break connectivity, you have a way back in. (5) Check logs after applying: journalctl -xe or tail -f /var/log/syslog to catch errors immediately.

D.1 /etc/fstab — Filesystem Table

Format: DEVICE MOUNTPOINT FSTYPE OPTIONS DUMP PASS
# Device    Mountpoint    Type   Options              Dump  Pass
/dev/sda1   /             ext4   errors=remount-ro    0     1
/dev/sdb1   /data/anihpj  ext4   defaults,noatime     0     2
UUID=xxx    /backup       xfs    defaults             0     0
//nas/anihpj /mnt/nas     cifs   credentials=/etc/.nas,rw,uid=1000  0  0

# OPTIONS EXPLAINED:
# defaults = rw, suid, dev, exec, auto, nouser, async
# noatime  = don't update access time (performance boost!)
# nodiratime = don't update dir access time (even faster)
# noexec   = prevent executing binaries (security for /tmp)
# nosuid   = ignore SUID bits (security)
# ro       = read-only mount
# _netdev  = wait for network before mounting (NFS, CIFS)

# DUMP: 0=no dump, 1=dump this filesystem
# PASS (fsck order): 0=skip, 1=root (first), 2=other (parallel)

D.2 /etc/passwd & /etc/shadow

passwd Format: name:passwd:UID:GID:GECOS:home:shell
root:x:0:0:root:/root:/bin/bash
alice:x:1001:1001:Alice Smith:/home/alice:/bin/bash
anihpj:x:2001:2001:anihpj Service Account:/opt/anihpj:/usr/sbin/nologin

# shadow Format: name:password:lastchange:min:max:warn:inactive:expire:reserved
alice:$6$salt$hash:19500:0:99999:7:::    # SHA-512 hashed
# $6$ = SHA-512, $1$ = MD5, $5$ = SHA-256, $y$ = yescrypt (modern)
# lastchange = days since 1970-01-01
# min=0 (can change anytime), max=99999 (never expires)

D.3 /etc/sudoers — Sudo Configuration

Format: USER HOST=(RUNAS) TAGS: COMMANDS
# ALWAYS use visudo to edit — it validates syntax before saving!

# User alice can run ANYTHING as root
root    ALL=(ALL:ALL) ALL
alice   ALL=(ALL:ALL) ALL

# Group anihpj-admins can run everything without password
%anihpj-admins  ALL=(ALL) NOPASSWD: ALL

# django-dev can ONLY restart anihpj and read its logs
django-dev  ALL=(ALL) NOPASSWD: /usr/bin/systemctl restart anihpj, /usr/bin/journalctl -u anihpj

# anihpj user can run specific commands as postgres user
anihpj  ALL=(postgres) NOPASSWD: /usr/bin/psql anihpj_db, /usr/bin/pg_dump anihpj_db

# Include directory (preferred for app-specific rules)
@includedir /etc/sudoers.d

D.4 /etc/ssh/sshd_config — SSH Server Hardening

Key Hardening Directives
# Port (change from 22 to reduce automated attacks)
Port 2222

# Disable root login (ALWAYS do this!)
PermitRootLogin no

# Key-based auth only (disable passwords!)
PasswordAuthentication no
PubkeyAuthentication yes

# Disable empty passwords
PermitEmptyPasswords no

# Limit users who can SSH
AllowUsers alice bob django-dev
AllowGroups ssh-users anihpj-admins

# Idle timeout (auto-disconnect after 5 min idle)
ClientAliveInterval 300
ClientAliveCountMax 0

# Max authentication attempts
MaxAuthTries 3

# Disable older insecure protocols
Protocol 2
HostKey /etc/ssh/ssh_host_ed25519_key

# Verify: sshd -t  (test config before reloading)

D.5 /etc/nginx/nginx.conf — Nginx Configuration

Key Directives & Contexts
# Global context
user www-data;
worker_processes auto;          # one per CPU core
pid /run/nginx.pid;
error_log /var/log/nginx/error.log warn;

# Events context
http {
    # Performance
    sendfile on;
    tcp_nopush on;
    keepalive_timeout 65;
    gzip on;

    # Security
    server_tokens off;           # hide nginx version

    # Include virtual hosts
    include /etc/nginx/sites-enabled/*;
}

# Server context (virtual host)
server {
    listen 80;
    listen [::]:80;
    server_name anihpj.com;
    root /opt/anihpj/static;

    location / {
        proxy_pass http://127.0.0.1:8000;
        proxy_set_header Host $host;
        proxy_set_header X-Forwarded-For $proxy_add_x_forwarded_for;
    }
    location /static/ {
        alias /opt/anihpj/static/;
        expires 30d;             # cache static files
    }
}

D.6 & D.7 PostgreSQL Configuration

postgresql.conf — Key Performance Settings
# Connection (match your app's needs)
max_connections = 100              # too high = RAM waste
shared_buffers = 512MB             # 25% of system RAM

# Memory for operations
work_mem = 16MB                    # per-operation sort memory
maintenance_work_mem = 256MB       # for VACUUM, CREATE INDEX

# Write-Ahead Log (WAL)
wal_level = replica                # needed for backups
max_wal_size = 2GB

# Query planning
random_page_cost = 1.1             # 1.1 for SSD, 4.0 for HDD
effective_cache_size = 3GB         # 75% of system RAM

# Autovacuum (critical for performance!)
autovacuum = on
autovacuum_max_workers = 3
pg_hba.conf — Client Authentication
# Format: TYPE  DATABASE  USER  ADDRESS  METHOD

# Local socket connections (no password needed)
local   all        postgres                    peer
local   all        all                         md5

# IPv4 local connections
host    anihpj_db  anihpj    127.0.0.1/32      md5
host    all        all       10.0.0.0/8         scram-sha-256

# AUTH METHODS:
# peer    → OS user matches DB user (socket only)
# md5     → password hashed with MD5 (legacy)
# scram-sha-256 → modern secure hashing (preferred)
# trust   → NO password (DEVELOPMENT ONLY!)

D.8 /etc/crontab & Crontab Format

Format: m h dom mon dow user command
# ┌────────── minute (0-59)
# │ ┌──────── hour (0-23)
# │ │ ┌────── day of month (1-31)
# │ │ │ ┌──── month (1-12)
# │ │ │ │ ┌── day of week (0-7, 0=Sun)
# │ │ │ │ │
# * * * * * command

# Examples:
0 2 * * * root /usr/local/bin/anihpj-backup.sh    # 2 AM daily
*/5 * * * * anihpj /opt/anihpj/health-check.sh     # Every 5 min
0 0 1 * * root /usr/local/bin/monthly-report.sh    # 1st of month
@daily root /usr/bin/certbot renew                 # Shortcut: daily
@reboot anihpj /opt/anihpj/startup.sh              # On boot

# Special strings: @yearly, @monthly, @weekly, @daily, @hourly, @reboot

D.9 systemd Service Unit File

anihpj.service — Complete Example
[Unit]
Description=anihpj Django Application (Gunicorn)
After=network.target postgresql.service
Requires=postgresql.service

[Service]
User=anihpj
Group=www-data
WorkingDirectory=/opt/anihpj

D.10 /etc/sysctl.conf — Kernel Parameters

Key Security & Performance Tuning
# Network security
net.ipv4.ip_forward = 0                    # disable routing (unless router)
net.ipv4.tcp_syncookies = 1                # prevent SYN flood attacks
net.ipv4.conf.all.rp_filter = 1            # anti-spoofing
net.ipv4.conf.all.accept_redirects = 0     # ignore ICMP redirects
net.ipv6.conf.all.disable_ipv6 = 1         # disable IPv6 if not needed

# File handles (for high-traffic servers)
fs.file-max = 65535

# Swappiness (0-100, lower = less swap use)
vm.swappiness = 10                         # use RAM first, swap only when needed

# Apply: sysctl -p /etc/sysctl.conf        # load settings
# List all: sysctl -a

D.11 Security Impact Analysis — What Each Config Means for Safety

🔒 Security Hardening Decision Tree for Each Config File
┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│  CONFIG FILE           │  RISK IF MISCONFIGURED                       │
│ ─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────── │
│  /etc/fstab            │  'noexec' missing on /tmp → attackers can   │
│                        │  execute malware from temp directory.        │
│                        │  Fix: add 'noexec,nosuid,nodev' to /tmp      │
│ ─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────── │
│  /etc/passwd           │  Shell set to /bin/bash for service accounts │
│                        │  (like 'anihpj') → attacker who compromises  │
│                        │  the app gets a shell.                       │
│                        │  Fix: set shell to /usr/sbin/nologin         │
│ ─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────── │
│  /etc/shadow           │  Empty password hash → account has NO        │
│                        │  password → anyone can log in!               │
│                        │  Check: grep '::' /etc/shadow (should be 0) │
│ ─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────── │
│  /etc/sudoers          │  'ALL=(ALL) NOPASSWD: ALL' → any compromise  │
│                        │  = instant root. Use least privilege!        │
│  /etc/ssh/sshd_config  │  PermitRootLogin yes + PasswordAuth yes →   │
│                        │  brute-force attacks WILL succeed eventually.│
│                        │  Fix: key-only auth, disable root login.     │
│  /etc/nginx/nginx.conf │  server_tokens on → leaks nginx version to   │
│                        │  attackers → they check CVE databases.       │
│                        │  Fix: server_tokens off;                     │
│  postgresql.conf       │  listen_addresses = '*' + no pg_hba.conf     │
│                        │  restriction → database exposed to internet. │
│                        │  Fix: bind to 127.0.0.1 or private IP only.  │
│  /etc/sysctl.conf      │  net.ipv4.ip_forward = 1 → server becomes    │
│                        │  a router (if not intended, security risk).  │
│                        │  net.ipv4.tcp_syncookies = 0 → vulnerable    │
│                        │  to SYN flood DoS attacks. Set to 1!         │
└──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

📊 Config Files Quick Tips

📝
Always Backupcp file.conf file.conf.bak before editing. A typo in fstab can make your system unbootable.
✅
Always Testnginx -t, sshd -t, visudo validates. Never reload a service before testing config syntax.
🔍
man 5 is your friendman 5 fstab, man 5 sshd_config, man 5 crontab — section 5 is file formats. The exam has man pages!

E.1 Full Dockerfile for anihpj

Production-Ready Multi-Stage Dockerfile
FROM python:3.12-slim

ENV PYTHONDONTWRITEBYTECODE=1 \
    PYTHONUNBUFFERED=1 \
    PIP_NO_CACHE_DIR=1

WORKDIR /app

# Install system dependencies
RUN apt-get update && apt-get install -y --no-install-recommends \
    gcc libpq-dev && \
    rm -rf /var/lib/apt/lists/*

# Install Python dependencies (cached layer)
COPY requirements.txt .
RUN pip install --no-cache-dir -r requirements.txt

# Copy application code
COPY . .
RUN python manage.py collectstatic --noinput

# Create non-root user
RUN addgroup --system --gid 2001 appgroup && \
    adduser --system --uid 2001 --ingroup appgroup appuser && \
    chown -R appuser:appgroup /app
USER appuser

EXPOSE 8000
HEALTHCHECK --interval=30s CMD curl -f http://localhost:8000/health || exit 1
CMD ["gunicorn", "anihpj.wsgi:application", "--bind", "0.0.0.0:8000", "--workers", "3"]

E.2 Gunicorn systemd Service Unit

/etc/systemd/system/anihpj.service
[Unit]
Description=anihpj Gunicorn Application Server
Documentation=https://docs.gunicorn.org/
After=network.target postgresql.service redis.service
Requires=postgresql.service

[Service]
User=anihpj
Group=www-data
WorkingDirectory=/opt/anihpj
Environment="PATH=/opt/anihpj/venv/bin"
EnvironmentFile=/etc/anihpj/env
ExecStart=/opt/anihpj/venv/bin/gunicorn \
    --workers 3 \
    --worker-class sync \
    --bind 127.0.0.1:8000 \
    --timeout 120 \
    --access-logfile /var/log/anihpj/gunicorn-access.log \
    --error-logfile /var/log/anihpj/gunicorn-error.log \
    --log-level info \
    --capture-output \
    anihpj.wsgi:application
ExecReload=/bin/kill -s HUP $MAINPID
ExecStop=/bin/kill -s TERM $MAINPID
PrivateTmp=true
NoNewPrivileges=true
Restart=on-failure
RestartSec=5s
KillMode=mixed
TimeoutStopSec=30

[Install]
WantedBy=multi-user.target

E.3 Celery Worker Service

/etc/systemd/system/anihpj-celery.service
[Unit]
Description=anihpj Celery Worker
After=network.target redis.service
Requires=redis.service

[Service]
User=anihpj
Group=anihpj
WorkingDirectory=/opt/anihpj
Environment="PATH=/opt/anihpj/venv/bin"
EnvironmentFile=/etc/anihpj/env
ExecStart=/opt/anihpj/venv/bin/celery \
    -A anihpj worker \
    --loglevel=info \
    --concurrency=4 \
    --queues=default,high_priority
ExecReload=/bin/kill -s HUP $MAINPID
Restart=on-failure
RestartSec=10s

[Install]
WantedBy=multi-user.target

E.4 Nginx Virtual Host (HTTP + HTTPS)

/etc/nginx/sites-available/anihpj
# HTTP → HTTPS redirect
server {
    listen 80;
    listen [::]:80;
    server_name anihpj.com www.anihpj.com;
    return 301 https://$server_name$request_uri;
}

# HTTPS
server {
    listen 443 ssl http2;
    listen [::]:443 ssl http2;
    server_name anihpj.com www.anihpj.com;

    ssl_certificate /etc/letsencrypt/live/anihpj.com/fullchain.pem;
    ssl_certificate_key /etc/letsencrypt/live/anihpj.com/privkey.pem;

    # Security headers
    add_header X-Frame-Options "SAMEORIGIN" always;
    add_header X-Content-Type-Options "nosniff" always;
    add_header X-XSS-Protection "1; mode=block" always;

    client_max_body_size 10M;

    location /static/ {
        alias /opt/anihpj/staticfiles/;
        expires 30d;
        add_header Cache-Control "public, immutable";
    }

    location /media/ {
        alias /data/anihpj/media/;
    }

    location / {
        proxy_pass http://127.0.0.1:8000;
        proxy_set_header Host $host;
        proxy_set_header X-Real-IP $remote_addr;
        proxy_set_header X-Forwarded-For $proxy_add_x_forwarded_for;
        proxy_set_header X-Forwarded-Proto $scheme;
    }
}

E.6 Logrotate Configuration

/etc/logrotate.d/anihpj
/var/log/anihpj/*.log {
    daily
    missingok
    rotate 30
    compress
    delaycompress
    notifempty
    create 640 anihpj www-data
    sharedscripts
    postrotate
        /usr/bin/kill -USR1 $(cat /run/anihpj/gunicorn.pid) 2>/dev/null || true
    endscript
}

E.7 Crontab for Backups & Health Checks

/etc/cron.d/anihpj
# Database backup — daily at 2 AM
0 2 * * * anihpj /opt/anihpj/scripts/backup-db.sh >> /var/log/anihpj/backup.log 2>&1
# Media files sync to backup server — every 6 hours
0 */6 * * * anihpj rsync -az /data/anihpj/media/ backup-server:/backups/anihpj/media/
# Health check — every 5 minutes
*/5 * * * * root /opt/anihpj/scripts/health-check.sh || /usr/local/bin/alert.sh
# SSL certificate renewal — weekly
@weekly root certbot renew --quiet --post-hook "systemctl reload nginx"

E.10 Full Deployment Automation Script

deploy.sh — One-Command Production Deployment
#!/bin/bash
set -euo pipefail
APP_DIR="/opt/anihpj"
TIMESTAMP=$(date +%Y%m%d_%H%M%S)

log() { echo "[$(date '+%H:%M:%S')] $*"; }

log "🚀 Starting anihpj deployment..."

# Backup database
log "📦 Backing up database..."
sudo -u postgres pg_dump anihpj_db > "/backups/anihpj_db_${TIMESTAMP}.sql"

# Pull latest code
cd "$APP_DIR"
log "📥 Pulling latest code..."
git pull origin main

# Install dependencies
log "📦 Installing dependencies..."
source venv/bin/activate
pip install -r requirements.txt

# Run migrations
log "🗄️ Running migrations..."
python manage.py migrate --noinput

# Collect static files
log "📁 Collecting static files..."
python manage.py collectstatic --noinput

# Restart services
log "🔄 Restarting services..."
sudo systemctl restart anihpj
sudo systemctl restart anihpj-celery

# Health check
log "🏥 Running health check..."
sleep 3
if curl -sf http://localhost:8000/health > /dev/null; then
    log "✅ Deployment successful!"
else
    log "❌ Health check FAILED! Rolling back..."
    git checkout HEAD~1
    sudo systemctl restart anihpj
    log "⚠️ Rolled back to previous version."
    exit 1
fi

E.11 Production Monitoring Setup

📊 Essential Monitoring for anihpj Production
# 1. SYSTEM MONITORING — CPU, Memory, Disk
sudo apt install prometheus-node-exporter
# Exposes metrics at http://localhost:9100/metrics
systemctl enable --now prometheus-node-exporter

# 2. APPLICATION MONITORING — Gunicorn logs
# Monitor via: systemctl status anihpj, journalctl -u anihpj -f
# Add to gunicorn: --statsd-host=localhost:8125 for metrics

# 3. DATABASE MONITORING — Slow queries
sudo -u postgres psql -c "ALTER SYSTEM SET log_min_duration_statement = 1000;"
sudo -u postgres psql -c "SELECT pg_reload_conf();"
# Check: tail -f /var/log/postgresql/postgresql-*.log

# 4. DISK SPACE ALERT — Simple cron-based monitor
cat > /usr/local/bin/check-disk.sh << 'SCRIPT'
#!/bin/bash
THRESHOLD=90
USAGE=$(df -h /data/anihpj | awk 'NR==2 {print $5}' | tr -d '%')
if [ "$USAGE" -gt "$THRESHOLD" ]; then
    echo "DISK ALERT: anihpj at ${USAGE}%!" | mail -s "DISK ALERT" admin@anihpj.com
fi
SCRIPT
chmod +x /usr/local/bin/check-disk.sh
echo "*/30 * * * * root /usr/local/bin/check-disk.sh" > /etc/cron.d/disk-alert

# 5. SERVICE UPTIME CHECK — Every 5 minutes
cat > /usr/local/bin/check-services.sh << 'SCRIPT'
#!/bin/bash
for svc in anihpj anihpj-celery nginx postgresql redis; do
    systemctl is-active --quiet "$svc" || \
        echo "$svc DOWN at $(date)" | mail -s "SERVICE ALERT" admin@anihpj.com
done
SCRIPT
chmod +x /usr/local/bin/check-services.sh
echo "*/5 * * * * root /usr/local/bin/check-services.sh" > /etc/cron.d/service-alert

E.12 Production Security Hardening Checklist

🔒 Pre-Go-Live Security Audit for anihpj
[ ] 1. SYSTEM HARDENING
   [ ] SSH: key-only auth, no root login, non-standard port
   [ ] UFW: only ports 22, 80, 443 open, default deny incoming
   [ ] fail2ban: enabled for SSH with 3-attempt ban
   [ ] Automatic security updates: dpkg-reconfigure unattended-upgrades
   [ ] Kernel hardening: /etc/sysctl.conf with secure defaults

[ ] 2. APPLICATION SECURITY
   [ ] DEBUG=False in production (.env file)
   [ ] SECRET_KEY is >50 chars, random, NEVER in git
   [ ] ALLOWED_HOSTS restricted to actual domain names
   [ ] Database password is strong, not default
   [ ] CSRF_COOKIE_SECURE=True, SESSION_COOKIE_SECURE=True
   [ ] SECURE_HSTS_SECONDS=31536000 (1 year)
   [ ] Admin panel: internal IPs only (nginx allow/deny)

[ ] 3. FILE PERMISSIONS
   [ ] /opt/anihpj/ owned by root:root, 755/644
   [ ] /data/anihpj/media/ owned by www-data (writeable)
   [ ] /etc/anihpj/env chmod 600 (secrets!)
   [ ] No .git directory in document root

[ ] 4. DATABASE SECURITY
   [ ] PostgreSQL: 127.0.0.1 only (not 0.0.0.0)
   [ ] pg_hba.conf: scram-sha-256 (not md5/trust)
   [ ] Regular pg_dump backups with retention
   [ ] Backup files stored off-server (rsync)

[ ] 5. SSL/TLS
   [ ] Valid SSL cert (certbot + Let's Encrypt)
   [ ] Auto-renewal: @weekly certbot renew
   [ ] HSTS header enabled, HTTP→HTTPS redirect

[ ] 6. LOGGING & MONITORING
   [ ] Logrotate for all log files
   [ ] Centralized logs (rsyslog to log server)
   [ ] Disk alerts at 80%, service checks every 5min
   [ ] External uptime monitoring (UptimeRobot)

[ ] 7. BACKUP & RECOVERY
   [ ] DB backup tested (restore to test server!)
   [ ] Application code in git (off-server)
   [ ] Media files synced to backup server
   [ ] Documented restore procedure
   [ ] Test restore within last 30 days

F LFCS Exam Preparation Guide

Your complete roadmap to LFCS certification success. This guide covers an 8-week study plan, lab environment setup, recommended resources, and exam-day strategy — everything you need to walk into the exam confident and prepared.

F.1 8-Week Study Plan

WeekFocus AreaContentPractice Tasks
1Linux BasicsPart 1 (Ch 1-4)Navigate filesystem, create/edit files, understand FHS, practice basic commands for 2 hours daily
2Essential CommandsParts 2-3 (Ch 5-11)Master grep/sed/awk pipelines, write 5 shell scripts, practice text processing on real log files
3Users & PermissionsPart 4 (Ch 12-14)Create/modify/delete users & groups, configure sudo, set ACLs, practice permission scenarios
4Processes & ServicesPart 5 (Ch 15-17)Create systemd units, manage processes with kill/nice, analyze logs with journalctl
5NetworkingPart 6 (Ch 18-21)Configure static IPs, set up firewalls (UFW/iptables), troubleshoot DNS, practice with ip/ss commands
6StoragePart 7 (Ch 22-25)Partition disks, create LVM volumes, format/mount filesystems, configure autofs and swap
7ServicesPart 8 (Ch 26-30)Configure SSH, Nginx, PostgreSQL, set up email/time services, deploy anihpj on a fresh VM
8Security + ReviewParts 9-12 (Ch 31-45)Configure SELinux/AppArmor, harden systems, practice full mock exams under time pressure

F.2 Practice Lab Environment Setup

🖥️ Your LFCS Lab Setup
# RECOMMENDED SETUP:
# 1. Install VirtualBox (free) on your main computer
# 2. Create TWO VMs:
#    - Ubuntu 22.04 LTS Server (primary practice environment)
#    - Rocky Linux 9 (for Red Hat family differences)
# 3. Allocate per VM: 2 CPUs, 4GB RAM, 20GB disk
# 4. Create a snapshot after initial install (easy reset!)
# 5. Use shared folders to transfer files between host and VMs
# 6. Practice in the terminal ONLY — no GUI, just like the real exam

# ESSENTIAL: Take a snapshot before each practice session
# VirutalBox: Machine → Take Snapshot → name it "Week1-Baseline"
# If you break something: Machine → Restore Snapshot → back to clean state

# SIMULATE EXAM CONDITIONS:
# - Disable copy/paste between host and VM
# - Turn off mouse integration (terminal-only navigation)
# - Set a 2-hour timer for mock exams
