Free PDF book by William Shotts. The definitive beginner's guide. Read chapters 1-10 for core skills, reference the rest.

F.4 Day Before The Exam

🎯 Day-Before Checklist: (1) Review your weakest LFCS domains — use the chapter practice questions in this guide. (2) Practice WITHOUT autocomplete — the exam terminal has basic bash completion but no fancy plugins. Build muscle memory for full command paths. (3) Review man pages for: useradd, crontab, fstab, sshd_config, systemd.unit. (4) Get a good night's sleep — cramming doesn't work for hands-on exams. (5) Verify your exam environment: stable internet, webcam working, quiet room, government ID ready.

F.5 Exam Day Strategy

🏆 The Winning Strategy for LFCS Exam Day

(1) First 5 minutes: Skim ALL questions. Mark them mentally: easy (do first), medium, hard (save for last). (2) Work in waves: Do all easy questions (20 min) → all medium (60 min) → all hard (30 min) → review (10 min). (3) Verify EVERY task: After creating a user: id username. After editing fstab: mount -a. After configuring a service: systemctl start then status. (4) Check persistence: If the task says "permanent" or "persistent," did you write to the config file? Did you enable the service? (5) Don't panic-reboot: Rebooting takes time. Only reboot if the task explicitly requires it or you've completely locked yourself out of SSH. (6) Man pages are your friend: The exam provides man pages. Use / to search, n/N to navigate. (7) Leave no blank: Even partial configurations earn partial credit. Something is better than nothing.

⚠️ Common Exam-Day Mistakes: ❌ Running commands as root when the task asks for a specific user. ❌ Forgetting to enable services with systemctl enable. ❌ Editing config files but not restarting/reloading the service. ❌ Not testing SSH config changes from a second terminal before closing the current session. ❌ Spending 20 minutes on one hard question while 10 easy ones go unanswered.
📊 LFCS Exam Scoring — What You Need to Know

The LFCS exam is performance-based — you perform real tasks on live Linux systems, not multiple-choice. Scoring is automated: each task has specific criteria (e.g., "user alice exists with UID 1500", "nginx is running and enabled"). You earn points for each criterion met. Partial credit is awarded — even if you don't complete a task perfectly, do as much as you can. The passing score is 66%. The exam has approximately 20-25 tasks across all domains. You have 2 hours. That's about 5 minutes per task — use your time wisely. The most important skill: verify your work after every single task.

❌ Time-Wasters to Avoid

Reading man pages cover-to-cover instead of searching with /. Writing elaborate bash scripts when a one-liner pipe would work. Rebooting to "fix" problems (wastes 2-3 minutes per reboot). Trying to memorize every flag — use --help for quick reference. Starting with the hardest question first.

✅ Smart Time Management

Use man -k keyword to find the right man page fast. command --help for syntax reminders. Do easy questions first (builds confidence + guarantees points). Flag hard questions and return later. Keep a terminal open with watch df -h or watch systemctl status for persistent monitoring tasks.

H Docker & Container Fundamentals

Containers are the natural evolution of Linux system administration. Understanding Docker builds on every LFCS skill: processes, filesystems, networking, and resource management. This appendix bridges the gap between traditional Linux admin and the containerized world.

🐳 Why Docker Matters for LFCS — Even Though It's Not Directly Tested

While LFCS primarily tests Podman (see Chapter 40), understanding Docker is essential because: (1) Docker images and Podman images are OCI-compatible — they work interchangeably. (2) Most tutorials and documentation use Docker commands — knowing the mapping to Podman helps you learn faster. (3) Docker's architecture (daemon, registry, images, containers) is the conceptual foundation for all container platforms. (4) The skills transfer directly: docker build = podman build, docker run = podman run. (5) In production, you'll encounter Docker — even if LFCS tests Podman, the real world uses both. Pro tip: alias docker=podman makes your Docker knowledge work with Podman instantly.

H.1 What is Docker? — Containers Explained

Docker is a platform to package, distribute, and run applications in isolated environments called containers. A container bundles code, runtime, tools, libraries, and settings into one portable unit. Unlike VMs, containers share the host OS kernel — starting in milliseconds (vs minutes), using MB of disk (vs GB). Docker uses Linux namespaces for isolation and cgroups for resource limits — the same primitives you learned in Parts 5 and 7.

🔧 Docker Troubleshooting Quick Reference
  • 🔴 Container won't start: docker logs container-name — check for errors. docker inspect container-name — verify mounts and env vars.
  • 🔴 Can't connect to container: docker port container-name — verify port mapping. ss -tlnp | grep PORT — is port already used?
  • 🔴 Image build fails: Check Dockerfile syntax. docker build --no-cache -t name . — force clean rebuild. Check network: can you reach apt repositories?
  • ✅ Clean up everything: docker system prune -a --volumes — removes ALL unused containers, images, networks, volumes. Frees GB of space.

H.5 Docker Volumes — Persistent Data

Containers are ephemeral — data is lost when the container is removed. Volumes (Docker-managed) and bind mounts (host directories) provide persistence. Volumes survive container deletion and can be shared between containers. Critical for databases!

# Create a volume and use it
docker volume create anihpj-data
docker run -v anihpj-data:/var/lib/postgresql/data postgres:15
# Data survives: docker rm postgres-container → volume still exists!

# Bind mount (host directory)
docker run -v /host/path:/container/path nginx

# Manage volumes
docker volume ls        # list all volumes
docker volume inspect   # see details (mountpoint on host)
docker volume prune     # remove unused volumes

H.6 Docker Compose — Multi-Container anihpj Stack

📋 docker-compose.yml — Complete anihpj Development Stack
version: '3.8'
services:
  db:
    image: postgres:15
    environment:
      POSTGRES_DB: anihpj_db
      POSTGRES_USER: anihpj_user
      POSTGRES_PASSWORD: securepass123
    volumes:
      - postgres_data:/var/lib/postgresql/data

  web:
    build: .
    command: gunicorn anihpj.wsgi:application --bind 0.0.0.0:8000
    volumes:
      - .:/app
      - static_volume:/app/staticfiles
    ports:
      - "8000:8000"
    depends_on:
      - db
    environment:
      - DATABASE_URL=postgresql://anihpj_user:securepass123@db/anihpj_db

  nginx:
    image: nginx:alpine
    volumes:
      - ./nginx.conf:/etc/nginx/conf.d/default.conf
      - static_volume:/static
    ports:
      - "80:80"
    depends_on:
      - web

volumes:
  postgres_data:
  static_volume:

# Commands:
# docker compose up -d      → start everything
# docker compose down       → stop and remove
# docker compose logs -f    → follow all logs

📦 OCI Image Format — What's Inside a Container Image
┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│  OCI IMAGE = tar.gz archive with specific internal structure          │
│                                                                      │
│  anihpj-v2.tar.gz (what 'docker save' or 'podman save' produces)     │
│  ├── blobs/                                                           │
│  │   └── sha256/                                                      │
│  │       ├── a1b2c3d4...  ← Layer 1: Ubuntu base (compressed tar)    │
│  │       ├── e5f6g7h8...  ← Layer 2: apt packages                    │
│  │       ├── i9j0k1l2...  ← Layer 3: pip packages                    │
│  │       └── m3n4o5p6...  ← Layer 4: application code                │
│  ├── index.json           ← Entry point: which manifest to use       │
│  ├── manifest.json        ← Lists all layers + config                │
│  └── oci-layout           ← Magic file: {"imageLayoutVersion":"1.0.0"}│
│                                                                      │
│  KEY INSIGHT: A "Docker image" and a "Podman image" are IDENTICAL    │
│  at the byte level. Both follow the OCI spec. This means:             │
│  • docker pull nginx → docker save → podman load → podman run nginx  │
│  • podman build -t app . → podman push → docker pull → docker run    │
│  • Complete interoperability between the two ecosystems              │
└──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

I Kubernetes Deployment of anihpj/jobpost

Kubernetes (K8s) is the natural next step after mastering containers. Where Docker runs a single container, K8s orchestrates fleets of containers across multiple servers. This appendix shows you how to deploy the full anihpj stack on Kubernetes — connecting the LFCS skills you've learned to the cloud-native world.

I.1 What is Kubernetes? — Harbor Master Analogy

🚢 The Shipping Port Analogy
┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│  🐳 DOCKER = A SINGLE SHIP (container)                               │
│  ☸️ KUBERNETES = THE HARBOR MASTER who manages the ENTIRE FLEET       │
│                                                                      │
│  Without K8s (Docker alone):                                         │
│  • You manually decide which server runs which container             │
│  • If a container crashes, YOU restart it manually                   │
│  • If traffic spikes, YOU spin up more containers by hand            │
│  • Rolling update? Stop old, start new, pray no downtime             │
│                                                                      │
│  With K8s:                                                            │
│  • You declare: "I want 3 copies of anihpj running at all times"     │
│  • K8s places them on the best nodes, monitors health, restarts dead │
│  • Traffic spike? K8s auto-scales (HPA)                              │
│  • New version? K8s does a rolling update with zero downtime         │
│  • Node fails? K8s migrates pods to healthy nodes automatically      │
│                                                                      │
│  🎯 K8s = Linux process supervision (systemd) at DATACENTER SCALE    │
└──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

I.4 Key K8s Resources for anihpj

📦
Deployment

Manages identical pods. "I want 3 replicas of anihpj:v2." Handles rolling updates with zero downtime.

🔗
Service

Stable IP/DNS for pods. Pods come and go, but the Service IP stays the same. ClusterIP (internal), NodePort, LoadBalancer.

⚙️
ConfigMap

Non-sensitive config (DB host, debug flags). Separate config from code. Update without rebuilding image.

🔐
Secret

Sensitive data (passwords, API keys). Base64-encoded (not encrypted — use etcd encryption for production!).

💾
PersistentVolumeClaim

Request storage. "I need 20GB for PostgreSQL." Survives pod restarts. Like a disk request ticket.

🌐
Ingress

HTTP routing. "anihpj.com → anihpj-svc:8000." SSL termination, path-based routing, name-based virtual hosting.

I.5 Complete anihpj Deployment YAML

📋 anihpj-deployment.yaml — Production-Ready
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: anihpj-web
  labels:
    app: anihpj
spec:
  replicas: 3                    # 3 copies always running
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: anihpj
  template:                       # Pod template
    metadata:
      labels:
        app: anihpj
    spec:
      containers:
      - name: anihpj-app
        image: anihpj/anihpj:v2  # Built from Dockerfile
        ports:
        - containerPort: 8000
        envFrom:
        - configMapRef:
            name: anihpj-config
        - secretRef:
            name: anihpj-secrets
        resources:
          requests:
            memory: "256Mi"
            cpu: "250m"
          limits:
            memory: "512Mi"
            cpu: "500m"
        livenessProbe:
          httpGet:
            path: /health/
            port: 8000
          initialDelaySeconds: 30
---
apiVersion: v1
kind: Service
metadata:
  name: anihpj-svc
spec:
  selector:
    app: anihpj
  ports:
  - port: 8000
    targetPort: 8000
  type: ClusterIP

I.7 Production anihpj K8s Architecture

☸️ Full anihpj Production Stack on Kubernetes
┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│  INTERNET → INGRESS (Nginx) :443                                      │
│      │ anihpj.com → anihpj-svc                                       │
│      ▼                                                                │
│  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐       │
│  │  SERVICE: anihpj-svc (ClusterIP) — Load balances 3 pods  │       │
│  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘       │
│      ├────────────┬────────────┐                                      │
│      ▼            ▼            ▼                                      │
│  ┌────────┐ ┌────────┐ ┌────────┐  Deployment: replicas=3           │
│  │ POD 1  │ │ POD 2  │ │ POD 3  │  anihpj:v2, resources: 256Mi-512Mi│
│  │anihpj  │ │anihpj  │ │anihpj  │  livenessProbe: /health/           │
│  │:8000   │ │:8000   │ │:8000   │                                     │
│  └───┬────┘ └───┬────┘ └───┬────┘                                     │
│      └──────────┼──────────┘                                          │
│                 ▼                                                     │
│  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐       │
│  │  SERVICE: postgres-svc (ClusterIP:5432)                   │       │
│  │  STATEFULSET: postgres (1 replica + PersistentVolume)     │       │
│  │  ConfigMap + Secret → env vars injected into pods         │       │
│  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘       │
│  NAMESPACE: production | All isolated from dev/staging              │
└──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
🔧 Worker Node Components — What Runs on Each Node: (1) kubelet: The primary node agent — registers the node with the API server, receives pod specifications, and ensures containers are running. It reports node and pod status back to the control plane. Think of it as a local "systemd for containers." (2) kube-proxy: Manages network rules (iptables/IPVS) so that pods can reach each other and external traffic can reach services. It implements the Service abstraction. (3) Container Runtime: The software that actually runs containers — usually containerd or CRI-O (not Docker directly anymore). Kubelet talks to the runtime via the CRI (Container Runtime Interface).
🎉 anihpj WITHOUT vs WITH Kubernetes — The Real Difference
  • ❌ Before K8s: Deploy = ssh to server, git pull, pip install, migrate, systemctl restart. Server crashes at 3 AM? YOU wake up and fix it manually. Traffic spikes? SSH in and start more processes by hand.
  • ✅ With K8s: kubectl apply -f deployment.yaml. Pod dies → auto-restarted. Node fails → pods migrate. Traffic spikes → HPA auto-scales. K8s automates the operations work you mastered in LFCS.

I.8 Helm — The Kubernetes Package Manager

Helm is to Kubernetes what apt is to Ubuntu — a package manager that installs, updates, and manages applications. Instead of writing raw YAML for every component, Helm uses Charts (pre-packaged K8s applications with configurable values).

📦 Helm Quick Reference — Deploying anihpj with Helm
# Install Helm
curl https://raw.githubusercontent.com/helm/helm/main/scripts/get-helm-3 | bash

# Add a chart repository (like apt repository)
helm repo add bitnami https://charts.bitnami.com/bitnami
helm repo update

# Deploy PostgreSQL with one command
helm install anihpj-db bitnami/postgresql \
  --set auth.database=anihpj_db \
  --set auth.username=anihpj_user

# List installed releases
helm list

# Upgrade a release (change values)
helm upgrade anihpj-db bitnami/postgresql --set primary.persistence.size=50Gi

# Rollback to previous version
helm rollback anihpj-db 1

# Uninstall
helm uninstall anihpj-db

# Create your own chart
helm create anihpj-chart
# Edit values.yaml, templates/deployment.yaml, templates/service.yaml
helm install anihpj-prod ./anihpj-chart --set image.tag=v3

J LFCS Practice Exam — 50 Questions

50 real exam-style questions spanning all LFCS domains. Each question is designed to test exactly what the real exam tests — practical, hands-on Linux administration tasks. Time yourself: 120 minutes for all 50 questions.

🎯 How to Use This Practice Exam for Maximum Benefit

(1) Simulate real conditions: Disable copy/paste, use terminal only, set a 2-hour timer. (2) Grade yourself: After each question, verify your answer with the solution. Give yourself 2 points if you got the exact commands, 1 point if you had the right idea but wrong syntax, 0 if you couldn't solve it. (3) Track weak areas: If you score below 7/10 in any section (J.1-J.5), review that Part of the guide and re-do the chapter practice questions. (4) Retake after studying: Come back 1 week later and try again — your score should improve. (5) Focus on speed: The real exam gives about 5 minutes per task. These questions should take 2-3 minutes each — practice until you can solve them quickly. (6) Read the error messages: The most important exam skill is reading what the terminal tells you. Errors are hints!

J.1 Essential Commands (10 Questions)

Q1

mkdir -p /var/www/anihpj; chmod 755 /var/www/anihpj; chown anihpj:www-data /var/www/anihpj; ls -ld /var/www/anihpj
📖 Explanation

ACLs & LDAP: The LFCS exam emphasizes practical, hands-on skills — exactly what this question tests. Practice this until you can complete it without consulting documentation. 🔐 Linux Permissions
  OWNER   GROUP   OTHER

  4 2 1   4 0 1   4 0 0  = 754

Q2
Find all .log files in /var modified in the last 7 days and display their sizes in human-readable format.
Click for answer
find /var -name "*.log" -mtime -7 -exec ls -lh {} \;
📖 Explanation

ACLs & LDAP: This is a core skill tested on the LFCS. Understanding not just the command but WHY it works this way helps you adapt when exam tasks combine multiple concepts. find searches the actual filesystem in real time. Use 2>/dev/null to suppress "Permission denied" noise. Combine with -exec to act on results. LFCS Exam Tip: Read every exam task TWICE before touching the keyboard. Missing a single detail like "UID 1500" or "GID 2000" means zero points — even if your commands are otherwise perfect.

Q3

ACLs & LDAP: This is a core skill tested on the LFCS. Understanding not just the command but WHY it works this way helps you adapt when exam tasks combine multiple concepts. awk is a full programming language optimized for columnar data. -F: sets the delimiter; numbers like $1, $2 reference fields by position. Clone a git repository from https://github.com/anihpj/anihpj.git to /opt/anihpj, create a new branch "hotfix", make a commit, and push it.
Click for answer
git clone https://github.com/anihpj/anihpj.git /opt/anihpj; cd /opt/anihpj; git checkout -b hotfix; echo "fix" >> README.md; git add .; git commit -m "hotfix: critical patch"; git push origin hotfix

💡 Git Workflow: clone (download) → checkout -b (create branch) → modify → add (stage) → commit (save) → push (upload). This is the exact LFCS workflow for Git tasks.

📖 Explanation

ACLs & LDAP: This is a core skill tested on the LFCS. Understanding not just the command but WHY it works this way helps you adapt when exam tasks combine multiple concepts. git tracks content changes, not just filenames. git log shows history; git diff shows unstaged changes; git status shows current state. LFCS Exam Tip: Read every exam task TWICE before touching the keyboard. Missing a single detail like "UID 1500" or "GID 2000" means zero points — even if your commands are otherwise perfect.

After completing all 50 questions, calculate your score to identify weak areas.

J.1 Essential CommandsQ1-Q1020___/20≥14

📊 How to Score: Give yourself 2 points for exact correct commands. 1 point for right idea but minor syntax error. 0 points for incorrect or no answer. LFCS passing is 66% — aim for ≥70/100 here. Retake weekly to track improvement.
⚠️ Top 7 LFCS Mistakes from Practice Data

(1) Forgetting -r with cp/rm for directories. (2) useradd without -m (no home dir). (3) Editing fstab without running mount -a. (4) Creating systemd units without systemctl daemon-reload. (5) Configuring SSH without sshd -t first. (6) Using iptables on modern distros (use nft/ufw). (7) Forgetting systemctl enable — start alone doesn't survive reboot.
